Okay, I’ve got a video coming out, but here are my early thoughts on Jev. 

The first thing to know is that it’s not a large language model. It doesn’t produce text, it outputs decisions.

The decision types are (roughly) choice, score, and yes/no. 

It is roughly at the intelligence level of Sol or Opus for making these decisions. 

The question is: why are people so excited about this? A couple of reasons: 

The most important one is that so much of what we actually do in AI is making these types of decisions. Especially for enterprise-type work and AI harness-type work where we have to do things like classification and labeling constantly. This is things like deciding if this particular email is spam or if this person with an account on your platform is about to cancel. 

Within your AI harness, it's things like deciding which model you should use for a particular task. In cybersecurity, there are millions of use cases for this, where we're trying to categorize types and classifications of different inputs and the chances of something being dangerous, etc. 

When you step back and look down at most AI work, there is just a massive amount thatreduces down to making these decisions at scale. 

And that's the second reason people are so excited. 

This system is almost instantaneous and almost free. They're charging $42 per billion input tokens, and they are not charging for output tokens at all. That means you can make thousands or tens of thousands of requests in a lot of cases, like processing entire databases of customer interactions or processing tens of thousands of emails or whatever, and you might get a bill for like $0.12. Or maybe far less. 

And the round-trip time for making requests is in the hundreds of milliseconds. With an early sweet spot of around 200 ms. 

And when you combine these two, it means this system, or a system like it, is likely to be a new cornerstone for all AI work being done anywhere. 

The first step is to zoom out and take a look at all the different work that you're doing in whatever domain or whatever application, etc. Decompose how much of that work actually consists of making thousands or millions of these types of judgments and classifications. 

This includes your hook system inside of an AI harness, where you can do things on user prompt submit, before and after tool use, model routing, as I mentioned earlier: the classification and labeling of all your session data to find things you might need to improve or fix, etc. 

And then the next step is to essentially retool all that work so that it is going through one or more of these decision phases before handing off to an LLM. And it doesn't have to be one or the other. I have some implementations that are LLM-first, passed off to Jev for decisions, and then maybe back to an LLM, and some are doing kind of vice versa. LLMs and this type of system work really well together for tons of use cases. 

One of the things I've already made massive progress on, and that has me most excited, is fully updating my eval system to include this as a layer. 

Evals have two branches, roughly:

1. Asserts that are deterministic and very fast

2. Judgment, which breaks down into rubrics and tournaments

Rubrics are essentially center mass for this Jev system. They are basically a set of options that AI chooses for you based on the context given and how smart the system is. Like picking how happy or upset a customer is on a five-level scale. 

And then there are tournaments which have the system pick between two options, given the context and the intelligence of the model. 

But until now, these types of operations have all been done with LLMs, which are very slow and very expensive. 

What I, and many others I'm sure, are building is a way to have multi-staged evals where a vast majority of the work can be done by this system, basically instantly and for free, while shoveling out to an LLM if it is specifically needed.

Very realistic overview. Hard to discern hype from reality about Jev so here are some bitter facts:

- Jev can’t write text: it’s not an autoregressive model, so forget about anything related to coding or writing
- Jev can’t see (yet): text only, althought there is nothing fundamentally preventing it from being multimodal. I’m sure they will add support for images?
- Jev can ONLY choose a set of predefined actions: the good thing about computer and browser use is that by very nature it’s a STATE -> ACTION model. The problem with long running state action models is that the reasoning and state understanding becomes extremely important.
- Jev is extremely cheap and fast

It opened up my eyes into what’s possible. We are often stuck in optimizing problems inside the box. This is one the real “think outside the box” solutions to problems we have been trying to solve.

I am extremely hyped about the future of computer and browser use. Latency matters, and people are clearly hyped about it.

We can surely combine some sort of global state understanding (LLM) with super fast actor model (System One). Obviously it’s possible - FSD and robotics companies have solved this already.

How hard can it be to apply the same thing to browser use?

t:
别再只看全网对 Jev 疯狂刷屏、自己却连第一行代码都不知道怎么接了。

今天把大家问得最多的实操问题彻底讲透：
怎么把这个不写废话的新模型，真正无缝插进你正在用的 Codex、Hermes 或者 Claude Code 里？
把这套“大小脑协同架构”接通，
你的 Agent 选错工具和技能的概率直接砍掉一半以上，单次判断只要 150 毫秒，输出 Token 彻底免单！

先搞清楚一个底层的认知误区：
Jev 从底座上就不是用来写文案、写长篇代码的，它连一个字都不会打；
它只输出三种强类型：Choice（单选）、Score（打分）、Noul（布尔判别）。
如果直接拿它当聊天机器人，你连第一步都跑不通；
但如果你把它当成主模型身边的“前置小脑（System 1 快思考）”，它就是今年最凶猛的物理外设：

1️⃣ 在 Codex / Claude Code 里的极简接入姿势：
不需要自己手搓网络请求，官方和社区早就把管道焊好了：
• 姿势 A（官方 Skill 路线）：在终端直接敲一行命令：
`npx skills add typesafe-ai/skills --skill typesafe-ai`，在配置里填好 `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`，在日常开发中直接让它负责任务路由与危险命令拦截；
• 姿势 B（标准 MCP 路线）：安装社区开源的 `jev-mcp`（例如 `npx -y github:jkudish/jev-mcp`），把它作为本地 MCP Server 挂载，大模型在需要多分支决策时，会自动调起 Jev 毫秒级返回结论；
2️⃣ 在开源之光 Hermes Agent 里的神仙用法（实测错误率砍半）：
Hermes 最大的特点是拥有 180 多个离散 Skills，
以前的主流做法是把这 180 多个技能的说明全喂给大模型，模型天天在看哪个技能该用，不仅又慢又烧 Token，还经常瞎选；
现在社区直接上了 `hermes-jev-skills` 插件：
在主模型被唤醒前（Pre-LLM Hook），Jev 花 150ms 扫一遍用户需求，直接把 180 个技能瞬间收敛到最精准的 1 到 2 个！
官方 Cookbook 实测数据极其残暴：
选错技能的翻车率直接从 16.8% 断崖式跌到 7.3%，无中生有滥载技能的比例从 9.8% 压到 4.0%！
3️⃣ 三个立刻能帮你省下大钱的绝杀场景：
• 绝杀一：上下文无损脱水（Context Compaction）：
很多 Agent 处理长任务喜欢让大模型做摘要，结果把关键代码细节全摘要没了；用 Jev 直接给历史上的每条 Tool 结果打分，过期的、无意义的调用直接物理级剔除，真正有用的保留字面原文，零幻觉衰减；
• 绝杀二：高危操作硬核安检门（Guardrails）：
跑 Shell、删文件、推代码之前，先过一层 Jev 的布尔判别，150 毫秒识别命令危险等级，高危操作强制弹窗等人批，成本只是大模型调用的零头；
• 绝杀三：智能模型路由（Router）：
根据代码任务复杂度自动分流：简单的改动分给本地小模型，真正需要深思的交给 Claude 3.5 / GPT-4o。

这就是 2026 年现代 Agent 最健康的工业形态：
别再让年薪百万的“博士后大脑”，天天去干传达室门卫的分类杂活！
让 Jev 负责在毫秒内看清意图、收敛选项、卡住风险，
让主模型退到深水区，专注做最硬核的逻辑攻坚。

架构一换，天地自宽。
今晚就把这行命令跑起来，你的 Agent 才能算真正长出了神经反射。

q.t:
发明了 ChatGPT 的 OpenAI 核心科学家，潜伏整整两年后，反手给整个聊天大模型行业敲响了丧钟。

Diogo Almeida（ChatGPT 与 RLHF 共同发明人之一）刚发的这条推文，开篇第一句就直击灵魂：
“在共同发明了 ChatGPT 之后，我一直在反问自己：为什么超人类水平的对话模型，至今没能带来真正的 AGI？”

带着 4000 万美元新融资杀回来的他，今天正式公开了闭关两年的全新成果——TypeSafe AI 与新一代前沿基座模型 Jev。
这绝不是又一个跑分微涨的普通大模型，
它的背后，藏着整个 AI 工业界一次极其反直觉的断代革命：
从“装模作样陪人聊天的慢速生成” $\to$ 转向“极速、零废话的确定性结构化决策”！

看懂他掀开的四层底层逻辑，你会发现他把现存的大模型缺陷肢解得极其彻底：

1️⃣ 第一层：最震撼的背叛——这个 AI 甚至“连一个字都不会写”：
在所有人的惯性思维里，大模型必须会出口成章、会写长篇大论；
但 Jev 走向了最极端的反面——它彻底阉割了自然语言生成能力，绝不吐半句废话！
因为在商业现实里，银行风控、诈骗识别、医疗初筛、路由分发，
根本不需要 AI 给你写一首抒情诗，业务系统只需要它在毫秒级内给出精准的概率分布与结构化判定；
2️⃣ 第二层：算术级暴击，输出 Token 彻底免费：
传统大模型之所以昂贵且奇慢无比，是因为它们被锁死在“逐字解码（Autoregressive Decoding）”的物理地狱里——每吐一个字就要把几十 GB 参数从显存里搬一次；
而 Jev 放弃了文字生成后，直接改用单次前向传播（Forward Pass）并行处理所有结构化问题！
结果是毁灭级的：推理速度暴涨 20 到 200 倍，API 成本断崖式暴跌 40 到 450 倍，
输出 Token 在物理层面上直接等同于免费！
3️⃣ 最狠的第三层：消灭幻觉的秘密武器——RLCD 概率校准：
大模型最让人不敢用的死穴，是它在不知道答案时依然自信地胡说八道；
Diogo 亲手放弃了自己参与发明的旧 RLHF，自研了全新的 RLCD（基于校准决策的强化学习）——
模型输出的每一个数值和选项，都带着严格校准后的真实胜率与置信度；
它知不知道自己知不知道，在数学层面上被彻底焊死；
4️⃣ 真正的生产力不是陪聊，是“快系统 1 的极致收割”：
这才是他眼中的正道：
把昂贵、笨重、充满主观修辞的聊天模型，降维成一个极度坚硬、不可篡改、毫秒级响应的纯逻辑决策核心。

这场发布给所有还在迷信“聊天框就是一切”的从业者敲响了一记重锤：
过去三年，全世界都在逼着大模型去当一个满嘴跑火车的文学家；
而真正看懂工业终局的科学家已经开始转头造刀——
消灭毫无价值的语言泡沫，
用 450 倍的成本代差，把最精准的决策直接插进人类现实业务的每一根血管里。 https://x.com/CompleteSkeptic/status/2099925687465570372/video/1

知道了 Jev 能用在哪

这条直接帮你梳理这些场景适不适合你，
以及能不能自己跑通闭环：

1. 操作电脑  
适合已经在用 Codex / Claude Code，但嫌 computer use 又慢又卡的人。  

简单动作可以闭环：Jev 判断点哪里，Agent 直接执行；复杂界面仍建议留人工接管。

2. 操作浏览器  
适合要自动搜、比价、填表、做网页流程的运营和开发。  

目标窄、按钮有限时能闭环；
页面一乱、要自己理解新站点，就还得大模型补位。

3. 海量分流和分类  
适合客服、运营、公关这种每天要处理大量进件的人。  

高置信度可以全自动分部门、打标签；
拿不准的再转人工，这是最容易先跑通的闭环。

4. 模型路由  
适合自己做 AI 产品、背后挂了好几个模型的人。
  
闭环很完整：用户一句话进来，Jev 选模型，生成接口直接出活。

5. 内容批量分析  
适合创作者、增长，想搞清楚「什么内容真的涨」。 
 
单次分析不是闭环，只是出结论；把结果接回「写稿 → 打分 → 再写」才算闭环。

6. 信息流过滤  
适合时间线被广告、引战、回复侠刷屏的人。 
 
可以闭环：帖子出现 → Jev 判断 → 隐藏或留下，人不用再看第二眼。

7. 代码审查和安全门禁  
适合带团队的开发，以及会自动改代码、跑命令的 Agent

不建议全自动闭环。高置信度拦截可以自己完成，放行和合并还是留给人或大模型。

8. 交易决策  
适合在做策略、回测、交易机器人的人。  

演示里可以闭环：价格进来，买或卖出去。真金白银不要全交给它，低置信度和风控必须留人手。

9. 游戏和实时控制  
适合做游戏 AI、实时控制和高频 Agent 的人。
  
天生就是闭环：状态进来，100 毫秒给出动作，环境更新后再判断下一拍。

Jev 负责判断，
闭环成不成，看你有没有把「判断之后的那一下」接好~

ar.ti: Jev Makes the Checks You Skip Affordable
ar.tx:
Imagine a research agent that reads the wrong document, builds an argument around it, then spends another minute polishing the answer
You discover the problem at the end, after paying for every step that followed it
A check immediately after retrieval might have stopped the mistake from travelling further
Now repeat that question across the workflow: after a search, before a tool call, after a result, before the final answer
Every checkpoint costs something, so there is pressure to use fewer of them
That is the opportunity I see in Jev: making small, useful checks cheap enough to put where the mistakes begin
1 — The price changes where you can put judgment
TypeSafe introduced Jev on September 15 as a model for structured decisions inside software
You give it evidence and defined questions; it returns choices, scores or yes-probabilities that code can use directly
The current listed price is $0.042 per million input tokens, with output free. Official model specifications
Here is a hypothetical budget: 100,000 agent runs per month, five checkpoint requests per run, and 2,000 billed input tokens per checkpoint, including the questions
That adds up to one billion input tokens and $42 in Jev inference
 
That is $0.00042 per run for the five checkpoint requests
The assumption matters: at 20,000 tokens per checkpoint, the same calculation becomes $420
This budget covers Jev inference only; the writer model, search, tools, retries and human review still have their own costs
But it gives you a concrete question to investigate: could those checks prevent more than $42 of wasted work each month?
2 — Check the handoffs where errors spread
Consider a proposed research-to-article workflow
The research agent collects evidence, a writing agent drafts the article, and the result goes to an editor
I would start with these checkpoints:
 
These are proposed integration points, not results from a system I have benchmarked
Two have direct examples in TypeSafe's documentation: its retrieval cookbook separates useful evidence from conflicting material, while its citation cookbook checks whether the source actually supports a claim. Retrieval example · Citation example
Notice what happens when you catch a problem early: the next agent receives a better input, and you avoid asking it to produce polished work on top of weak evidence
3 — Ask several things about the same moment
A retrieved passage can be relevant, contain a usable fact, contradict the brief and include instructions aimed at the agent
Those are separate questions about the same evidence
Jev can evaluate independent questions together in one request. TypeSafe says adding questions usually changes latency very little, although the extra question text still costs input tokens. Parallel evaluation
That suggests a compact bundle at each checkpoint:
Relevant? → Useful evidence? → Contradiction? → Needs review?
Your code decides what to do with the results
Questions about a future tool result still have to wait for

t:
Jev  和开源本地大模型到底哪个更强？🔥

肯定很多人有这个疑问，我就直接在本地部署了 Laya 模型，做一个系统性的测试

先说结果：准确率方面Jev 完胜，速度方面 Laya 模型完胜

我设计了 100 条真实事件场景去做测试，因为 Laya模型只支持英文，所以对应的内容都是用英文去处理的，我设计的场景就是火星救援

1、整体设计的场景是多方面的 通过这两个模型判断紧急程度和事件处理方案的正确性

2、整体通过率都是百分之百 但是正确率本地模型只有 57% 左右，Jev 模型对事件的判断率能达到百分之百

3、在整体速度延迟方面 因为有网络因素 所以本地模型延迟最优，Jev 模型慢一些

4、模型量级方面 Laya模型只有 421M，对接 EV 模型的话是相对较小的 在很小的内存上就可以运行 而且支持 Mac M 系列的芯片

整体测试下来 让我感到惊喜的就是准确率，Jev 模型我其实在本地循环测试了将近 500 条到 1000 条的数据 准确率都可以达到 100%

而且我用 GPT6 去做了复核 数据准确性也可以达到 99%，说明在最基本的事件处理和判断上 JEV 模型还是遥遥领先的地位

后面我也会尝试把它部署到其他流程当中 比如 computer use 操作电脑的时候，具体效果有没有更加出色

q.t:
Jev 发布没几天，开源社区已经开始疯狂复刻了🔥

最值得推荐的五个模型：

1、Laya 421M：原生决策模型，支持 Mac

2、Decider-2B：最像 Jev，基于 Qwen3.5

3、NanoJev 0.6B：专门的 Decision Head

4、Reflex：Qwen3.5 + Direct Logits

5、System-One 4B：专门做概率校准

如果和我一样是苹果的芯片，我推荐： Laya 和 Reflex

下一步我准备选两个在本地运行 然后测试一下和Jev的差距

q.t:
Introducing Bespoke Nimble: an open data, open model, open recipe for an open Jev.

Code and info: https://github.com/bespokelabsai/nimble
Model: https://huggingface.co/bespokelabs/Bespoke-Nimble-9B

Data:
* A new data curation recipe called contrastive data curation.
* Slightly change facts to generate negative data. This pushes the model to discriminate better and become a better decision maker. The calibration is implicit.
* Didn't do ablations but I think this is a critical piece!
* This also means training data doesn't need probabilities.
* Data covered 10 categories, and is fully synthetic.
* This data is split into train and eval.

Training
* LoRA finetune of Qwen3.5-9B.
* Distillation-free: we use Jev to only evaluate.
* No RL yet!

Serving
* Parallel constrained decoding as suggested by  @NielsRogge and @harshagundal.

Results:
* The post-trained Qwen (Nimble) became substantially better on our curated eval: 66% for Qwen to 90% for Nimble. Jev is at 93%.
* 100ms on H100 and free to use on your macbook! Feel the AGI for free.
* 2 days of building in public. :)

Big caveat is that there is no standard benchmark to measure performance, and it's possible Nimble is much worse on other benchmarks compared to Jev. But it should be better than Qwen!

We thank @typesafeai for making Jev and the inspiring discussions in the community. Hope this release lifts all the boats and encourages more research and activity in this space.

q.t:
"DiffusionGemma as Jev" showcases the power of non-autoregressive architectures.

While Jev demonstrates the value of rapid decision models, running DiffusionGemma in this paradigm leverages canvas diffusion to evaluate structured choices in a single parallel pass:

⚡ ️Massive Parallelism: Denoises across an open canvas in a single step instead of sequential autoregressive token generation (~0.2s on a DGX spark).

🧠 Full Bidirectional Attention: Allows every option to attend to the full context concurrently, yielding well-calibrated decision distributions.

👁️ Multimodal Grounding: Inherits Gemma 4's spatial vision capabilities for complex visual and text decisions.

Read more about this approach here:

好多人觉得 Jev 非常牛逼，其实就是一个分类模型（在《图解大模型》里面称为表示模型，作者认为生成模型开始流行后，很多人就忘记了表示模型）。

达到这么低的推理延迟和成本也是很容易的。只要 prefill 一次，并行针对每个问题 decode 一个 token，输出 logprob 就行了。

当然，由于 RLHF 带来的分布崩塌，现在 LLM 输出的 logprob 并不能作为置信度。这就是为什么 Typesafe 采用了 RLCD，其实在学术界早就有 RLCR。

我把它加入了《深入理解 AI Infra》的算例，读过这本书的人肯定能一眼看出它该怎么实现。

q.t:
話題の Jev（TypeSafe AI）を自分の開発した法令検索サービス「条文くん」で試したので、良かったところも、ダメだったところもそのまま書きます。

■ Jev は何者か
ChatGPT や Claude のように文章を書く AI ではありません。文章を渡して「これは質問に関係あるか」「AとBどちらか」のような決まった形の質問をすると、答えを確率付きで返すだけの AI です。書かないので速くて安い。1回0.5秒くらい、料金は文章を書く AI の数十分の一。「ハルシネーションしない」と言われていますが、それは「決められた選択肢以外を返さない」という意味で、間違った選択肢を選ぶことは普通にあります。

■ どこで試したか
法令検索では、まず検索で候補の条文を100本くらい集め、そこから「本当に関係ありそうな25本」に絞ってから、AI に読ませて答えを作ります。この「100本を見出しだけ見て25本に絞る」工程を、今は Claude にやらせています。ここを Jev に置き換えたらどうなるかを、税務の質問120問で比べました。正解の条文が25本の中に何本残るかで採点します。

■ 結果
・Claude: 正解248本のうち218〜225本が残った（3回やって毎回少し違う）
・Jev: 230〜235本が残った（何回やっても同じ）
Jev のほうが正解を落としませんでした。しかも Claude は同じ質問でも回ごとに答えがぶれるのに対し、Jev は毎回同じ答えです。速さは数秒→0.5秒、費用は1問2円→0.1円。

■ なぜ Jev が勝ったのか
賢いからではありません。Claude に「最大25本選んで」と頼むと、20本くらいで「もう十分」と自分で切り上げてしまい、2本目3本目の正解を取りこぼします。Jev は100本を1本ずつ独立に採点して、機械的に上から25本取るので、席が全部埋まる。それだけの差です。
逆に、見出しの言葉が質問と一致せず、意味を考えないと関係があると分からない問題では、Claude のほうが正解しました。つまり判断の質は Claude が上で、Jev は取りこぼしの少なさで勝っています。

■ 効かなかったこと
・法律の知識がないと結びつかない判定は全然ダメでした。たとえば「この質問にはどの通達が関係するか」を選ばせると、確率が全部50%付近に固まって、判断になっていません。Jev は渡された文章どうしを見比べることはできますが、文章に書いていない知識で結びつけることはできません。公式も「世界の知識を持たない」と明記していて、それがそのまま出た形です。
・候補を100本から300本に増やしても良くなりませんでした。Jev が安いからといって沢山読ませればいい、というものではない。
・検索の代わりにはなりません。
検索エンジンは、50万条文の中から「この質問に関係ありそうな100本」を一気に探すための仕組みです。
一方、Jevは渡された文章を1本ずつ見て、「この質問に関係あるか」を判定する道具です。
つまり50万条文全部をJevで探そうとすると、質問のたびに50万本を1本ずつ判定させることになります。これでは検索の代わりにはなりません。
検索でまず100本まで絞る。その100本をJevで採点して、上位25本を選ぶ。
Jevが向いているのは、検索そのものではなく、その後の絞り込みです。

■ まとめ
Jev は「渡した文章の中で答えが決まる判定」専用の道具です。その用途では安く、速く、ぶれず、今回の1工程では Claude より良かった。ただし、文章を書く AI の代わりでも、検索の代わりでもない。1か所で勝ったからといって、何にでも効くわけではありません。

I’ve put a ton of tokens through Jev now, and...I have thoughts.

1. The big labs lost the script

TypeSafe’s intro video says, “We’re building prod, not God” — and can I just say? Hell yeah. @typesafeai built something for engineers like me, so I can build products for people like your mom (she says hi btw). They’re not trying to create “Machines of Loving Grace”; they’re trying to build things that let OTHER HUMAN BEINGS create new types of products.

The proof is in the pudding. When ChatGPT shipped, we were all blown away by…ChatGPT. When Jev shipped, we were all blown away by what everyone was making with it.

I cannot tell you how refreshing this is. It takes a sincere form of humility to believe that you, the creator of a technology, will not be the best at deploying the technology into the marketplace. The big labs, especially Anthropic, have proven not to have this humility…and now everyone hates AI. Thanks, Dario.

I guess what I’m saying is: Diogo for president.

2. Ultra-smart classifiers were genuinely a missing primitive.

I don’t know how this got missed. Diogo calls it “machine-native intelligence,” and that’s really what it is. I cannot tell you how much bending and twisting I've had to do with LLMs to get them to act like a classifier when they just weren’t. I’m absolutely shocked this is the first time this “type” of model has come to market.

These models will unlock AI utility for entire industries: robotics, trucking, aviation, meteorology, finance, defense, retail…even your smart coffee mug is going to use this.

3. It’s still too expensive

Jev is really, really cheap compared to LLMs. But you don’t use it like an LLM. In my full self-driving example, or any robotics example, you’ll be making decisions several times per second continuously. The #1 value proposition of a model like this is speed and cost.

To be clear, at current pricing, the model will still be successful and well integrated. It will be able to replace a number of tasks that were already being performed (poorly) by LLMs. However, to unlock industrial-scale demand (Jevons paradox), I believe it needs to be roughly 10x cheaper.

Currently, Jev is $0.042/M input, which is actually 7x more expensive than a cache read on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.006). If our industrial application requires decisions at 10 Hz and we provide only 10k of context, that would cost $0.0042/second to operate, or $15/hour, $600/week, etc.

The good news is Diogo said on a recent AMA that they have substantial margin at their current pricing and have already considered dropping the cost further. I hope it's a lot further.

4. Latency is a real limiter

I really hope TypeSafe AI works with an edge network provider to improve the co-location of models and reduce network latency. Ultimately, these models really need to run on-device. I would even be willing to pay some kind of recurring license fee to have a great closed model running on my own hardware, just so I can reduce the TTD (Time To Decision) as much as possible. Imagine running a model like this at 60 Hz, or even 120 Hz.

At that point, we’re looking at a new kind of logic gate — we can’t even imagine what that will be like.

In summary, this one really is a game changer for everyone building AI products, and, assuming cost and latency are further improved…it’ll be a game changer for everyone doing anything.

Jev is a classifier

Example: I asked Jev what color is this iPhone

Jev gives me this:
- 80% orange
- 10% red
- 10% blue

The total is 100.

I set 5 options: blue, orange, red, green, and yellow.

The question and the options are the schema.

Jev does not say "This is orange." It says it is 80% sure.

Jev is a decision model
tr: Jev is a classifier at its truest being that's what it is. I won't get into the architecture and stuff like that because honestly, I don't even understand it that well but essentially you define an input, let's say you have this iPhone as an input, right? And that's the input and then the output is a schema. So we could have the schema be what color is the iPhone is the question almost? And it has a blue, orange, red, green, yellow as the output options for that question. And the classifier, Jev, then looked at this phone in a text format and says, hmm, what, is this orange? Is it red? Could be red. But then it says, okay, this is about, I'm pretty confident it's 80% orange but it could be 10% red or it could be 10% blue, which adds up to 100. And it's the probabilities of those choices. So it's not just going to be a 100% affirmative, this is orange, this is blue, this is red. It's a, hey, I'm 80% confident that this is orange or this is red. And the best way to illustrate that is with this email example.

Almost everyone I know is spending more time thinking about evals, these days, than we did a year ago.

For the past two years, we've been speed-running computer science/software engineering history, trying to figure out how to build useful, robust, real-world systems that leverage LLMs. (Re-inventing lots of wheels, as always happens during a big computing transition.)

Last year at this time, it seemed like the big, general questions we were asking mostly revolved around how to think about the loops, tool calls, and context management triad of problems.

Now, a lot of my conversations are about evals. Evals unlock scaling, maintainability, modularity, cost management, legal/compliance, and research into new architecture directions. Probably a bunch of other stuff, too. But building good evals is not a competence that most software engineers have (yet).

Some really helpful notes on how Typesafe/Jev might fit into our toolkits, below, including some thoughts on evals ...

q.t:
some thoughts on jev

1) i tend to think that twitter hype is not relevant for ai product releases; especially when someone claims to be doing something novel with the architecture

2) but, i think that jev is interesting in principle; it is a low cost, fast classification service, and it claims to be about equivalent to gpt-5.6-terra in performance

3) something interesting here is that this is what most ai services looked like in 2022; cohere sold a classification api, an embedding api, a reranker

4) the problem was that, in addition to not being as effective as gpt-3 and then gpt-4, these services were much harder to use as a developer

5) you had to decide which apis to use, then write the code to glue them together; so, you got less performance for more work

6) but now, we can imagine coding agents making it much easier to select and integrate a cheaper service with specialized characteristics

7) evals are still a bottleneck, though; you need some way to automatically compare performance between services using their apis

8) and, enterprise companies often have a hard time building evals that reflect their actual use cases; it's not a core expertise

9) but, the better coding agents get at integrating and switching between services, the more valuable those evals become;

10) this means companies have more reason to figure out the evals problem;

11) maybe that means getting rights to use customer data for testing, or getting better at purchasing synthetic test data, or something else

12) so, i think there is an interesting world where coding agents create more market for specialized api services, even specialized model services

13) which can compete either on cost or on capabilities; with the winner determined by cost basis or specialized data, etc...

14) note, it might be unclear but if specialized models services becomes an important direction, i expect the frontier labs to have an edge on cost basis

15) and, i think that, at least for now, these specialized model services probably do not provide enough of a cost difference to be relevant

t:
Ran a dumb experiment last night: used Jev by @typesafeai (a decision/classifier model, not a text-gen model) to write C++.

At every step I gave it the finite set of grammatically valid next tokens and let it just... pick one. No free-form generation, no hallucinated syntax, purely "choose from this legal set." It's not built for this, that's what made it fun.

Got a working piece of C++ out of a model that fundamentally does not generate text. Not claiming this is how you should write code, and it's slower and dumber than just using an actual code model. But it's a neat proof that a classifier constrained tightly enough can stumble into looking like a generator.

Novelty over utility here, but it's the kind of dumb experiment that tells you more about a model's actual guardrails than the official demos do.
Jev making its blazingly fast classification responses

补充一下 Jev 的输入和输出，具体可以怎么放进程序里。

输入可以是自然语言文本，也可以是结构化信息。调用时主要提供两部分：state 放需要分析的内容，比如一段聊天记录、一份报错信息，或者包含多个字段的对象；questions 定义你要问什么，以及判断标准和候选项。

比如 state 放用户的消息，questions 问这条消息应该交给哪个部门处理，再给出技术支持、账单、销售三个选项及各自的说明。

输出通过 JSON 返回，目前主要有三种。

Choice 用来选一个选项。比如技术支持、账单、销售的概率分别是 70%、20%、10%，最终 choice 就是技术支持。程序也能读取完整分布，知道其他选项有多少可能性。

Score 用来按标准评分。比如把故障分成三个等级：0 是轻微显示问题，1 是影响功能但有替代办法，2 是完全阻塞。如果概率分别是 10%、20%、70%，分数就是：

0 × 0.1 + 1 × 0.2 + 2 × 0.7 = 1.6

这个分数可以直接参与排序，或者和其他评分组合计算优先级。

Noul 用来判断一个条件是否成立，返回 0～1 的概率。比如问消息是否包含求助意图，得到 0.9，再由程序设定阈值，决定是否触发后续操作。

Choice 和 Score 还会返回 confidence，根据概率分布的集中程度计算。90%、5%、5% 表示明显偏向一个选项，34%、33%、33% 就很难选。

我想到一个很适合的场景，就是判断群聊里的 agent 该不该被唤醒回复。

把最近的聊天记录、有没有被 @、agent 的角色，以及它刚刚是否已经回复过这些信息放进 state，再问当前是否适合由 agent 参与。

有人明确求助，或者问题正好属于 agent 负责的范围，就可能得到较高的值。如果只是群友闲聊，或者问题已经被别人解决，就让它保持安静。超过设定阈值，再调用负责生成回复的大模型。

这样也能处理没人 @ 它，但上下文里确实需要它帮忙的情况，不用只靠关键词和固定触发词。

还可以在同一次请求里并行判断该不该回复、问题有多紧急、应该交给哪个 agent，把这些结果交给代码，决定具体唤醒谁、以什么优先级处理。

q.t:
能不能把 Jev 这类模型直接结合进编程语言，作为一种函数执行方式？

开发者定义输入参数、计算目标和返回类型，函数被调用时，把参数交给模型，内部的计算或语义判断由模型完成，结果直接回到程序里。

比如 calculatePriority(task, context) 返回优先级分数，参与后续排序；shouldRetry(error, context) 返回是否重试，用于 if 判断；classifyIntent(message) 返回枚举，决定接下来执行哪个分支。

现在封装一层 API 就能尝试其中一部分。如果语言和类型系统直接支持，就可以明确声明哪些函数执行普通代码，哪些函数交给模型，调用时仍然使用熟悉的参数和返回值。

这样写业务逻辑时，遇到那些很难穷举规则、但用自然语言又能说明白的判断，就可以直接定义成函数。写清楚要算什么、传入必要的上下文，让模型完成这部分计算，不用再手工展开成几十个 if else。

Jev Ultrafast is insane for WebMCP.

q.t:
We just ran Jev on our WebMCP benchmark.

The result: basically broke the benchmark.

Jev + Mercury 2.5 (a fast, low-cost LLM) using WebMCP solved 100% of the tasks at roughly 112× lower model cost than GPT-6 Astra using computer use with code execution. Compared to Astra using screenshot-based computer use, the model cost was 245× lower (!). 

We also compared Jev operating the browser with and without WebMCP. 

We used Browser Use’s open-source Ultrafast, with some improvements to the harness to make it more reliable across the benchmark. 

Jev’s browser-control accuracy on its own was not amazing - adding WebMCP nearly doubled the number of solved tasks, from 25/49 to 49/49, while reducing model cost by 18% (more on why below).

The benchmark and methodology are fully open and reproducible.

Full results: https://webmcp.com/benchmark

A few words on how the Jev + WebMCP harness works and why this is exciting:

Jev receives text as input and a set of discrete options it can choose from.  With WebMCP, those options are the tools exposed by the website. At each step, Jev sees the task, the available tools and previous results, then picks what to do next.

The limitation is that Jev can’t generate arbitrary text, which you need for tool arguments. For example, it can choose the search_products tool, but it can’t generate the search query itself.

So we split the work: Jev picks the tool and Mercury 2.5 generates the arguments if needed. 

This works well because turns out most of the cognitive load in these tasks is around choosing the right action. The argument generation itself is relatively simple, so we can delegate to a small and very fast model. We used Mercury, which outputs 1,000+ tokens/sec and is very cheap.

The result is a pretty simple combination: Jev for tool selection + Mercury for arguments + WebMCP for the interface. It ends up being very reliable, very fast, and very cheap.

A few words about Ultrafast and why do we think it underperforms:

Without WebMCP, Jev chooses from the page’s controls: which button to click, which field to fill, or which option to select. 

But choosing a valid button is different from choosing the right next step. The agent still has to navigate menus, understand forms, recover from errors  and recognize when the task is actually complete.

Our hypothesis is that WebMCP makes the decision space much simpler. Instead of figuring out a sequence of clicks through a website, Jev chooses explicit actions that directly advance the task. 

@typesafeai itself documents weaker accuracy on questions requiring multiple reasoning steps. WebMCP moves much of that complexity into the website’s tools, leaving Jev with clearer decisions and fewer opportunities to go wrong (in a sense WebMCP "compresses" a sequence of clicks into one tool call).

Our modified Ultrafast setup solved 25/49 tasks - that is a result for our particular implementation and benchmark, not a universal limit on Jev or Browser Use. We are open to more harness optimization to get this result to perform better, feel free to directly contribute to the benchmark here: https://github.com/nekuda-ai/WindTunnel

Browser-use ultrafast: https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast

q.t: when a designer gets access to Jev

t:
Since Jev launched Tuesday, there’s apparently a new thing at @every “Jev boys.”

Ever since the launch there’s been this flock of self-proclaimed “Jev boys” who carry Jev on hand at all times and constantly ask it what to do. They have their entire personality revolve around Jev, TypeSafe, and calibrated probabilities. When we went around talking about what people were trying this week, 4 or 5 of them said some variation of “I live by the Jev and die by the Jev.”

Just about an hour ago, I asked someone to do something and one of the Jev boys was bold enough to say “if Jev says I do it, otherwise I don’t.” I told him if he asked Jev instead of just doing the thing I was going to lose my mind.

He asked it anyway and it said to do it.

Thank god for that at least.

But then the other Jev boy asked the same question and Jev gave him a different answer.

He immediately pulled up the probability and started explaining that Jev was only 63% confident, so technically it was a judgment call.

I told him that yes. That is what being a person is.

Later, another Jev boy asked Jev whether he should go to a meeting. Jev said no.

He did not go to the meeting.

When someone asked where he was, he posted the Jev output in Slack.

At lunch, I watched two Jev boys ask Jev where they should eat. They got different answers and spent five minutes comparing confidence scores instead of picking somewhere.

One of them actually said “I’m going with Jev on this one.”

The other said “your Jev is wrong.”

I don’t even know what that means.

Now they’ve started asking Jev questions about each other.

Someone asked Jev if another person’s idea was good.

false

The person whose idea it was then asked Jev whether that was constructive feedback.

false

Neither of them has spoken since.

This afternoon one of the Jev boys told me he doesn’t make decisions anymore, he “routes them through Jev.”

I asked if he was joking.

He asked Jev.

It said false.

It has been three days since launch.

I really hope this dies off soon. I haven’t seen anything outside Every about “Jev boys,” so I’m guessing it’s just an Every thing.

Unless one of you has more information.

ChatGPTのように文章を書くAIではなく、「判断」だけを超高速・低コストで返すAIモデルです。

例えばメールを読ませて、

・営業／請求／サポートのどこに振る？
・緊急度は1〜5のどれ？
・返信が必要な確率は？

システムがそのまま使える「判断結果＋確率」。

活用先としては、

・問い合わせの自動振り分け
・営業リードの優先順位付け
・不正取引や異常検知
・契約書や申請書の要確認判定
・コンテンツ審査
・AIエージェントが「次に何をするか」の判断など。

組み込み方も分かりやすくて、

メール受信
↓
Jevが「誰が対応するか・緊急度・返信要否」を判断
↓
請求チームへ振り分け
↓
必要ならSlack通知
↓
ChatGPTやClaudeに返信文を書かせる
↓
自信が低いものだけ人間が確認

ChatGPT → 「このメールへの返信を書いて」
Jev → 「返信は必要？誰が対応する？どれくらい急ぐ？」

何でもできるAIを速くしたのではなく、

AIエージェントが普及するほど、こういう「判断専用AI」はかなり重要になりそう。

t:
Jev 发布还不到一周，OpenJEV 也开始扎堆了。

我整理了 8 个目前比较有代表性的项目：

1. SemIf

最省事的一派。直接拿现成 Qwen，在模型准备回答 A / B / C 时截住，不让它继续生成文字，只读取每个选项的分数，再换算成概率。

不用重新训练模型，更像是把传统大模型换了一种用法。

https://github.com/TheoLeeCJ/SemIf

2. Simple Jev

思路和 SemIf 类似，但进一步省掉重复计算。

同一段材料只让模型读一次，后面的多个问题共用这部分结果，再分别算答案概率。

作者也说得很清楚，它复刻的是 Jev 的接口和用法，不代表准确率、速度和概率校准已经做到 Jev 水平。

https://github.com/featherless-ai/simple-jev

3. Laya

直接放弃「会写字的大模型」，改用更像传统分类器的编码模型，再加专门的决策头。

模型只有几亿参数，可以做得非常快，但复杂任务还有明显差距。比如一次从 77 个选项里选答案，Laya 准确率 42.5%，Jev 是 87.0%。

https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya

4. Von

也是从头做一个专门的决策模型。

Von 只有约 4 亿参数，不生成文字，一次前向直接处理 Choice、Noul 和 Score，更像一个能读自然语言的新一代分类器。

项目自测里，本地 GPU 单次判断已经能压到几十毫秒。

https://github.com/wfzyx/von

5. Verdict

体积更小，只有约 1.5 亿参数。

作者专门处理了两个问题：模型答错了还报很高的置信度，以及把 A、B 选项前后换个顺序，答案就跟着变。

这条路线很看重判断结果和概率能不能稳定。

https://github.com/Heman10x-NGU/Verdict-open-jev

6. Kev

Kev 选择了保留大模型，直接拿 Qwen 改。

它给 Qwen 加了专门的决策结构，同一份输入只读一次，多个问题分别给出概率。第三方此前逆向 Jev 时，也猜测 Jev 可能采用类似设计。

Kev 拿训练时没见过的新题测试，8B 版准确率约 78%，Jev 约 86%。差距还在，但已经能看出这条路线确实能跑通。

https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev

7. Nimble

Nimble 更偏「靠训练把 Qwen 练成 Jev」。

它用 Qwen3.5-9B，再准备大量「只改一个事实，正确答案就翻转」的数据做后训练。

在 324 个没参与训练的测试样本里，Nimble 有 90.1% 选中了参考答案，Jev 是 93.2%。不过作者也提醒，它报出来的概率目前还没有完全校准。

https://github.com/bespokelabsai/nimble

8. OpenJev

这条最不一样，直接用了 DiffusionGemma。

它先把多个答案位置留空，再像扩散模型补图一样，一次把答案填出来，不需要一个 token 一个 token 往后生成。

在 RTX PRO 6000 上，作者测到单请求中位延迟约 94ms。

https://github.com/razorback16/openjev

---

看下来，OpenJEV 已经很明显分成了四派：

1. 直接读现成大模型的答案分数
2. 重新训练专用决策模型
3. 把现有大模型改造成决策模型
4. 用扩散模型直接填答案

「不吐 token，只给概率」这个表面形式确实不难复刻。

真正拉开差距的还是准确率、泛化和概率校准。模型敢报 90%，这个 90% 到底有多可信，才是最难的部分。
Playing with @typesafeai Jev a lot this morning and I think 70% of my application budget will shift away from OpenAI to it once I'm confident in their uptime.

t:
看大家都在讨论Jev，一起来了解一下

这个模型的特点是由于它的构建模式决定的：

1、输出空间事先由 schema 定义
调用时你先声明"允许的答案是什么"，目前主要三类：
- Choice：有限选项中选一个工单归类到 {退款, 技术故障, 投诉}
- Score：数值/量表打分   比如 紧急程度 0–100
- Bool ：是/否 + 概率   比如  这段输入是否含 prompt 注入？

因为输出只能落在预定义集合里，所以"不会幻觉、不会类型错误"是结构上的必然

2、并行采样，非自回归
Jev 不是逐 token 生成的 transformer LLM，而是一次前向传播并行给出所有输出。这就是它延迟 70–500 ms（对比前沿 LLM 3–329 s）、快 40–200 倍的根源。

3、训练方法 RLCD（Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions）

RLHF 优化"人类评分者喜欢的回答"；
RLVR 优化"可验证的正确输出"；
RLCD 优化"认识论上诚实的概率"——即模型说 80% 置信时，真实准确率就应接近 80%。

这个校准很关键，因为模型输出的置信度可以直接当阈值用（比如 <0.7 就转人工）。

具体逻辑可以看我贴的图

-----------
理解了这个模型，那么不难识别，Jev有四个特别适合它特征的使用场景：
1、问题可枚举
2、量大或高频
3、对延迟/成本敏感
4、置信度能直接当阈值用。

满足其中三条就值得考虑使用Jev

我目前认为特别适合的一些场景：

1. 用户用自然语言写规则的"个人分类器"

过去个性化推荐需要训练排序模型，现在用户一句话"不看引战、不看币圈"就是一个分类器。

可以推广到邮件分拣、通知优先级、评论区管理、家长控制、RSS/新闻聚合。

2. 调用大模型之前的"前置门"

每个 Agent 循环里都有大量廉价判断被浪费在 LLM 上：这个请求要不要调 LLM、走哪个模型（便宜/贵）、要不要检索、检索回来的 chunk 相不相关、这轮工具调用成功没有、任务完成了吗、该不该停下来问用户。把这些交给 Jev，LLM 只在真正需要生成时才被唤醒，整体成本和延迟能砍掉一大截。语义缓存的"命中判断"也属于这一类。

3. 对结构化数据做"语义列"
比如：简历初筛（"有 3 年以上 Go 经验？"）、合同条款存在性检查、电商评论的属性抽取（"是否提到尺码偏小"）、客服工单归因、问卷开放题编码、日志/告警的异常标注。特点是：一次性把整张表跑一遍，几分钟、几美元搞定，然后就能用 SQL 查了。

4. 每个请求都要过的安全护栏

Prompt 注入检测、PII 检测、毒性判断、输出是否越权——这些必须在 100 ms 级完成、必须对每条请求都做、误判可以用置信度阈值分层处理（高置信直接拦，中间转人工）。校准过的概率就非常有用。

5. 大规模评测与标注

LLM-as-judge 现在的痛点是又贵又慢，做不到全量。Jev 可以对每条输出打分、比较 A/B 两个 prompt 的偏好、给训练数据打标签、监控线上模型质量。它自己就是靠校准训练出来的，做 judge 的一致性比 LLM 更好。

6. 实时交互和控制

AI玩游戏和交易机器人是这个方向的两端：游戏 NPC 的行为决策、直播弹幕的实时审核、客服对话中的情绪升级检测（该不该转人工）、机器人/IoT 的高层决策、根据用户操作动态调整 UI。共同点是决策必须跟上事件流的节奏。

7. 数据工程中的模糊匹配实体消歧（A 和 B 是不是同一家公司）、跨系统字段映射（这个列对应哪个标准字段）、去重、数据质量分级。这些传统上要么写规则要么训小模型，Jev 用自然语言描述规则就能上，而且能跑全量。

I've been testing @typesafeai Jev. 
And I found a way to make it good.

Jev is not an agent. It's very good at figuring out what needs to be done, but actually executing actions that move towards that goal is its biggest weakness.

I found a workaround and it 10x'd its performance.

> You need to "predict outcomes, not steps towards an outcome."

It really matters for many use cases. 
Most problems require multi-step planning, and solving them is an interconnected graph of choices. And without this change in perspective, using it for such problems is simply impossible.

This is how this thinking is applied when trying to solve Tetris:

Asking it to "Play Tetris" won't work. It requires Jev to make a plan by itself and execute actions towards that plan.

Asking it "Which button to press" is better, but changing this question to "Where should this piece land" magically bypasses its weakness in multi-step planning.

Even better would be asking "Should you win or lose" and executing actions towards that GENIUS goal, but if we could do that for any problem, we wouldn't really need AI in the first place.

I’m yet to find a solution for more complex decision trees, where one outcome deeply changes the next. Solving that is what would actually make workflow automation with models like Jev work.

The most interesting thing about all of these Jev demos to me is just how many incredibly smart and creative people there are on X.

I'm seeing people use it to self-drive cars, launch rockets, solve rubix cubes, build programming languages, write viral tweets, search postgres w/ natural language, control browsers and OS, improve speech to text, detect fraud, scrape content and more.

It's hard not to have a bit of imposter syndrome. When you give the best designers and developers tools like this it's a genuine superpower that makes it very hard to compete with!

How does Jev work?

Jev takes two things: your input and an output schema.

The schema gives the structure of the answer you want.

I send an email. 

My schema asks for two fields: is spam, and a category from marketing, finance, or spam.

Jev returns:
- is spam: 0.90
- category: spam

That is a 90% chance of spam.

Jev selects the category only from the list I give it. It writes no sentences. 

The 0.90 is a number object, so my code can use it immediately without extra processing.

Jev shows no reasoning. You get the answer and nothing more, so some people do not trust it.

Use Jev for choices your code must make fast and at low cost: spam or normal, buy or no buy, reply or escalate.

t:
What does it cost to sort 1,700 emails with Jev?

I gave JEV each full email object: 
- Subject
- body
- sender

No special changes.

Jev sent back 4 values for each email:
- Category: work, shopping, finance, security
- Priority: low to urgent
- Spam score: a percentage
- Reply score: how much the email needs a reply from me

One user wrote that their account had a violation. JEV gave it a 90% reply score.

The run used 4.2 million input tokens and 500,000 output tokens.

The final cost was 18 cents. The total time was 12 seconds.

q.t:
Resumo geral do Jev, use cases do Visor e o que abre em outras áreas com exemplos que consegui explorar com o Claude:

É um modelo da TypeSafe que não devolve texto e nem expõe raciocínio - basicamente um modelo de decisão via API, pay as you go, com latência baixa e preço ínfimo.

Você manda um estado (JSON com fatos) e perguntas com tipo e ele devolve um structured JSON.

Nele, você tem três opções:

NOUL: probabilidade de “sim”.
pergunta: “Um cachorro é um animal?“
resposta: { probability: 0.99, confidence: 0.97 }
O booleano é você quem tira: if p > 0.9.

SCORE: um nível numa escala que você define, com a probabilidade de cada nível.
pergunta: “Quão completa é esta descrição de bug?”, níveis: sem passos / passos sem resultado esperado / completa.
resposta: { score: 1, probabilities: [0.12, 0.71, 0.17], confidence: 0.74 }

CHOICE: uma opção entre até 255, com a probabilidade de cada uma.
pergunta: “Qual time atende este ticket?”, opções: financeiro, suporte, comercial.
resposta: { choice: “financeiro”, probabilities: {…}, confidence: 0.88 }

Com relação ao preço, aqui deu $0.03 por cerca de mil decisões, mas depende do seu input - o output é free.

A condição é uma pergunta em linguagem natural, o contexto é o state que você monta, e o resultado entra no seu fluxo como um logical gate:

"Essa compra parece fraude?" antes de mandar para o antifraude por ex
"Esse ticket de suporte pede reembolso?" 
"Essa mensagem tenta injetar prompt?" 
"Esse trecho do diff faz rescue para devolver nil?" (num cenário de dev tool)  

Pode servir como um filtro na frente de outro serviço, modelo ou pessoa, barato o bastante para rodar em qualquer request.

No Visor, alguns usos possíveis interessantes:

“essa cobrança mensal é assinatura cancelável?” acertou 88%, 93% quando era relacionado à seguros. 

Já atribuir compra à fatura, 65% contra 82% das regras internas do Visor. 

Categorização automática no pdf entre 140 opções com histórico inteiro, 41% (bem pior que o gemini). 

Usar como roteador de tools no chat piorou o custo porque o cache do Gemini já cobria 86% do prefix.

Alguns constraints que testei e melhoraram muito o resultado:

- uma decisão por pergunta
- um Choice largo perde para vários Noul pequenos compostos em código
- um SQL com um aggregate passando pro Jev julgar o resumo teve resultados interessantes
- pedir pro claude testar com uma api key no local foi BEM interessante
- corte de confiança em toda chamada do Jev - estando abaixo, ou a chamada caiu, roda o fluxo anterior 
- lembre de limpar PII antes de enviar o state

A parte boa é o que isso abre em outras áreas, que eram onde a IA não conseguia fazer de forma escalável/rápida.

Com decisão a centavos por milhar e abaixo de um segundo, algumas coisas se tornam possíveis:

Moda e casa: “essa peça é do estilo que o usuário costuma salvar?” 

Estilos do próprio catálogo, com a probabilidade/rank de similaridade de cada um.

Conteúdo e comunidade: “esse comentário quebra a regra de moderação?” 

Severidade e confiança podem decidir entre publicar, avisar e revisar sem ninguém ter o trabalho

Qualquer produto com muita decisão pequena e pouca gente. 

- suporte classificando tickets
- marketplace que normaliza anúncio de vendedor e manda o incerto para revisão. 
- seguro e crédito com o caso claro automático e o duvidoso para o analista. 
- recrutamento que pontua evidência de competência e não currículo bonito. 
- busca que reordena candidatos por relevância.
- app de IA generativa que checa cada entrada e saída antes de mostrar.

Em resumo: onde hoje existe uma fila de tarefas para passar por julgamento humano, um limiar fixo para decisões, ou uma chamada de LLM para uma resposta de sim ou não, cabe uma chamada pro Jev com corte de confiança possivelmente mais "correto".

Vercel Labs 工程师 Chris Tate 给 json-render 接入 Jev，开始试验让 AI 在运行时直接组合 UI。

json-render 会提前准备好按钮、卡片、输入框、数据和动作。Jev 不需要像大模型一样逐 Token 写完整 JSON，只负责决定用哪些组件、怎么排序、放在哪里，再交给正常的 UI 渲染器。新界面默认一次判断选出主要组件，需要时再用第二次判断安排布局。

未来 App 的界面可能根本不用完全写死。UI 可以变成运行时决策，同一个 App 面对不同用户、任务和状态，临时拼出不同的页面。Jev 这次演示已经把完整生成时间压到 1 秒以内，至少让这种交互开始有了实时感。

Runway 上月底发布的 Solaris 也在赌类似方向，只是路线更激进。Solaris 用世界模型逐帧生成整个界面，直接绕过传统代码和组件；Jev 仍然使用开发者提前写好的组件和动作，只动态决定怎么组合。

一个想让软件变成实时生成的视频世界，一个更像让软件拥有一张随时重组的脸。

t:
some underrated points + important second order effects of the wildly successful Jev launch

1. Data is the bottleneck! TypeSafe calls themselves a “data research lab”. 

To build a general purpose classifier or actor of any kind, you need to painstakingly curate and create tons of high-quality data (Traces, Examples, Evals/Environments/Worlds, Simulations). 
This helps the model learn these distributions so it can do good work for users. This is especially true for building domain specific, vertical agents.

Look at the data. Every team looking to build better agents will need help + tooling to help them with this. If teams can spend more time building good data, then they will build better models & agents.

2. The explosion of ultra-cheap, always-on Monitoring + Data Mining of Agent Traces at scale

To build better agents, we need to understand them at scale. We also saw the large need to real-time monitor and flag bad behavior during the OpenAI-HuggingFace Incident. Models like Jev help us do this because they’re very fast and cheap for classification.

There’s a simple pipeline here:
Gather Traces —> Label Them aggressively —> Make Evals/Environments from them (optional) -> Fine-Tune Cheaper Model.

Part of data hygiene is understanding data at scale. We sort of had the tooling to do this before by fine-tuning small models or sending smart agents to read lots of traces. 
We’ll still use agents to mine traces because Jev has limitations like context window length, but this is a great tool for:
- humans to define dimensions up front on what they care
- using Jev to triage data across important dimensions for further review.

3. We are never escaping Jevon’s paradox

Models like Jev just help us do more. Classify more traces, monitor more actions in real-time. This is all net-new addition of compute and will happen at massive-scale over every piece of data agents create. 

This is all very exciting because though we’ll use more compute, we’ll understand much more to build better systems.

t:
JEV TIP 003:

When an agent marks an attempt as failed, send JEV:

> task contract
> failure report
> failed strategy
> proposed retry strategy
> criteria for what counts as a legitimate retry

If the retry doesn’t meet the criteria, force a replan, escalate, or stop.

q.t:
JEV TIP 002: 

Run JEV outside the loop to track task drift.

On each state transition, send the task contract + the delta + a checklist to classify drift.

Wire the signal into a fuse to trip after a crossed threshold, and then it can redirect, escalate, or pause the agent.

q.t:
"DiffusionGemma as Jev" showcases the power of non-autoregressive architectures.

While Jev demonstrates the value of rapid decision models, running DiffusionGemma in this paradigm leverages canvas diffusion to evaluate structured choices in a single parallel pass:

⚡ ️Massive Parallelism: Denoises across an open canvas in a single step instead of sequential autoregressive token generation (~0.2s on a DGX spark).

🧠 Full Bidirectional Attention: Allows every option to attend to the full context concurrently, yielding well-calibrated decision distributions.

👁️ Multimodal Grounding: Inherits Gemma 4's spatial vision capabilities for complex visual and text decisions.

Read more about this approach here:
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57250

使用 Jev 模型 判断任务和时长，到底是真的程序在运行 还是 Agent 出问题，自动终止任务和重试

整体的执行流程和判断逻辑：

 1、监控 Pi 是否持续产生模型输出、工具进度或生命周期事件。

 2、如果持续有进度，判断为正常运行，继续等待。

 3、如果长时间没有进度，调用 TypeSafe 判断是正常慢任务、需要用户处理，还是疑似卡住。

 4、TypeSafe 判断正常时继续等待；判断不确定时提醒用户。

 5、判断为卡住时终止当前请求，并自动重试一次。

 6、重试仍失败时停止自动操作，提示用户切换模型、检查网络或手动处理。

 7、如果 Pi 进程本身死锁，则交给外部系统级 Watchdog 重启

我相信很多用 PI 的人都遇到过，PI 在执行长时间任务的时候没有任何反应，只有终止当前任务才能继续

我在社区也看到了相关的解决方案，可以使用插件去监测时间消耗，我自己的处理方案是把对应的等待时间都调小，但是只是治标不治本，后面我就尝试使用 Jev 模型去做判断，没想到真可以

t:
TypeSafe'in Jev modeline 2048 oynattım. Videoda oynayan ben değilim.

Soldaki Terminal'de kararları görüyorsunuz, sağdaki tarayıcıda oyun gerçekten oynanıyor. Kendi kurduğum taklit bir tahta değil, herkesin girip oynadığı siteden. Her hamlede dört yönün yanındaki çubuklar modelin o yöne ne kadar meylettiğini gösteriyor, altında seçtiği yön ve kararın kaç milisaniye sürdüğü yazıyor. Ortalama 300-400 milisaniye, yani saniyenin üçte biri. Videoyu izlenebilir olsun diye kasıtlı olarak yavaşlattım; model beklemese saniyede 2,5 hamle yapıyor.

Kararı veren TypeSafe'in Jev modeli, ve bu bir sohbet robotu değil. Cümle kurmuyor, açıklama yazmıyor. Ona tahtanın halini ve dört seçeneği veriyorum, bana bu dörtten birini geri veriyor. Dışına çıkması mümkün değil.

Küçük bir ayrıntı gibi duruyor ama sıradan bir yapay zeka modeline "bana sadece yukarı, aşağı, sola, sağa yaz" dersin, ilk seferinde "Yukarı" yazar, ikincisinde "up", üçüncüsünde "Sanırım yukarı gitmek mantıklı çünkü..." diye üç cümle döker. Uygulama da orada patlar. Burada o ihtimal hiç yok, çünkü model yazmıyor, verilenler arasından seçiyor.

Sıradan bir modele de "sadece şu dört şıktan birini söyle" diyebilirsiniz, hatta bunu garantiye alan yöntemler var. Ama orada elinizde cümle kuran bir makine vardır, siz onu dışarıdan zapt edersiniz. Burada zapt edilecek bir şey yok. Model kalem tutmuyor, sadece şıklardan birini işaretliyor.

Gerçek hayatta şu şekilde kullanılabilir. Bir şirkete günde on bin destek mesajı geliyor diyelim. Her mesajın doğru departmana gitmesi lazım: fatura, iade, teknik arıza, kargo. Aslında iş tam olarak 2048'deki iş, tek fark seçeneklerin dört yön değil dört departman olması. Model mesajı okuyup listeden birini seçiyor, yanına da ne kadar emin olduğunu koyuyor. Emin olmadığı mesajları ayırıp insana bırakabilirsiniz.

Maliyet tarafı da burada anlam kazanıyor. Bu kurulumda 1 dolara yaklaşık 20 bin karar alınıyor, her biri saniyenin üçte birinde. On bin mesajlık günün faturası yarım dolar civarı.

Kodu GitHub'da açık olarak yayınladım, linki yanıtta.

Bu arada konu 2048'i iyi oynaması değil. İleriyi hesaplamıyor, sadece o anki tahtaya bakıp bir yön söylüyor. Videodaki kayıt 60 hamlede kesiliyor, skor 324. Mesele kararın kendisinin ne kadar ucuza ve ne kadar hızlı alındığı.

Generative UI?

You don't always need to generate new UI to be creative. You can simply make existing UI more fun to use.

This might actually be more important than generative UI. Reconfigurable UI?

q.t:
很多人没看懂爆火的JEV是什么？

所以我做了一个 50 秒的演示视频，带大家把海外刷屏的 JEV 以及它背后的底层架构看透👇（见下方视频）

JEV 是前 OpenAI、参与 ChatGPT / RLHF 的 @CompleteSkeptic（Diogo Almeida）创办 @typesafeai 后的第一款模型

他在 OpenAI 时发现了一个致命矛盾：
通过人类偏好微调（RLHF）训练出来的自回归大模型，存在严重的模式崩溃（Mode-dropping）、过度自信与幻觉，且串行逐字生成的延迟极大，根本无法胜任严肃的机器自动化生产

为此，他们花了两年研发了专为自动化设计的 System 1 基础模型 JEV，核心架构创新非常激进：

• 单次并行计算（One Parallel Pass）：
如同当年 Transformer 取代 RNN 一样，JEV 彻底抛弃了逐 Token 串行吐字的自回归机制，采用全新的模型架构与采样器，一次性并行击发所有预设选项

• 强化学习校准决策（RL for Calibrated Decisions）：
引入全新的训练算法，输出媒介不再是自然语言文本，而是直接输出经过置信度校准的概率分布

• 代码级可靠（TypeSafe）：
彻底根除幻觉，输出自一致、确定性高，可作为强类型对象直接被程序调用

• 100 倍提速与极端降本：
延迟降至 0.1 秒以内（快到能直接插入 60 FPS 游戏循环）；输入每 10 亿 Token 仅 42 美元，输出 Token 彻底免费

视频里我把传统自回归的 8.5 秒延迟瓶颈、JEV 的并行矩阵运算，以及实时控制小游戏实测，全拉通做了可视化, demo参考 @MatijaSosic 

聊天需要慢推理，自动化需要快直觉，Building Prod, not God 确实不是一句空话🫡

Here is the full walkthrough if you want to watch it work. 

A real support ticket goes in, and Jev comes back with the team that owns it, a frustration score, and a probability that it reads as urgent. The confidence value on each answer decides what gets handled automatically and what a person sees.
tr: Everybody, this is Sean Roberts from Netlify, and today I wanted to talk to you about JAV, the first system one model built by TypeSafe.ai. And I wanted to kind of give my point of view around how I think it's cool and how we have to think about using this versus using an LLM traditionally. First of all, before we go too deep, I think it's important to talk about the system one naming. So there's this concept of system one, system two thinking, and it's very intentional that they called it this. So system one thinking, is fast, quick decision making, or system two thinking, is more methodical, slower type of decision making. And what they're saying is JAV is much faster at giving quick decisions, and thus it's a very specifically designed system one model. So let's dive into this. So we've used LLMs to get decisions before. So we give it a prompt, the LLM gives us a lot of content back, and then we use JSON schema type of methodologies either very simple, having the provider do the JSON schema parsing or doing it ourselves. Unfortunately, in many cases, falling back to regex to extract certain things. And then also when things fail, we also have to account for retrying loops and making sure that that happens. And that's kind of a lot to get a single decision from a specific prompt. Now let's think about this problem and how you'd use a system one model to think about solving it. So first is our state. State can be any text data that represents the situation. In this case, I'm building something for a support agent, and I just use the support ticket itself as that state. Next, I want to ask a few questions about that state. So for example, in my processing of support ticket, I want to know how the team should handle this? How frustrated is that user? And how urgent is this? Each question asks one thing, and there's no paragraph needed here. So for example, the teams, I know the finite list of teams that it should pick from how frustrated a customer is is a very simple scale. And urgency is a simple yes or no answer. Then we give it take three different shapes. A choice, a score, and a null. A choice is given the finite set of options, these are the ones that I want to know about. A score is given the different ranges or levels on an axis. I want you to score the probability of each of those. And then a null is the probability of yes or no. The answer is actually the how sure the model is of any given answer you supply it. So whenever you're asking a question, you also have to give all of the answers. And then what it's going to do is give you the probability of each of those answers. Now, let's look at the question we asked earlier and the answers that we got back from it. So for our support ticket, we asked which team should handle this, and we gave it three different teams, and it returned to us for each of those teams that said, this is the confidence for billing. This is the confidence for the technical team and the confidence for the sales team. And in this case, it's highly confident. This is the billing team support ticket. We also asked how frustrated the customer seemed, and we gave it a scale. It gives a confidence level of each entry on that scale. And then finally, we asked for a null for the urgency determination, which is basically the confidence of yes, this is urgent or the confidence that no, this is not urgent. Let's look at this in the form of the code that we would send. So like we said before, we determined our state, which in this case is just going to be the ticket verbatim exactly as it came in. And then we asked the three questions, which are keyed by the, the object in the questions object. So for the department, we have a specific question on which team should handle this and we gave it the three finite answers. And then we asked for a score and urgent, we asked for a null. And no, you don't have to add criteria, yes or no, and no, just it knows that it's a yes or no. And when we send this, it's all processed at once. And the three questions are processed in parallel. Now let's check out the response. Like we saw before, where we're going to see the model give us confidence readings and make a determination by selfless confidence readings. This is what that actually looks like. And we're going to see that it chose from the list of available options at billing with this confidence score is what we should, you know, is the answer for, for that department gives us a score for the confidence of the frustration and a null for the urgency. And like we mentioned before, the choice is going to pick from the probability of the options you offered, a score is going to determine the position on a scale. And the null is going to be a number between zero and one where one is yes and zero is no. These three judgments happen very fast. There's no natural language returned back. There's nothing to parse. There's no markdown. There's nothing to strip out, right? This is given our inputs that we hav

t:
Did my OSS-Jev called Verdict, beat Official Typesafeai 's Jev ?, and Laya (the best performing OSS Jev) on their own benchmark?

When I first tested Verdict 1.0(my earlier attempt of oss-jev) earlier this week, it scored 26.10% accuracy. Uniform random guessing on that split is 26.90%, meaning the model was literally worse than a coin toss.

I dug into the failure and traced it to an option-pointer misalignment. I scrapped that setup and rebuilt Verdict 2.0 with ModernBERT-base (149.6M parameters), symmetric permutation-KL loss to eliminate option-order bias, and strict case hashing to keep the test set clean.

I just finished evaluating on the 2,000 held-out enterprise decisions from LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions.

1. Top-1 Accuracy: 77.10%

Ahead of both Laya's 421M ModernBERT-large (76.60%) and TypeSafe AI's Jev (72.70%). A 149.6M base encoder outperforming a model with 2.8x the parameters, on less than half the memory.

2. Solved the "Soft-Label Trap"

The benchmark scores Brier against soft human panel distributions and scores ECE against hard right or wrong. Those two objectives pull in opposite directions. Laya answers both with a single probability vector and lands at 0.2140 ECE.

Verdict 2.0 splits the output into two heads:
• Distribution head: 0.0636 Brier, 0.1513 ECE, 29% below Laya
• Confidence head: 0.0144 ECE (1.44%) and 0.7664 AUROC

3. Permutation Stability: 4.76% Flip Rate

Kev(another better oss jev version) reported a 7.41% flip rate when option positions were shuffled. Verdict 2.0 drops this to 4.76% across 2,918 permutations via symmetric KL training.

4. Production Gating with Selective Classification

Calibrated confidence enables safe automation thresholds:
• At 80% coverage: accuracy rises to 83.44%
• At 60% coverage: accuracy reaches 89.00%
• At 50% coverage: accuracy reaches 91.40%

Deterministic code can auto-route routine decisions and escalate low-confidence cases to humans.

5. Runs in the Browser via WebGPU

At 149.6M parameters it runs locally in browser tabs and edge runtimes, with no cloud dependency and no inference fees.

I Will be writing a full technical Article on the dual-channel calibration math, the option-pointer wiring fix, and training dynamics. If you want to catch the breakdown when it drops, drop a follow.

Link for the post-trained model and github repo are in the comments

t:
Jev 生态 72 小时：从 46 条到 160 条

Jev 把「判断」变成了一个足够便宜、可以在代码里直接调用的原语。然后开发者社区在 72 小时内把这句话翻译成了项目。

一、最热的方向：上下文压缩

tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction 现在 3,169 星，是目前最大的 Jev 项目。思路是把摘要换掉：不再让 LLM 重写一遍历史，而是让 Jev 给每条工具调用和结果打分，判断「这条还需要吗」，不需要就删，剩下的原文照旧。

实测 Claude Code 从 156,000 tokens 压到 62,000，使用率 78% → 31%，16 条里 10 条原文保留。已经出现 Codex 移植版和 Pi 移植版。

争议也最大：@theo 拿到 2,276 赞反对，认为压缩是重建而不是过滤，「根本不懂上下文管理」。

二、平台级仓库开始接入

· vercel-labs/json-render（16,439⭐）：生成式 UI 框架，compose 路径用 Jev 挑组件和动作
· vercel-labs/fx（3,057⭐）：Zig 写的类 Unix coding agent，内置 typesafe_permission_reviewer
· vercel-labs/ai-python（183⭐）：官方 Python SDK 的 evaluation op 支持 Jev
· cline/plugins：官方插件集里有  jev-browser
· Atomic（805⭐）：把 Jev 做成一级 structured-output provider，与其他 provider 共用 resolver

我拒掉 Coder 和 Mastra 的理由值得说明：它们只出现在价格表和模型能力目录里 ——  那是「认得这个模型」，不是「用它做决策」。

三、新长出四个领域

金融交易（本轮新开分类）
· Monad 上的链上交易机器人：Jev 看价格喂价决定买卖，每个 300ms 区块下一笔真实订单，代码和前端全开源
· Jevinik：抓实时行情与 Valyu 证据，判断某只股 30 天是否上涨
· jev_stock：港股短期方向预测，附首个交易日回测脚本

数据库
· jev() 是 PostgreSQL 扩展：WHERE jev(people, 'could work from home')，不要索引、不要 embedding
· DuckDB 扩展：给任意 CSV / Parquet / 表逐行分类，1000 行约 10 秒

创意
· jevinci：让 Jev 并行预测每个像素的颜色来作画，置信度决定笔触宽度

成本对照也开始出现了
· 724 条广告拆解 37 个品牌，提示词/格式/offer/CTA/落地页错配，9 分钱
· 3M 条回放事件 → 3,247 个会话、132 次暴怒点击、213 个修复 PR，$2.17
· 384 条新闻 → 给 15 个品牌挑今天该跟的选题，$0.19（同期 Opus 5 只跑了 4 条，花了 $0.77）

四、开源复刻潮

· jaredpalmer/kev（125⭐）：Qwen2.5-0.5B 上的迷你 Jev，MacBook 能训练能跑
· NanoJev（165⭐）：0.6B，输出完整概率分布、零 token 解码，附训练管线与数据集
· 中文社区盘点出至少五款：Laya 421M、Decider-2B、NanoJev 0.6B、Reflex、System-One 4B
· 另有兼容 Jev 的公开 API（Qwen3.6-35B-A3B）和「把任意 HF 模型 Jev 化」的库

五、最有价值的其实是反对意见

· @jiayuan_jy：研究一天后新鲜感回落 —— 「这好像就是一个更快的通用分类器，LLM 完全可以做到」，而且在世界知识不全的情况下，复杂场景的准确率要打问号
· @anderslie：Jev 快的关键不是训练而是推理技术（并行解码），任何开源权重模型都能改推理引擎暴露类似接口
· @iwashi86：用约 1 万次 API  调用反推 Jev 内部结构
· @0xBOYD：X 上热火朝天，Reddit 上只有 3 条帖子、其中 2 条还是他自己发的 —— 渠道不同，结论会完全不同

最后说清楚：这份清单不背书任何项目。160 条里有大量 0 星、一天写完的仓库，README 里的数字也不一定有出处。我为此加了两条规则 ——  同一作者的收录上限是滚动 7 天 3 条，共同发布日期视为风险信号。采用之前请自己跑一遍。

q.t:
Yes, classifiers existed. BERT, DeBERTa, GLiNER, fine-tuned heads. Most of them were specialized. Pick the labels, train, ship. Changing the rules at runtime meant another training run.

What we did not have was a general-purpose classifier at Terra / Sonnet 5 level intelligence.

You could fake it by asking an LLM for JSON, but that was slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated.

Jev is that missing piece. Labels defined in code, typed answer plus confidence, no extra LLM call.

Classification is not new. What is new is a general-purpose classifier this intelligent, this fast, and this cheap.

【Jevとは何か】

•ChatGPT系の研究に関わったDiogo AlmeidaのTypeSafe AIが、2年のステルス後に出した「System One」モデル。チャット用ではなく、ソフトが直接使う判断専用。
•文章をトークン生成せず、状態（テキスト等）に対して Choice / Score / Noul を並列評価し、選択肢・点数・確信度だけ返す。
•公称は70〜500ms、LLM比で20〜200倍速・40〜400倍安。入力 $0.042/百万トークン、出力は計測不能として無料。数字はJev向きタスクでのベンダー評価。
「ハルシネーションしない」の意味
•スキーマ外のラベルや壊れたJSONは出せない（タイプ安全）。
•候補の中から間違った答えを選ぶことはある。形式保証 ≠ 意味的正解。
向く用途
•エージェントのゲート：ツール許可、ポリシー違反、jailbreak、途中成果物の品質判定。「作るのはLLM、通すかはJev」。
•高頻度ルーティング：チケット振り分け、緊急度、詐欺スコア、請求・セキュリティの優先度。
•大量データの一括判定：ログ・契約・記事を安く全件スコアリング（例：777判断を0.7秒未満）。
•低遅延ガードレール：入力・出力の危険度を100ms前後で差し込む。
•相場まわりなら、予測そのものではなく「材料かノイズか」「出すか出さないか」「発注前のルール違反か」。
向かない用途
•チャット、長文、コード生成、説明、多段の自律計画、画像。より賢いChatGPTではない。
計算資源は減るか
•1判断あたりは減る。自己回帰生成がなく、複数質問を1回で並列処理し、出力が極小だから。
•ただし名前の由来（ジェヴォンズ）どおり、安くなると「毎回検証」「全件検査」が増え、総計算量は増える。
•既存のLLM分類の置換 → 資源減。今までやらなかった常時ゲート → 総量増。
•現時点はホストAPIのみ。ローカル実行・オープンウェイトなし。出力無料の持続性は未証明。
使い方の要点
•仕事を小さな判断に分解し、低確信度だけ人間か大型LLMへ上げる。
•閾値は自前データで校正する。誤分類が高い領域では第1段フィルタ以上にしない。

One of the best businesses to build with Jev is a local services matcher.

It's a form with a classifier behind it. 

Someone types what they need, and they get matched with a company near them before they close the tab.

Here's the whole setup:
1) Pick your area and a category with steady inbound. Driveway power washing is a good one.

2) Load Jev with the local businesses and what each one actually does.

3) Put a form in front of it. Someone types that they need their driveway power washed.

4) Jev reads that against every business you loaded and returns percentages on which ones fit.

5) The person gets the match in seconds, on the page, before they've gone anywhere else.

6) That person becomes your client later, because you were the one who answered.

Step 6 only works because of step 5. Every "get an instant quote" form on the internet promises an answer and then sends "we'll email you by end of day."

The speed is the thing the client notices. 

It tells them you're not trying to waste their time, and you're not trying to waste your own.

Find the inbound that's piling up somewhere, put Jev at the front of it, and answer people while they're still on the page.

X 上也突然被这个模型刷屏，它就叫 Jev

Jev 和我们熟悉的 GPT、Claude 很不一样，他不是为了聊天而生的

也不是为了写文章或者是生成代码，它只负责一件事：

帮操作或者模型，快速做决定

比如 Agent 运行的时候，可以让 Jev 判断该用哪个模型、加载哪个 Skill、Tool Call 风险高不高，下一步继续还是重试。

我列出了几组比较夸张的数据：

1、延迟：70–500ms
2、价格：$0.042 / 1M 输入 Token
3、官方 Benchmark：最高 193× 更快
4、成本：最高 444× 更便宜

这个方向我觉得挺有意思，以后的 Agent 可能根本不需要所有事情都交给 GPT、Claude 这种大模型。

A new benchmark called  JevBench just dropped.

for models whose output is a bounded software decision rather than open-ended prose and follows TypeSafe’s 15 Sept release of Jev, which takes application state plus fixed choices and returns a typed answer with probabilities instead of prose.

This benchmark's score deliberately combines Intelligence, Calibration, Speed and Cost because deployment can fail even when raw accuracy is high.

e.g. GPT-5.6 Luna records substantially higher hard-case accuracy than Jev 1.13.0, yet Jev leads the composite because the benchmark also prices latency, calibration and cost.

The geometric mean prevents exceptional performance on 1 axis from fully compensating for a weak one.

The result is evidence about a narrow typed-decision workload, not evidence that Jev is generally more capable than GPT-5.6 Luna.

People look at this and keep saying "you need to sell/market yourselves well" (pro tip: none of the ppl saying this, understand what this is all about)

But, that's what the laya author is actually doing right now pretty cleverly (or naively) by overstating and broadening the claims of their work, because their 2025 work wasn't "Jev/Jev-like" at all. It shared "one" ingredient with jev, RL for a non-generative prediction, but it was not the general jev-like system now being implied, and even that wasn't novel.

First, Jev isn't just "a classifier + RL". It takes arbitrary state + typed questions (yes/no, choice, score) and returns calibrated probability distributions in parallel. RLCD trains for calibrated decisions and the same model is meant to generalize across many task types.

Their sales RL agent was embeddings -> small network -> PPO -> one 0-1 sales conversion probability, trained on synthetic sales chats. RL Classification itself wasn't new as well. DQN Classifiers were done in 2020, PPO multi-label classifications were demoed in 2022, much before their work, so it was building on that work already, not a novel approach.

tr: I'm Diego Almeida, founder of Typesafe AI, and at OpenAI, I co-created ChatGBT and RLHF, the post-training algorithm behind most frontier AI. Our team trained the first models to be superhuman at instruction following, what we now call Chat. And we asked ourselves, are models that are superhuman at Chat AGI? The answer was obviously not, but the trillion dollar question is why not? RLHF has led to LMs that are optimizing for human preferences and include issues such as mode dropping, overconfidence, and an overall lack of reliability. These flaws mean that LMs require humans in the loop, and almost no true automation can be done. At Typesafe, we've spent two years building in stealth, and we're finally ready to share our new type of foundation model that's optimized for automation. System 1 models. With a new architecture, new sampler, and new training algorithm, reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions. Movements are clear if you see them side by side. Ask a System 1 model a ton of structured questions, just like you would an LM. Get the answers back near instantly. Meanwhile, LMs take hundreds of times longer to finish responding. Look at how the LM generates sequentially, which is great for a natural conversation, but totally useless for computers. LMs extract intelligence from the tiny straw of auto regression, and similar to the jump that transformers made over RNMs, We are replacing sequential computation with parallel, because that is obviously the future. Our System 1 models output decisions with probabilities and confidence instead of words, and they can't hallucinate. They're a lot more like code, reliable, fast, self-consistent, and Typesafe. This opens up a whole new world of possibilities and applications. Today, we're releasing JIV, the first public System 1 model. It's 100 times faster, so real-time AI is finally possible. This is cheaper with input tokens priced at $42 per billion tokens, and output tokens are free because they're finally too f***ing cheap to meter. JIV is super smart, and its intelligence per dollar is literally off the charts. This is just the beginning. We're excited to see what you build with JIV. As we say at Typesafe, we're building prod, not God. We're waiting seconds for responses or paying for words you never asked for. Side effects may include fewer retries, fewer parsers, fewer broken schemas, and intelligence running inside every software loop. Your software may begin moderating every message, routing every ticket, reviewing every document, and making millions of background decisions that were previously too slow or expensive to automate. Entire software categories may be rewritten in the process. As costs fall, usage may increase dramatically. Ask your developer if your industry is ready.

after Jev, I'm seeing threads about the comeback of encoder-only models, which I don't get. What we should be celebrating is the comeback of discriminative models. Both encoder and decoder can be forced to have discriminative outputs. Most jina models today are discriminative and decoder-only.

I haven't tried Jev yet, just got off the waiting list an hour ago. Internally we tried to mimic Jev's I/O, and the closest thing we have is jina-reranker-v3.5, a listwise reranker with discriminative outputs. It's natural to formulate a question-decisions as a prompt, where the "yes"/"no" decisions aren't embedded independently but always in the context of the question. For embedding models it's hard to mimic that interface, because you lose the context. For classic bi-encoder pairwise reranker it’s also not possible, only jina-v3/v3.5 listwise reranker make them remotely close to Jev’s IO.

Need to try more and read more later.

Seems to me that the best application for @typesafeai System One models will be: *the AI router / controller* of the system. Let me explain... 

This demo by @allietheicon of Jev's real-world capabilities is incredibly cool.

Traditionally in automation engineering there are 3 main building blocks: sensors (get info), actuators (perform actions) and controllers (decide what to do). It seems to me that a very compelling AI system design going forward will have System One-like model right at the input of the system playing a role of controller/gateway/router that then decides incredibly fast: 1) perform a deterministic action, 2) delegate to an LLM, 3) loop back or exit.

Performance characteristics match well with a general concept of a router. In a way it's reminiscent of Karpathy's "cognitive core" idea

It'll be interesting to see the architectures that will pop-up: system-one + LLMs + code-mode + realtime. https://x.com/karpathy/status/1938626382248149433

q.t:
The race for LLM "cognitive core" - a few billion param model that maximally sacrifices encyclopedic knowledge for capability. It lives always-on and by default on every computer as the kernel of LLM personal computing.
Its features are slowly crystalizing:

- Natively multimodal text/vision/audio at both input and output.
- Matryoshka-style architecture allowing a dial of capability up and down at test time.
- Reasoning, also with a dial. (system 2)
- Aggressively tool-using.
- On-device finetuning LoRA slots for test-time training, personalization and customization.
- Delegates and double checks just the right parts with the oracles in the cloud if internet is available.

It doesn't know that William the Conqueror's reign ended in September 9 1087, but it vaguely recognizes the name and can look up the date. It can't recite the SHA-256 of empty string as e3b0c442..., but it can calculate it quickly should you really want it.

What LLM personal computing lacks in broad world knowledge and top tier problem-solving capability it will make up in super low interaction latency (especially as multimodal matures), direct / private access to data and state, offline continuity, sovereignty ("not your weights not your brain"). i.e. many of the same reasons we like, use and buy personal computers instead of having thin clients access a cloud via remote desktop or so.

One of the playground examples was a rudimentary chat.

It wasn’t until two years later that OpenAI released a productized version with ChatGPT which of course changed the world

The big themes I've been working on this year are: multi-model systems, specializing models for specific tasks, "thinking fast and slow" using multiple models/loops/prompts together in one application, and co-design of harnesses/tooling and models.

The big release today from @typesafeai touches on all of these! Their new model, Jev, fills a big, big gap in our multi-model toolkit.

I'm obsessed with building realtime systems. Voice agents, physical AI, new kinds of human-in-the-loop software.

We often build voice agent front-end loops that need to drive a variety of backend systems, ranging from extremely big and slow (for example, coding agents) to super-fast and specialized (think vision systems and classifiers).

When we're doing things like updating a dynamic user interface, we want to generate small bundles of error-free, strongly typed, structured data ... many times a second. But we also want to leverage the flexibility and natural language abilities of LLMs.

I think of this as pulling out a subset of the context from the long-running human interaction (voice and text conversation), combining that context with other state the application is managing, prompting an LLM, and getting back structured data. We build with this pattern a lot. (There's a whole section of the Pipecat docs about the `UIWorker` pattern.) 

But even small-ish, fast LLMs take a few hundred milliseconds to generate ~100 tokens of structured data one token at a time. However, this is a parallelizable operation and it's right in Jev's wheelhouse.

This is the first model release in a while that feels to me like a genuinely new architecture solution to one of our big, interesting, hairy, real-world pain points as we figure out how to design new, AI-native systems.

I also really love the fact that the second post in the thread below starts out: "The gains aren’t free: Jev can't generate text".

One of the things that drives me crazy about some of the scaling-is-all-you-need discourse around models is that there are *always* systems engineering trade-offs, and they *really* matter.

There are lots and lots of exciting things to build in this new era of LLMs and generative AI. Making things that are fast enough, reliable enough, and affordable enough that people will actually use them is going to require creative exploration of a very wide design space!

I'm super-excited about Jev. Congratulations to the Typesafe team.

■ 補足
Jevの面白さは「小さいLLMを高速化した」ことではなく、そもそも生成方法が違う点。

通常のLLMはtokenを1つずつ生成しますが、Jevは自由文を作らず、あらかじめ定義した候補に対する確率をまとめて返す。なので「fraud > 90%なら人間に回す」のように、そのままシステムへ組み込みやすい。

公称では応答70〜500ms、特定タスクで40〜200倍高速、入力100万token $0.042、出力tokenは無料。

ただし「ハルシネーションしない」は、何でも正解するという意味ではないです。自由文を生成しないので、想定外の形式を返しにくいという話。第三者テストでも速度・コストは圧倒的でしたが、一部の判定精度は既存LLMが上でした。

GPT / Claude系は複雑な推論・生成、Jev系は大量・高速な分類や判定。この棲み分けはAIエージェント時代にかなり相性が良さそうです。

tr: I will say that I might speedrun through this, feel free if you don't disagree with something to yell out. It's way more fun for me if things get interactive. Otherwise, I will go through this. First, can I have a vague show of hands of who knows what RLHF is? Oh, excellent. I might be able to skip through that part quickly and get into the interactive stuff. So my name's Diego Almeida. I'm talking about what's next after RLHF. More accurately, I think this should be called what's next after the chat GPT era that I think we're all in. And my hint for you guys is it is not the quad code era. I will justify this later on, but I actually believe them to be part of the same era. Why should you listen to me? I was co-author to, what is basically OpenAI's greatest hits, at least published hits, co-author to GPT for chat GPT, RLHF slash instructor GPT. The team I was part of basically invented post-training as a concept, so very qualified on a lot of this stuff. But what makes me somewhat unique here is that I'm one of the few people at OpenAI who actually hates on chat GPT. Thank you. I don't hate chat GPT as a product to be clear. I think chat GPT is a world-changing product that will probably stay with us for the rest of time unless something better comes up. But I also acknowledge its limitations. I think a lot of what's happened in the state of the field can be traced back to minor decisions we made in making the algorithms behind chat GPT. I feel like the question that's relevant to everyone in AI right now is what's actually going on. There's a lot of differing opinions, and I think it's really useful to map out the spectrum and figure out how can smart people have such different opinions. There's CULT1. AI is not just going well, it's going insanely well. Every single benchmark we surpass human level, and as far as we can measure, we are continuously surpassing human performance, basically every new benchmark, and it's only getting faster and accelerating. You have every, can I see my mouth, excellent. Basically every NLP benchmark is getting crushed, and not only that, allegedly the time that LLMs can operate autonomously is growing exponentially. On the other hand, you have AI is not just going poorly, it's going insanely poorly, AI is a bubble, it's basically generating no value, it's just circular financing deals, et cetera, et cetera, and if AI is so great, why is everything just like a chat app right now? Or like a cloud code thing? And a lot of the people have actually kind of given up on what was the old guards terminology of a transformative AI revolution. People aren't really talking about that anymore, they're talking about it being massively valuable, like B2B SaaS. So the only thing that everyone agrees on is like there's just these extreme points of view and like nothing in between, and everyone basically thinks AI is insane, but like for different reasons, and what I would want to talk about is what is the sane view of AI? Let's take all the evidence of like CULT1, it's going super well, take all the evidence of CULT2, it's going super poorly, like you know map them out and try to explain what explains that divide. Like what is the simplest possible explanation of why some things are too good to be true and some things are not just bad, they are so bad that we would still employ human workers to do like kind of like dumb tasks. No offense to any of them, a lot of these tasks on the right seem way, way, way easier than the stuff on the left. Like how can we be solving like unsolved math problems, but still customer service requires like humans in the loop in order to actually like make decisions? This I think is like kind of like a wild state of affairs and in my opinion, anyone who works adjacent to AI should have an answer to this because this is like the evidence in the field right now. I would normally pause and ask people if they want to yell out their thoughts on this but I don't think we have time for that and I've been told to not take Q and A until after but I'll just give you my answer to this which is in my opinion the simplest explanation. All the stuff in the left is not just a task that happens to have a human in the loop. In the left, the task, the goal of it is to please the human in the loop. These tasks are intrinsically human in the loop tasks. The like Claude code's job is not to just make code work. The way it converses would be totally different. The goal is to please the human in it and on the other side all of these tasks that seem way more basic, the goal is to not have removed the human loop. Ideally it would be running in the background in a server that you never even look at and ideally it eventually becomes like legacy software that you don't really worry about. So and this is the divide between assistance and automation. Lesson one for my talk is that today's AI, everything inherited from RLHF is incredible at the human in the loop stuff but not for automation ta
