I spent some time looking through what people are actually building with Jev on GitHub.

The ecosystem is moving surprisingly fast, and the most interesting pattern isn't using Jev as another LLM.

It's using Jev as a fast decision layer around existing systems.

Here are 10 of the most popular and interesting Jev-related repos I found:

① browser-use/jev-ultrafast — ★4.8K
Probably the clearest example of where Jev fits.
Jev handles browser actions and target element selection, while a small LLM is only called when text actually needs to be generated.
Observe → Decide → Execute → Repeat.
https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast

② tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction — ★2.7K
Uses Jev to identify unnecessary tool calls and results in Claude Code history and compact them while preserving the important context.
Really interesting use of Jev inside the coding-agent harness itself.
https://github.com/tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction

③ TheoLeeCJ/SemIf — ★1.5K
An independent open-source exploration of the same general idea behind fast choice evaluation.
It uses open models to directly evaluate probabilities across possible choices and can run locally.
Not the official Jev model, but an interesting direction for understanding where this architecture could go.
https://github.com/TheoLeeCJ/SemIf

④ vinnylarouge/jevlike — ★850
Another independent research project exploring how to train small models to evaluate variable sets of choices simultaneously.
Again, not an open-source version of TypeSafe's Jev, but interesting research around the same decision-model paradigm.
https://github.com/vinnylarouge/jevlike

⑤ jarrodwatts/jev-trader — ★800
An experimental trading bot using Jev to make trading decisions on Kuru on Monad.
It's primarily a dry-run/mock experiment and obviously doesn't prove profitability, but it's a good example of putting Jev inside a continuous decision loop.
https://github.com/jarrodwatts/jev-trader

⑥ TianyuCodings/NanoJev — ★310
A Qwen3-0.6B-based parallel decision model with open weights and training code.
One of the more interesting attempts to explore Jev-like decision models locally.
https://github.com/TianyuCodings/NanoJev

⑦ thruwire/foreman — ★280
Jev acts as a supervisor for Codex.
Codex writes the code while Jev continuously evaluates whether the work is complete, whether verification is needed, whether the agent is stuck, or whether human intervention is required.
Jev doesn't replace the coding agent — it watches it.
https://github.com/thruwire/foreman

⑧ fhshaik/typesafe-mario — ★260

q.t:
We just ran Jev on our WebMCP benchmark.

The result: basically broke the benchmark.

Jev + Mercury 2.5 (a fast, low-cost LLM) using WebMCP solved 100% of the tasks at roughly 112× lower model cost than GPT-6 Astra using computer use with code execution. Compared to Astra using screenshot-based computer use, the model cost was 245× lower (!). 

We also compared Jev operating the browser with and without WebMCP. 

We used Browser Use’s open-source Ultrafast, with some improvements to the harness to make it more reliable across the benchmark. 

Jev’s browser-control accuracy on its own was not amazing - adding WebMCP nearly doubled the number of solved tasks, from 25/49 to 49/49, while reducing model cost by 18% (more on why below).

The benchmark and methodology are fully open and reproducible.

Full results: https://webmcp.com/benchmark

A few words on how the Jev + WebMCP harness works and why this is exciting:

Jev receives text as input and a set of discrete options it can choose from.  With WebMCP, those options are the tools exposed by the website. At each step, Jev sees the task, the available tools and previous results, then picks what to do next.

The limitation is that Jev can’t generate arbitrary text, which you need for tool arguments. For example, it can choose the search_products tool, but it can’t generate the search query itself.

So we split the work: Jev picks the tool and Mercury 2.5 generates the arguments if needed. 

This works well because turns out most of the cognitive load in these tasks is around choosing the right action. The argument generation itself is relatively simple, so we can delegate to a small and very fast model. We used Mercury, which outputs 1,000+ tokens/sec and is very cheap.

The result is a pretty simple combination: Jev for tool selection + Mercury for arguments + WebMCP for the interface. It ends up being very reliable, very fast, and very cheap.

A few words about Ultrafast and why do we think it underperforms:

Without WebMCP, Jev chooses from the page’s controls: which button to click, which field to fill, or which option to select. 

But choosing a valid button is different from choosing the right next step. The agent still has to navigate menus, understand forms, recover from errors  and recognize when the task is actually complete.

Our hypothesis is that WebMCP makes the decision space much simpler. Instead of figuring out a sequence of clicks through a website, Jev chooses explicit actions that directly advance the task. 

@typesafeai itself documents weaker accuracy on questions requiring multiple reasoning steps. WebMCP moves much of that complexity into the website’s tools, leaving Jev with clearer decisions and fewer opportunities to go wrong (in a sense WebMCP "compresses" a sequence of clicks into one tool call).

Our modified Ultrafast setup solved 25/49 tasks - that is a result for our particular implementation and benchmark, not a universal limit on Jev or Browser Use. We are open to more harness optimization to get this result to perform better, feel free to directly contribute to the benchmark here: https://github.com/nekuda-ai/WindTunnel

Browser-use ultrafast: https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast

@fakegingerbitch asked and I checked.

Here is what I quickly found:

TypeSafe sells its AI model Jev on one promise: when it says "70% likely", it's right about 70% of the time.

I tested that on 8 real datasets — loan defaults, bankruptcies, medical diagnoses, marketing responses. 16,500 predictions.

It fails on 7 of 8.

Jev is 10× more miscalibrated than CatBoost, a standard model anyone can download for free. On average it's no more useful than guessing the overall rate for every single case.

And it fails in one direction: it thinks bad things are about twice as likely as they really are. Loan defaults, bankruptcies, disease — all overstated, on every dataset.

German loan data: applicants flagged "critical account" repay 83% of the time. Jev says 26%.

The fix takes 120 rows of data and a textbook method from 2017. 

It removes three quarters of the error. A model that was actually calibrated would gain nothing from that.

Calibration is something you measure. Not something you announce.

TypeSafe AI came out of stealth with Jev, and access is behind a waitlist.

I built an open source version Verdict (Open-jev) you can run right now in a browser tab: And its a real post trained model..(link in comments)

It is a post trained 151M parameters model. ModernBERT-base with a GLiClass head. Instead of token-by-token autoregressive decoding or JSON string parsing, it takes an input text and candidate options, then returns calibrated probabilities and an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome in a single forward pass.

Some of The numbers:

Calibration: 0.83% adaptive expected calibration error on 1,000 held-out cases. I trained with a multi-class Brier score term, then tried standard post-hoc temperature scaling. Temperature scaling degraded the metrics, so the model ships with temperature 1.0.

Order invariance: reversing the option list flips 3.0% of predictions across 1,000 cases. For reference, another open Jev reproduction measured a frozen Qwen3.5-4B at 27.8% flips on the same perturbation, though on their own 36-case fixture rather than mine. Full bidirectional attention evaluates the candidate list simultaneously instead of scanning left to right.

Shuffled-context control: Pairing questions with the wrong document drops accuracy from 95.0% to 22.4% and drives abstention from 21.8% to 72.7%, confirming the model actively conditions on the context.

Latency: 89ms median in-browser via WebGPU, and 35.6ms via ONNX on CPU at 5 candidates.

The negative results:

I ran 12 use cases on public data across both checkpoints and three label framings three passed the promotion gate. Passage re-ranking hit 11.9%, jailbreak screening 34.9%, and phishing detection 57.5%. 

On 337 cases from TypeSafe's public evaluation set, Jev reaches 90.8%, a 26B diffusion model reaches 88.4%, and Verdict reaches 48.1%.which is expected since its just 151M param model but working on trying it on bigger scale as well.

A 151M encoder is calibrated, order-invariant, and fast, but it lacks broad world knowledge. 

In a tiered architecture where a cheap model gates an expensive one, knowing exact failure boundaries is essential. 48 of the 50 classification errors fall below a 0.95 confidence threshold, making the gate predictable.

For the next steps i will be testing the same harness on a larger backbone a bigger model with more params to see whether order invariance holds at scale or depends strictly on bidirectional attention.

In my mind, the excitement and potential around Jev is related to that of model routing and posttraining - in a world where intelligence is abundant, how do you best optimize it for a
specific task? 

By optimizing the harness, model weights, or model architecture itself, you can push the frontier of accuracy / cost / latency

.@jonptaylor recorded a detailed walkthough of Jev vs GPT-5.6 Luna as the "operator" element of a Pipecat speech interface pipeline.

GPT-5.6 Luna:

  - 81.3% command accuracy
  - 1,008 ms median latency

Jev
  - 92.6% command accuracy
  - 296 ms median latency
  
A few notes here ...

1) We expected to see a big latency benefit. But the higher accuracy is maybe more interesting. Jev (with a bunch of code wrapped around it) is much better at turning messy transcriptions from a noisy speech environment into correct command structs.

The very hand-wavy explanation here is something like: LLM tool calling is an amazingly flexible, general capability but is only one thing that LLMs are trained to do. Jev is trained to do a narrower thing: to produce probabilities over a fixed set of options.

If we can express our tool calling requirements as fixed set of choices, it's perhaps not surprising that the model trained specifically and only to evaluate choices does a better job at that task.

Some keywords to talk to your friendly neighborhood LLM about this topic, if you're interested in a deeper dive, are: discriminative vs generative models, calibrated probabilities, constrained decoding, and closed-set vs open-set prediction.

Note that this is GPT-5.6 Luna without reasoning enabled. With reasoning, today's LLMs are going to do much better on evals like this. Reasoning lets models build a scratch pad of options, which is massively helpful in classification tasks. But we generally can't use models in reasoning/thinking mode for applications like voice agents or voice user interfaces, because the latency is too high.
  
2) An application-specific eval lets us make informed choices about whether we're getting measurable benefits from different models and different architectures. It's gotten a lot easier to build pretty good, very specific evals as part of agent development. Fable and Astra know how to do this and mostly get things right without a lot of guidance.

3) Using Jev feels more like programming than using an LLM does. Mostly, with LLMs, we're doing "context engineering." Which is just a fancy way of saying we're trying to feed the LLM a big pile of natural language and hoping we're aiming for the right part of the latent space.

In most of our sophisticated agents, there's a lot of code to do this context engineering: constant summarization, switching prompts for different parts of the conversation, etc. But the end result is always just really long prompt strings!

With Jev, we're sending the model natural language, but in addition we're doing very explicit mapping between application state and Jev's input data structures.
tr: Oof, jeff is a pretty big step forward for voice interfaces, and if you're building one the results are quite hard to ignore. We've been trying it out in Jamcat, our experimental thing for music generation and live jamming, built of course with Pipecat. Everything is controlled by voice, so latency and accuracy aren't background details, they're a core part of a good performance. If the app misunderstands you or responds late, you don't just notice some lag or delay, you miss the beat and maybe clear the dance floor. Here's the TLDR of how Jamcat works. Pipecat coordinates three specialists, the producer, which decides which sound should be played, the composer, that turns your text and audio prompts into music, and finally the operator, Jamcat's silent UI worker, which turns spoken commands into UI actions driving the whole experience. The operator is the immediate place where jeff has the biggest potential. Before we were using GPT 5.6 Luna, a fast, capable, general purpose LLM that handled commands by writing tool calls. Since Pipecat can orchestrate, well, anything, we swapped in jeff and measured what changed. The latency gain is almost immediately noticeable, it's night and day, but the accuracy is actually the more interesting story, at least to me, because of where it comes from, and that's bad speech recognition. By the time our operator receives a transcript from the user, it's likely some of the words have been incorrectly heard. This is really normal and LLMs are pretty good at figuring out what you actually intended to say. Play the core us becomes play the chorus. On mute becomes unmute and so on. The right corrections are not a guarantee, though, and can lead to an LLM making the wrong decision, taking too long to figure it out, or just ignoring it entirely. Now, most speech-to-text providers do accept a key term list to bias a user's input, but they typically recommend concentrating on 20-50 of the most important, with a hard cap of around 500 tokens. That helps, but it isn't a silver bullet. A fixed list can pull recognition both ways, and it can't know dynamic elements such as what you named a track or seen about 30 seconds ago. Our operator will likely always have to cope with a bad transcript. Now, this isn't the fault of the speech-to-text services, those are brilliant, but when you are working in noisy environments or with different accents and so on, getting a good transcript is really important for voice UI, and this is where Jeff can make a huge difference. The user's input can remain conversational and open-ended, but the controls our app has over the UI is not. The app already knows the valid commands and things that it can act on, so Jeff can choose among those and make the probabilistic bets as to what action the user actually wanted based on the state of our session. So, we built out this little benchmarking tool, or to be more accurate, it's an experiment, I guess, since we don't really have all that much data, but the idea was to see what Jeff could improve about the Jamcat experience. It runs 230 commands against the same live bot, that's 100 clean commands, the same 100 again, but with realistic speech-to-text mistakes, and 30 lines of ordinary chatter where the right answer is to do nothing. Every case runs through Jeff and the baseline, and it only counts if the command and its arguments were correct. That lets us look at clean speech, misheard speech, ordinary talk, and everything combined, and see where each approach is stronger. And we can see how with a blunder like Play the Core Us, Jeff recovers it to chorus in just 294 milliseconds, whereas our baseline takes 1.2 seconds and returns no command. So these overall numbers are interesting and pretty useful, but it does hide the real story. If you break the benchmark down by what speech-to-text handed us, things start to come a little bit more into focus. On clean commands, both systems were perfect. On ordinary talk, both stayed quiet every time. The gap appears when the speech-to-text gets the words wrong. The LLM returned no command on 39% of these garbled inputs. Jeff, though, did that on just 6%. For a chat model, doing nothing can, of course, be the safe choice, but in a live Jam situation like we have here, well, it's a bit more risky. The biggest gap was on words that merely sound alike, like pose for pause or stomp for stop. Jeff recovered 80% of those, whereas the LLM recovered just 10. And this is why Jeff fits the Jamcat use case so well. It can choose between things the app already knows, so that's mute or unmute, bass or chords, verse or chorus, even when the transcript it receives is messy. But it's not all sunshines and rainbows, though. The flip side is that Jeff picks, it doesn't write. It can't simply return an open-ended number or a new name, and long command chains do distract it. That's why these results don't come from just Jeff alone. They come from the pipecat harness we've built around it. Insi

Anyone testing Jev on messy business workflows?

For the last 9 hours, I haven’t stopped testing different marketing use cases for Jev.

Here are 6 of the most interesting ones I found:

1. SEO/AEO opportunity detection:

Pull ideas from customer calls, sales calls, internal meetings, and old content. Jev took 40 ideas, checked what was already covered, and cut them down to 10 worth pursuing.

2. Content deduplication:

Give it those 50 ideas plus your existing site. Jev can remove the 40 that overlap with content you already published, explain why, and send the remaining 10 into drafting.

3.Content quality scoring:

Run clips through Jev before publishing. In one test, it checked for complete thoughts, missing context, visual proof, and topic value in a 204ms median response.

4. X Content pattern analysis:

Feed it your published content plus performance data. Jev can compare engagement by hook, spot the formats that keep working, and tell you which patterns deserve more output.

5. Customer health scoring:

Combine account data, open issues, seat requests, and expansion signals. Jev can separate accounts that need attention from customers showing clear PQL signals like asking for more seats.

6. Product friction detection:

Run onboarding and customer data through the same layer every week. Jev can surface where new users keep getting stuck, then turn those recurring problems into a short list for product to fix.

q.t:
I shared 10 Jev use cases for marketers.

Here are 10 more:

11. Ad creative scoring - Feed it 100 ad variations. Jev can score which hooks, headlines, or angles are most worth testing first.

12. Social post filtering - Monitor thousands of posts. Jev can flag the ones worth replying to, reposting, or using as sales signals.

13. ICP detection - Give it a company, profile, or website. Jev can score how closely it matches your ideal customer.

14. Buying signal detection - Someone posts that they're switching tools, hiring, raising money, or struggling with a problem. 

15. Comment prioritization - Get hundreds of comments across LinkedIn, X, YouTube, or Product Hunt. Jev can score which ones deserve a reply first.

16. Review analysis - Feed it thousands of customer reviews. Jev can classify sentiment, complaints, feature requests, and purchase intent.

17. Influencer matching - Give it 5,000 creators. Jev can score which ones best match your product, audience, and campaign.

18. Sponsorship qualification - Feed it newsletters, podcasts, or creator media kits. Jev can score audience fit, relevance, and whether they're worth reviewing.

19. UGC selection - Give it dozens of videos, screenshots, and testimonials. Jev can score which ones are strongest for ads or landing pages.

20. Product Hunt monitoring - Scan launches, comments, and makers to find competitors, customers, partners, or interesting products.

The more repetitive marketing decisions you have to make at scale, the more interesting Jev becomes.

q.t:
知道了 Jev 能用在哪

这条直接帮你梳理这些场景适不适合你，
以及能不能自己跑通闭环：

1. 操作电脑  
适合已经在用 Codex / Claude Code，但嫌 computer use 又慢又卡的人。  

简单动作可以闭环：Jev 判断点哪里，Agent 直接执行；复杂界面仍建议留人工接管。

2. 操作浏览器  
适合要自动搜、比价、填表、做网页流程的运营和开发。  

目标窄、按钮有限时能闭环；
页面一乱、要自己理解新站点，就还得大模型补位。

3. 海量分流和分类  
适合客服、运营、公关这种每天要处理大量进件的人。  

高置信度可以全自动分部门、打标签；
拿不准的再转人工，这是最容易先跑通的闭环。

4. 模型路由  
适合自己做 AI 产品、背后挂了好几个模型的人。
  
闭环很完整：用户一句话进来，Jev 选模型，生成接口直接出活。

5. 内容批量分析  
适合创作者、增长，想搞清楚「什么内容真的涨」。 
 
单次分析不是闭环，只是出结论；把结果接回「写稿 → 打分 → 再写」才算闭环。

6. 信息流过滤  
适合时间线被广告、引战、回复侠刷屏的人。 
 
可以闭环：帖子出现 → Jev 判断 → 隐藏或留下，人不用再看第二眼。

7. 代码审查和安全门禁  
适合带团队的开发，以及会自动改代码、跑命令的 Agent

不建议全自动闭环。高置信度拦截可以自己完成，放行和合并还是留给人或大模型。

8. 交易决策  
适合在做策略、回测、交易机器人的人。  

演示里可以闭环：价格进来，买或卖出去。真金白银不要全交给它，低置信度和风控必须留人手。

9. 游戏和实时控制  
适合做游戏 AI、实时控制和高频 Agent 的人。
  
天生就是闭环：状态进来，100 毫秒给出动作，环境更新后再判断下一拍。

Jev 负责判断，
闭环成不成，看你有没有把「判断之后的那一下」接好~

q.t:
Jevのキラーアプリ、「意味で探す grep」を作った。

semgrep -e "顧客が怒っている" と打つと、"angry" も「怒」も含まない行まで拾ってきます。

正規表現の代わりに、TypeSafe AI の Jev（System One モデル）に 1 行ずつ「この行は○○の意味に合うか」を yes/no 確率で答えさせる。Jevの特性を活かして30 行をまとめて 1 リクエスト、200 行のログが 1 秒弱で返ります。依存ゼロ、Node 1 ファイル。

grepに準じるオプション体系。

・-e A -e B で OR、-a で AND、-v で AND NOT
・-r で再帰、-l でファイル名だけ、-A/-B/-C で前後の行、--color
・確率の閾値は --level loose / strict で調整

ベクトル検索と何が違うかというと、否定検索もできるし、話題の近さではなく「命題が成り立つか」を見るところです。「返金してほしい」と「返金処理が完了しました」は埋め込みではほぼ同じ距離ですが、「顧客が返金を求めている」という意味で引くと 0.98 と 0.10 に分かれます。だから AND や NOT がそのままブール演算として効きます。「返金の話だが要求ではない行」なども 1 コマンドで検索できます。

問合せは「意味」でおこなうので、多言語検索が普通に可能。日本語と英語の区別もフランス語もロシア語も、その混在文書からも検索できます。仏・露・独・西・中・韓14行を4言語（日・英・仏・露）の意味クエリで検証した結果、取りこぼしも誤爆もゼロで、どの言語で意味を書いても同様に機能します。

以下で試せます。
npx @uehaj/semgrep -e "ネットワーク障害" app.log

GitHub: https://github.com/uehaj/jev-semgrep

t:
但天下武功唯快不破, 这玩意从输入到输出最快只需要70ms!

所以完全可以用在高频的生产级场景, 比如接到堡垒机里面实时判断用户输入的shell命令是否存在危险(rm -rf /). 再加上输入每百万token只需要$0.042, 输出不要钱. 妥妥的新一代flash模型斩杀线(有的flash模型会被企业用作决策器).

说完了用途再来看它的架构, 传统大模型有多少token就要把激活参数过多少遍(前向传播)所以特别吃显存带宽, 而这个模型设计了一个特殊的并行采样架构, 只需要一次前向传播, 就能输出所有预设schema字段的离散预测与分支概率. 达成了极低的延迟.

而推出Jev的 TypeSafe AI 这个公司也很有噱头, 它是 Diogo Almeida 一手创办的, 就是他曾经在 OpenAI 的 InstructGPT 和早期 RLHF（基于人类反馈的强化学习) 团队中的贡献才有了如今的ChatGPT.

最后说一下目前模型的限制, 首先由于没有本土节点, 所以虽然它只需要70ms, 但是到美西这海底光缆延迟120ms是躲不掉的, 所以至少还是200ms打底. 另外, 模型被官方称为 System One 模型, 所以理想搭配还需要一个 System Two 模型用来进行战略判断, 然后生成策略当作提示词输入进去, 这样才能提升模型的输出质量.

另外, 官网还在申请使用, 不过vercel的AI Gateway已经能直接用了, 所以想测试的同学直接去vercel用就行.

t:
不知道中文圈有没有人解释过，Jev 这个 System One（第一系统）到底是什么意思。

这个概念来源于卡尼曼的《思考，快与慢》。书中把人的认知活动粗略分成两个系统：

第一系统是“快思考”，负责快速反应、直觉判断和近乎下意识的决策。

第二系统是“慢思考”，负责更复杂的全局分析、逻辑推理和需要集中注意力的问题。

Jev 的意思是，他们想给 AI 做一个类似“第一系统”的东西。

今天的大模型其实非常偏向第二系统。哪怕只是判断 A、B、C 三个选项哪个更合适，我们也经常让一个大型 decoder 模型读取上下文，在自然语言和 token 空间里进行推理，再生成一段文字或者 JSON，最后由程序把它重新解析成一个选项。

但很多任务根本不需要“说人话”。

如果问题只是：该调用哪个工具？哪个文件最相关？这个结果是否正确？应该继续、重试还是停止？那么机器真正需要的可能只是：

状态 → 判断 → 行动

而不是：

状态 → 自然语言思考 → 自然语言输出 → JSON → Parser → 行动

Jev 所代表的 System One 路线，就是试图砍掉中间这一大段语言生成过程，直接根据当前状态，对候选选项进行快速判断。

这让我觉得未来的 AI 很可能也会逐渐形成“快与慢”两个系统。

一个可能是很小、很快、常驻的 Jev-ish 模型，负责分类、路由、排序、工具选择、继续/停止以及大量近乎“下意识”的微决策。

另一个则是 Flash-ish 的大型生成和推理模型，负责真正困难、陌生、开放的问题，以及最终与人类进行自然语言交流。

前者可能根本不需要说人话，甚至不需要拥有传统意义上的“语言”。后者才需要承担语言、复杂推理和创造。

更有意思的是，慢系统解决过的问题还可以不断蒸馏给快系统：

第一次遇到陌生问题，需要认真思考；

做过一千次以后，就变成了直觉。

这和人类学习其实非常相似。

所以 Jev 最终这个产品或者品牌能不能活下来，我觉得反而没有那么重要。真正值得关注的是，它重新提出了一个被 decoder-only 大模型的成功暂时掩盖的问题：

自然语言也许是人与 AI 之间极好的通用界面，但未必是机器内部最高效的工作语言。

tr: Jev is so fast, it can play Doom. Every decision, where to move, where to aim, whether to hold down the trigger, Jev is making those decisions inside the software loop. Responding at about 100 milliseconds per battery of questions, it's able to make 10 decisions a second, which is fast enough to track enemies and fire effectively dodge projectiles. One model is fed a structured description of the situation. Health, nearby enemies, incoming projectiles, available pickups, everything a player needs to make informed decisions about what to do next in the game. With that game state as input, the model is asked to make small typed judgments, such as should the players trigger be held down right now, what is the player's highest priority goal right now, should the player be dodging, and others. We compose their answers into the player's next action, and keep repeating that loop as the game changes. The model has a default game strategy, generally telling it how to play the game somewhat effectively. But of course, because that's fed in this text, we can change that at any time. Let's try here, do not fire, simply dodge. We can see that immediately the player's behavior changes, because the model is making the same judgments, but now in the context of that new instruction. Not the best strategy, but hey, that's on us. t:
TypeSafe 新发布的 Jev，主打不生成文字，只返回选项、概率和置信度。光看这些功能，我确实会觉得，拿个 base 模型后训练，再接个分类头，也能做啊。分类器已经是很成熟的技术了。

预训练模型接分类头，本来就可以直接输出分类概率。把答案限制在 A/B/C，也能保证它不会输出 D。所谓零幻觉如果指的是这个，和模型能不能选对是两回事。

Jev 允许开发者用自然语言定义问题和候选项，可以理解为估计 p(选项 | 输入状态、问题、候选集)。这比只认固定标签的业务分类器通用，但同样可以作为 base 模型的多任务后训练目标。难点在于换到没训练过的任务以后，判断质量还能保留多少。
它把同一份输入上的多个问题独立、并行求值，省掉了逐 token 写出完整答案的过程。直接给候选项打分，确实可能比生成一整段 JSON 快很多。但分类头本来也不需要生成文本，单凭这个对比看不出新架构的贡献。公开材料也没说明底层如何共享计算，一次 API 调用不等于只跑一次前向传播。

它的训练方法 RLCD 强调概率校准。给出 80% 概率的那组预测，长期看应该大约有 80% 正确。分类准确率高，不代表概率可信，一个正确率 90% 的模型，也可能动不动就报 99% 的把握。

这个目标有实际意义。程序需要根据概率决定自动执行还是转人工，同样选 A，51% 和 99% 应该触发不同处理。

但校准也有成熟方法。交叉熵、Brier score 可以用于训练概率预测，温度缩放可以做后处理。目前这些公开材料没有给出 RLCD 的奖励函数、训练配方和消融实验，还没法判断它相对常规训练加校准，多解决了什么问题。

Jev 的 confidence 也是从选项概率分布计算出来的统计量。分布很集中，说明模型偏向某个答案，不能单凭这一点认定它可靠。

如果它能让开发者直接用自然语言定义分类任务，省去准备数据、训练和部署的工作，同时保持低延迟、低成本，这个产品当然有意义。成熟技术做成好用的服务，本身就能解决问题。

不过，既然主张新架构和新训练方法，就应该和经过多任务后训练、带分类头和校准、支持批量推理的模型比较。在未见任务上测准确率、校准误差，以及相同错误率下能自动处理多少请求，再比较延迟和成本。这样的结果才能说明 Jev 到底做到了什么。

t:
12 most valuable ways to use Jev: 

first setup:

· get access and an api key from http://typesafe.ai.
· install the official skill:
npx skills add typesafe-ai/skills --skill typesafe-ai
· give your coding agent one of the jobs below and say “build this using the typesafe skill.”

> 1. find landing page copy worth rewriting
· split your page into sections.
· score each for clarity and specificity.
· flag sections that leave the offer unclear.

> 2. check the sources behind a draft
· pair each claim with its source passage.
· ask whether the passage actually supports it.
· send weak matches back for review.

> 3. catch your coding agent calling unfinished work “done”
· define what finished looks like.
· check its recent actions before it stops.
· flag missing steps, like a test it never ran.

> 4. catch code that breaks your rules
· write rules like “never log customer emails.”
· check new code against those rules.
· flag the relevant changes for review.

> 5. test cheaper models on simpler requests
· list the models your app can use.
· have jev choose one for each task.
· compare quality and total cost with your usual model.

> 6. choose a browser agent’s next click
· give it the goal and available buttons.
· have it pick an action and target.
· refresh the options after the page changes.

> 7. find code changes that deserve extra attention
· feed it the changes in a pull request.
· check for broad impact and missing tests.
· move concerning changes up the review queue.

> 8. turn a bug backlog into next steps
· feed it open issues and their descriptions.
· classify urgency and possible duplicates.
· suggest “investigate,” “ask for details,” or “add to backlog.”

> 9. cut down the search results you need to read
· give it your question and retrieved results.
· score each result for relevance.
· open the strongest matches first.

> 10. sort emails by what they need
· define categories like invoice, support, and general.
· have jev classify incoming messages.
· route clear matches and keep uncertain ones for review.

> 11. spot urgent support requests
· check each ticket for urgency and frustration.
· choose the team that should handle it.
· flag customers who appear blocked from using the product.

> 12. filter weak examples out of training data
· define what a useful example looks like.
· check records for filler, incomplete answers, or other flaws.
· review what gets rejected before filtering the full dataset.

===

Claude Codeに並列タスク管理機能Projectsが導入

===

OpenAIが法律業務特化のAstra for Lawを発表

・GPT-6 Astraをベースに、米国の判例や法令など2億3000万以上のURLをカバーする法的検索レイヤーを搭載しています。
・データプライバシー保護を標準装備し、26のパートナー構築プラグインを利用して契約書レビューやIPO申請書の作成などを支援します。

AnthropicのAI研究開発の26%をClaudeが主導

・約3万のAIエージェントが研究やエンジニアリングに従事しており、AIによるAI開発（RSI）が加速している現状が示されました。

"output tokens are free because theyre too cheap to meter" is the line that should make people pause. when you constrain generation to a distribution over enum-like decisions instead of open-ended text, the output side of inference basically collapses - no long autoregressive decode loop, no KV growth per generated token. thats where the 20-200x comes from. its not a better LLM, its a different object optimized for a narrower job: decisions, not language. whether that job is big enough to matter is the real question, but the architecture argument is sound @CompleteSkeptic

这两天被Jev刷屏了，简单说就是一个非常擅长做选择题的大模型，不是替代以前的模型，其面向程序而非人类能够更好地实现AI自动化。

Jev想解决的问题是：现在的大模型（OpenAI、Claude、DeepSeek等）输出的都是"一段话"，人看没问题，但程序没法直接用，你让它判断"这个客户会不会流失"，它可能回你一篇小作文，可能格式不对，可能瞎编，而且永远一副很自信的样子

Jev 的做法：干脆不让它说话，直接做选择题。

你给它一堆信息，再给它一张"选择题答卷"：
1、这封邮件是投诉吗？是/否
2、紧急程度？高/中/低
3、该转给哪个部门？A/B/C

它只能在选项里选，所以不可能答非所问、不可能编造，而且每个答案都附带"我有 92% 把握"这样的数字，把握低的交给人处理，把握高的直接自动执行。

因为不用一个字一个字往外蹦，它一次性给出所有答案：
⚡ 0.1–0.5 秒出结果，比大模型快 40–200 倍
💰 价格便宜几百倍，输出直接免费

它不能干什么：写文章、写代码、聊天、复杂推理，统统不行，它不是来取代 ChatGPT 的。

它能干什么：那些量巨大、要求快、不能出错的"小判断"，审核内容、分拣工单、风控打分、从海量数据里筛东西，以及给别的 AI 当"监考老师"，检查它们有没有胡说。

对行业的影响：
→ 以后 AI 会分工：大模型负责"慢慢想、好好写"，Jev 这类负责"秒级拍板"
→ 现在大量公司拿大模型干分类、审核的活，又贵又慢，这块生意要被jev接管了
→ 便宜到几乎不要钱之后，以前"不值得用 AI"的地方都会用上，需求反而会爆发

if you're an applied AI operator, here are 3 practical Jev use cases I'm wanting to explore:

1) Jev as an 'advisor' for my agents
because Jev is so fast and cheap, you can run it alongside any agent you run to steer/stop it if it goes off track. I think Jev will unlock new levels of agent reliability because it's practically free, adds no latency, and can check against any criteria you need.

2) as a tool for your frontier agents
I have Astra in Codex a Jev tool that lets it pre-process data and save on tokens. rather than read files itself or delegating to smaller sub-agents, it can quickly run files through Jev and immediately screen files to make quick decisions.

3) auto-review for every task

q.t:
alright - just got Jev deployed for a real production use case, which now performs at fable level quality but 10x faster and saves a ton of money

context - a powerful capability of firstmate is that as an orchestrator it intelligently routes each task to an appropriate agent (permutation of harness, model, and reasoning effort) based on custom user preference

by default, that's done by the firstmate agent and the LLM would have to do some thinking, make tool calls to read dispatch rules, quota data etc and then do the dispatch. this is slow and does cost a bit of LLM tokens

i just replaced this dispatch process with Jev. it makes the same decision with no thinking or tool calls, done in ~200ms, and for the 25 tasks i evaluated this with, it gives the exact same answer fable would have given... 

there's still a tool call needed to invoke Jev, done by the firstmate agent which uses an LLM. but even with that counted, the saving from Jev still resulted in a -71% reduction in cost and -90% reduction in wall time of completing the whole dispatching process

Jev API calls themselves are almost free.. i made 100+ calls, and my usage dashboard still shows $0.01 (which i think means "haven't reached $0.01 yet"). if we just look at the part Jev replaced and not the whole system, then the saving is on the magnitude of ~100x

if you also have Jev and you use firstmate, set TYPESAFE_API_KEY in your .env file in your firstmate repo to activate this

exciting times! i think this is starting to enable a whole new architectural paradigm for software. LLMs are just a small part of it. more on that soon

q.t:
Since Jev launched Tuesday, there’s apparently a new thing at @every “Jev boys.”

Ever since the launch there’s been this flock of self-proclaimed “Jev boys” who carry Jev on hand at all times and constantly ask it what to do. They have their entire personality revolve around Jev, TypeSafe, and calibrated probabilities. When we went around talking about what people were trying this week, 4 or 5 of them said some variation of “I live by the Jev and die by the Jev.”

Just about an hour ago, I asked someone to do something and one of the Jev boys was bold enough to say “if Jev says I do it, otherwise I don’t.” I told him if he asked Jev instead of just doing the thing I was going to lose my mind.

He asked it anyway and it said to do it.

Thank god for that at least.

But then the other Jev boy asked the same question and Jev gave him a different answer.

He immediately pulled up the probability and started explaining that Jev was only 63% confident, so technically it was a judgment call.

I told him that yes. That is what being a person is.

Later, another Jev boy asked Jev whether he should go to a meeting. Jev said no.

He did not go to the meeting.

When someone asked where he was, he posted the Jev output in Slack.

At lunch, I watched two Jev boys ask Jev where they should eat. They got different answers and spent five minutes comparing confidence scores instead of picking somewhere.

One of them actually said “I’m going with Jev on this one.”

The other said “your Jev is wrong.”

I don’t even know what that means.

Now they’ve started asking Jev questions about each other.

Someone asked Jev if another person’s idea was good.

false

The person whose idea it was then asked Jev whether that was constructive feedback.

false

Neither of them has spoken since.

This afternoon one of the Jev boys told me he doesn’t make decisions anymore, he “routes them through Jev.”

I asked if he was joking.

He asked Jev.

It said false.

It has been three days since launch.

I really hope this dies off soon. I haven’t seen anything outside Every about “Jev boys,” so I’m guessing it’s just an Every thing.

Unless one of you has more information.

t:
这两天 被Jev刷屏，我最开始也以为它是又一个新模型。

看了一圈后，我觉得它有意思的点如下：

第一，它把“语言生成”改成了“决策原语”。
LLM 的默认接口是 chat completion，输出一段文本；Jev 的默认接口是 typed decision，输出 choice、score、probability、confidence。它不是给人读的模型，更接近一个能被程序直接调用的判断函数。

第二，它把“事后解析”改成了“天然结构化”。
过去让 LLM 做分类、路由、评分，经常是先让它生成 JSON，再校验、重试、修格式。Jev 直接在固定决策空间里返回答案，模型输出可以进入 if、switch、rank、filter、guard。

第三，它把“单次大推理”改成了“大量小判断”。
它不适合承担完整复杂任务，但很适合插在 Agent 系统的判断点里：这段记忆要不要进上下文？这个任务该走哪个模型？工具调用有没有风险？Agent 是否已经完成？这个文件值不值得继续读？这些判断数量很大，过去都被大模型硬扛。

第四，它把“答案”改成了“概率信号”。
Jev 返回的不只是结果，还有概率和置信度。系统可以根据置信度决定自动执行、交给强模型，还是交给人复核。AI 在这里不再只是一次性黑盒，而是一个能被调度的系统组件。

第五，它把“模型能力竞争”推向了“控制流竞争”。
Jev 的价值不在于比 Claude/GPT 更会写，而在于帮系统分配任务：什么时候用便宜模型，什么时候用强模型，什么时候继续搜索，什么时候停止。

接下来先做几个实验：
让 Jev 批量筛选候选记忆和检索结果，看看减少上下文时会不会漏掉关键证据；
让它参与工具和模型分流，测试低置信度时交给强模型复核是否划算；
再把 Agent 的执行检查拆成多个小问题，看看它能否及时发现遗漏要求、超出修改范围和缺少完成证据。

这几件事，分别能检验它的并行判断、概率分流，以及高频核验能力。

q.t:
Jev 这个 waitlist 还是很给力的，昨天申请，今天就能用上。

给已经拿到 API、但还不知道怎么玩的人整理了一份 Awesome Jev，目前我能确认到的 Jev 项目基本都在这里：

1. jev-ultrafast
Browser Use 做的高速浏览器 Agent。Jev 负责每一步判断「做什么、点哪个元素」，需要输入文字时才调用小模型。Google Flights 搜航班完整跑完约 7.1 秒。
https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast

2. typesafe-mcp
把 Jev 直接接进 Claude Code、Claude Desktop 和 Codex。Agent 可以随时调用 Jev 做 Choice / Score / Noul 这类结构化判断。
https://github.com/itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp

3. jev-mcp
另一个更偏实用工具的 MCP，已经封装好事实核验、Prompt Injection 检测和语义排序。
https://github.com/jkudish/jev-mcp

4. SemDecide
把 Jev 做成 Unix 命令行工具，可以直接拿来做语义判断、分类、打分、过滤和 Guard。很适合塞进脚本、CI 和数据流水线。
https://github.com/sharziki/semdecide

5. Jev Codex Router
先让 Jev 判断每一轮编程任务有多难，再自动决定交给便宜模型还是更强模型。作者用 237 个真实 turn 回放，自测成本降低约 60%。
https://github.com/0xNatoshi/jev-codex-router

6. Winnow
给 Claude Code 做「上下文垃圾回收」。Read、Bash、Grep 输出太长时，先让 Jev 判断哪些内容真的跟当前任务有关，再决定哪些需要进上下文。
https://github.com/GhalebDweikat/winnow

7. Jev Review
用 Jev 做代码审查前置筛选，先判断 correctness、security、reliability、兼容性和测试风险，再把重点问题交给更重的模型处理。
https://github.com/devagrawal09/jev-review

8. Blink
用 Jev 在代码库里做语义寻路。每到一层目录，就判断哪些文件或文件夹最可能和问题有关，再把更多 walker 分配过去。
https://github.com/ellipsis-dev/blink

9. neo4jev
把同样的思路用到知识图谱。Jev 给每条候选边打概率，再用 beam search 一步步找到最可能的路径。
https://github.com/jexp/neo4jev

10. jev-desktop
把 Jev 接到桌面自动化里。它读取 Accessibility Tree，判断该操作哪个控件、执行什么动作，再交给本地执行器。
https://github.com/lahfir/agent-desktop

11. TypeSafe AI Playground
一个专门拿 Jev 做实验的 Rust CLI，已经做了 PHI 检测、代码注释审查、实时语气分析、职业和行业分类等玩法。
https://github.com/markjaquith/typesafe-ai-playground

12. Prism
目前我看到最接近量化/交易场景的项目。它让 Jev 判断流动性池的 toxic flow、市场压力、均值回归可能性和流动性分布方式，目前默认还是 shadow/advisory，不直接驱动交易。
https://github.com/irfndi/prism-liquidity-agent

13. 1v1 Jev
直接做了一个 FPS，让 Jev 大约 9Hz 判断移动、瞄准、ADS、开枪和跳跃。属于最直观展示 Jev 低延迟决策能力的项目之一。
https://github.com/emrickgarrett/OneVOneJev

14. TypeSafe on Neon
拿 Jev 做模型 Router。请求先由 Jev 判断属于哪种任务，再转给 Grok 4.6 或 GPT-6 Astra 等模型执行。
https://github.com/andrelandgraf/typesafe-on-neon

看完这些项目，你大概也知道 Jev 可以怎么玩了，就是拿它反复做「要不要、选哪个、打几分、下一步干什么」。

真正需要生成代码、写文章和复杂推理时，再把任务交给传统大模型。

Feed some input (eg customer email, any other text, structured data) into it, define your questions ("which team should answer this email?") and dimensions ("sales, technical, fraud") and get back a response within milliseconds. No long reasoning, no exploding token costs.

Sure, that answer will still be generated by an LLM, complex questions may still require an (additional) LLM but this model is really mindblowing.
If you’re wondering how Jev is scaling to meet insane demand they could not possibly have predicted, the answer appears to be @modal — one of only 4 subprocessors listed on https://trust.typesafe.ai

t:
Jev really looks like it’s going to be a huge deal, and the next massive leap forward.

If you can have parallel cheap classification/decision making running alongside an LLM, you can hyper-focus the LLM on the things it is very good at, and strip out all the noise.

q.t:
I got access to Jev earlier today (thank you @hackgoofer).  I have run ~5,000 requests so far, (which cost me around $2!), across classification, model routing, intent, steering, and many other things.

tl;dr, Jev enables a new intelligent decision-making primitive, separate from deterministic code and LLM calls.  This allows a class of decision-making that was neither suited to dumb, unintelligent code, nor to slow, expensive LLMs.

It is super fast and cheap, and I think I will likely end up making a few Jev calls to every LLM call I make in my product. I think probably any company using LLM requests today can probably add a Jev call pre and/or post LLM calls to quite literally make their product much better for free, and have better tool calling behavior in many cases.  

I happened to have a personal benchmark for this as I’d been working on a ton of proactivity and classification tasks.  I have been using the deepseek flash and more recently gpt 5.6 luna family of models as reasonably smart classifiers with low latency.  Think questions like:

- Did this conversation output contradict something they’ve mentioned before?
- Should we send a followup message to this user based on our rules?
- It’s been a few seconds of silence.  Should we proactively send a message?

In the past, I’ve been forced to write a bunch of what I call decision chains, mostly because an LLM classification call is very expensive in TIME (avg 4s), and less importantly can cost quite a bit if run on every message.

Imagine a normal chat app.  If you added 4s to every response to figure out if the response is good before sending it out, that ends up being pretty bad.  So instead, I usually have to write some code that is a crude heuristic that runs quickly and decides whether to run the classifier.  Obviously this sucks because you call the classifier many times that you don’t want to, which makes your p95 bad, and you also miss cases with the heuristic, and you also have to manage all of these weird chains.

With Jev, it’s cheap enough, and fast enough (p50 ~150ms, p95 ~350ms in my testing!) that you can easily run it every turn.  Heck you can reasonably run it before generation AND post generation, for any application that isn’t realtime voice, and still feel snappy.

But this is just one use case.  Think: smarter model routing, better context packing, better responses, better observability for intent/tags/safety, smarter retries and so much more.  By simply thinking about the inputs and outcomes you want to enforce, you can use Jev to supercharge most model calls and reduce bad user outcomes.  The more “quirks” a model has, the more valuable it ends up being.

It’s a bit weird and unintuitive using Jev.  Generally, you want to decrease the # of questions you ask a classifier, or it makes more mistakes.  In fact, you might want to ask your questions kind of in a compound way, because the reasoning happens in a shared scratchpad of sorts.  Adding questions muddies the scratchpad and makes it take longer.  

With Jev, you feel incentivized to go the other way, to formulate your query as a set of independent questions.  It doesn’t feel like adding more questions decreases your performance on others.

You can go a bit deeper to improve tool calls.  Many model tools are things like turning on settings, or other things.  You can easily improve models that are not very good at tool calling with Jev, by simply figuring out when to run them.  You can do a pre-LLM call to figure out when to unfurl different tool definitions, in order to make your main LLM run better, you could run a background task with Jev + another LLM to reduce tool and context burden on your main LLM, and free it to be responsive.

I’ve only scratched the surface of my testing but very excited!

Jev 

意味着确定性结果不需要确定性执行

可能也说明了场景：有限空间内决策（可接受的决策空间有限），State → Action → Feedback

1. 如何定义有限空间

有限空间：状态空间可以很大，但决策空间必须足够有限

1️⃣「动作有限」

模型最终只能做少数几件事，比如：买 / 卖 / 持有

2️⃣ 「目标有限」

评价标准比较明确，比如：赚钱、点击、胜负、转化、通过率、延迟、成本。

目标越容易量化，越容易训练决策模型

3️⃣「反馈明确」

做完动作后，很快知道结果，比如：游戏里几秒就知道一次行动有没有效果

4️⃣「状态可观测」

虽然 State 可以非常复杂，但需要能够被结构化，例如：市场价格 + 成交量 + 波动率

2. 什么样的场景，值得用 Jev？

有限决策空间
可观测 State
快速 Feedback
高频 Decision

四个条件越同时满足，越适合

3. 那什么样的有限空间，值得用 Jev？

决策频率 × 反馈速度 × 决策价值

三个同时高，价值就出来了

t:
Jev 的这些场景，用 embedding、reranker 或传统分类器能替代多少？

Embedding 把文本变成向量，靠相似度就能做分类和路由。Reranker 把输入和候选放在一起打分，Qwen3 Reranker 还支持自定义指令，直接读取 yes/no 的 logits 算分数。

常见的专用 classifier 针对固定任务训练，直接输出类别概率。Jev 主打每次请求都能指定判断规则和选项，并行返回类型受约束的结果，减少为不同任务单独训练的工作。

所以分类、选项、概率输出，都算不上新东西。固定任务完全可以把这些现成方案拿来做替代基线。Jev 能否在规则变化后仍保持准确、快速，才值得比较。

只和逐字生成 JSON 的大模型比速度，基线还是太舒服了。

q.t:
补充一下 Jev 的输入和输出，具体可以怎么放进程序里。

输入可以是自然语言文本，也可以是结构化信息。调用时主要提供两部分：state 放需要分析的内容，比如一段聊天记录、一份报错信息，或者包含多个字段的对象；questions 定义你要问什么，以及判断标准和候选项。

比如 state 放用户的消息，questions 问这条消息应该交给哪个部门处理，再给出技术支持、账单、销售三个选项及各自的说明。

输出通过 JSON 返回，目前主要有三种。

Choice 用来选一个选项。比如技术支持、账单、销售的概率分别是 70%、20%、10%，最终 choice 就是技术支持。程序也能读取完整分布，知道其他选项有多少可能性。

Score 用来按标准评分。比如把故障分成三个等级：0 是轻微显示问题，1 是影响功能但有替代办法，2 是完全阻塞。如果概率分别是 10%、20%、70%，分数就是：

0 × 0.1 + 1 × 0.2 + 2 × 0.7 = 1.6

这个分数可以直接参与排序，或者和其他评分组合计算优先级。

Noul 用来判断一个条件是否成立，返回 0～1 的概率。比如问消息是否包含求助意图，得到 0.9，再由程序设定阈值，决定是否触发后续操作。

Choice 和 Score 还会返回 confidence，根据概率分布的集中程度计算。90%、5%、5% 表示明显偏向一个选项，34%、33%、33% 就很难选。

我想到一个很适合的场景，就是判断群聊里的 agent 该不该被唤醒回复。

把最近的聊天记录、有没有被 @、agent 的角色，以及它刚刚是否已经回复过这些信息放进 state，再问当前是否适合由 agent 参与。

有人明确求助，或者问题正好属于 agent 负责的范围，就可能得到较高的值。如果只是群友闲聊，或者问题已经被别人解决，就让它保持安静。超过设定阈值，再调用负责生成回复的大模型。

这样也能处理没人 @ 它，但上下文里确实需要它帮忙的情况，不用只靠关键词和固定触发词。

还可以在同一次请求里并行判断该不该回复、问题有多紧急、应该交给哪个 agent，把这些结果交给代码，决定具体唤醒谁、以什么优先级处理。

q.t:
Ran a dumb experiment last night: used Jev by @typesafeai (a decision/classifier model, not a text-gen model) to write C++.

At every step I gave it the finite set of grammatically valid next tokens and let it just... pick one. No free-form generation, no hallucinated syntax, purely "choose from this legal set." It's not built for this, that's what made it fun.

Got a working piece of C++ out of a model that fundamentally does not generate text. Not claiming this is how you should write code, and it's slower and dumber than just using an actual code model. But it's a neat proof that a classifier constrained tightly enough can stumble into looking like a generator.

Novelty over utility here, but it's the kind of dumb experiment that tells you more about a model's actual guardrails than the official demos do.

===

TypeSafe Jevの驚異的なユースケース【続報】

・構造化出力に特化した「Jev」の具体的な活用事例に関する続報です
・ブラウザ操作エージェントによるフライト検索が7秒で完了するなど、圧倒的な速度が実証されました
・架空ペルソナ150人への調査がわずか1.8円・5秒で終わるなど、コストパフォーマンスの高さも絶賛されています

===

MetaのMuseがビジネス向けコール機能を拡大【続報】

・大ヒット中のMetaのAIエージェント「Muse」に関する続報です
・米国ビジネス向けのアウトバウンドコール機能のベータ版が拡大されました
・産業セクターでのオーケストレーターとしての活用など、より複雑な業務フローへの組み込みが進んでいます
・既報の節約事例に加え、企業での実用性の高さが際立っています

===

Huaweiが100万GPUクラスタと新AIチップ計画【続報】

・米国の輸出規制下でAIチップ開発を進めるHuaweiに関する続報です
・2027年に次世代チップをリリースし、独自のネットワーク技術を用いて100万GPU規模のクラスタを構築する計画であることが報じられました
・規制下においてもAIインフラの開発スピードを加速させており、業界に驚きを与えています

===

動画生成を完全自動化するVideoClaw登場

・動画編集・生成を完全に自動化するツールVideoClawがローンチされました
・アイデアや素材を渡すだけで、計画から編集、Bロールの追加、音楽、キャプション付けまでを自動で行います
・ソフトウェア開発におけるコーディングエージェントの動画版として、クリエイターから注目を集めています

===

AI時代のOSSはコンパクトさが重要に

・AIによってコーディングコストが激減した現在、機能過多なライブラリの価値が低下しているという意見が話題です
・AIが簡単にグルーコードやボイラープレートを書けるため、不要なコードを抱えること自体がリスクになると指摘されています
・今後のOSSには高速・安定・セキュア・コンパクトであることが求められるという見解に多くの賛同が集まっています

===

AIエージェント利用履歴からクラス診断するツールが話題

・CodexやClaude Codeの過去30日間の利用履歴を読み取り、ユーザーの使い方を診断するツールが公開されました

While we are on the topic, the "confidence" stuff you have seen people post on JEV is also a farce. The "confidence" value the API returns is a derived metric from the predicted class probs... it does not "model" uncertainty like a bayesian net would.

https://x.com/neural_avb/status/2101594784490270785?s=20

q.t:
I was super intrigued when I noticed that JEV returns not just probs for candidate choices, but also a CONFIDENCE SCORE of it's prediction...

I was wondering if TypeSafe AI brought back Bayesian Networks or something to learn uncertainty.

Turns out - NO. Acc to their docs, confidence is just a derived metric from the classification scores. It carries ZERO extra information. Their demo page shows:

 confidence = (3 × largest probability − 1) / 2

Confidence is tightly coupled with the classification scores it is measuring the uncertainty for.

There is no magic here. The model can produce high probability on a wrong choice and just be confidently wrong.

t:
审查 1000 个代码 PR：
用传统的 Claude Opus 5 大模型，要花大约 14.5 美元；
而换成刚刚刷屏的 Jev，只需要整整 7 美分（约合人民币 5 毛钱）！
成本直接暴跌 200 倍，而且半秒钟内当场交卷。

Wasp 联合创始人 Matija 用一段仅仅 45 秒的极简解说，在推特上狂砍了 100 多万播放、被翻译成十几种语言。
官方发了一堆复杂长篇的学术推演把所有人看懵，
而 Matija 这一刀，直接切中了所有软件工程师的灵魂：
“这玩意儿根本不是又一个陪聊大模型！它就像我们在大学机器学习里学的‘逻辑回归（Logistic Regression）’——输入一段上下文，直接吐出概率和决策，中间没有半个字的废话！”

为什么全网做开发、做基础设施的人会在 24 小时内集体高潮？
看懂这三层硬核拆解，你会看清整个 AI 软件工程最深刻的一次范式转移：

1️⃣ 告别“脱裤子放屁”的自然语言内耗：
过去三年全行业都在犯蠢：
系统只需要知道一个用户是不是骗子、这行代码有没有 SQL 注入（一个 Yes/No 的判断）；
我们却非要逼着大模型花几秒钟吐出一篇几百字的分析小作文，
然后再让后端工程师抓耳挠腮地写正则表达式去提取结论！
慢得要死，贵得要命，还动不动因为模型发散而崩掉。
Jev 彻底把这一环给掐死了：输入数据，毫秒级返回一个确定性的选项或置信度分数；
2️⃣ 真实业务里的降维打击（实测数据极其残暴）：
开发者录屏实测：把一段真实的代码 Diff 丢给它，
一次 API 调用只要 0.00007 美元，半秒之内，14 个强类型的安全检查清单伴随精准的概率同时返回：
是否存在硬编码密钥？是否有越权隐患？是否有重大破坏性变更？
整个过程快到像本地静态代码扫描一样顺滑，但背后拥有大模型的深度常识；
3️⃣ 真正的“AI 软件底层积木（Software Primitive）”：
这是 Matija 强调的最值钱的一点：
各种 LLM 是生成式模型（像个文学家）；而 Jev 是人类等待了三年的纯逻辑决策原语。
它输出的不是不可控的文字，而是代码能直接吞进去的布尔值和浮点数——
它快到能直接塞进工单队列做 0.1 秒的优先级分流，
甚至快到能塞进实时动作游戏和区块链交易的确认窗口！

很多非技术人还在困惑：一个不会写自然语言的模型到底有什么用？
但在真正每天扛着高并发和高昂 API 账单的工程师眼里，
这个放弃了写小作文、把决策成本打到几分钱的新物种，
才是真正能把 AI 无缝焊进现代化软件工业血肉里的终极齿轮。 https://x.com/MatijaSosic/status/2100190746389135772/video/1

We are going to see some ridiculous stuff built from this as well.

t:
Prod, not God.

Such a refreshing departure from the hubris of the like of Dario. 

If you're still confused about what makes Jev refreshing, this is your answer. Something we can actually build with.

q.t:
I’ve put a ton of tokens through Jev now, and...I have thoughts.

1. The big labs lost the script

TypeSafe’s intro video says, “We’re building prod, not God” — and can I just say? Hell yeah. @typesafeai built something for engineers like me, so I can build products for people like your mom (she says hi btw). They’re not trying to create “Machines of Loving Grace”; they’re trying to build things that let OTHER HUMAN BEINGS create new types of products.

The proof is in the pudding. When ChatGPT shipped, we were all blown away by…ChatGPT. When Jev shipped, we were all blown away by what everyone was making with it.

I cannot tell you how refreshing this is. It takes a sincere form of humility to believe that you, the creator of a technology, will not be the best at deploying the technology into the marketplace. The big labs, especially Anthropic, have proven not to have this humility…and now everyone hates AI. Thanks, Dario.

I guess what I’m saying is: Diogo for president.

2. Ultra-smart classifiers were genuinely a missing primitive.

I don’t know how this got missed. Diogo calls it “machine-native intelligence,” and that’s really what it is. I cannot tell you how much bending and twisting I've had to do with LLMs to get them to act like a classifier when they just weren’t. I’m absolutely shocked this is the first time this “type” of model has come to market.

These models will unlock AI utility for entire industries: robotics, trucking, aviation, meteorology, finance, defense, retail…even your smart coffee mug is going to use this.

3. It’s still too expensive

Jev is really, really cheap compared to LLMs. But you don’t use it like an LLM. In my full self-driving example, or any robotics example, you’ll be making decisions several times per second continuously. The #1 value proposition of a model like this is speed and cost.

To be clear, at current pricing, the model will still be successful and well integrated. It will be able to replace a number of tasks that were already being performed (poorly) by LLMs. However, to unlock industrial-scale demand (Jevons paradox), I believe it needs to be roughly 10x cheaper.

Currently, Jev is $0.042/M input, which is actually 7x more expensive than a cache read on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.006). If our industrial application requires decisions at 10 Hz and we provide only 10k of context, that would cost $0.0042/second to operate, or $15/hour, $600/week, etc.

The good news is Diogo said on a recent AMA that they have substantial margin at their current pricing and have already considered dropping the cost further. I hope it's a lot further.

4. Latency is a real limiter

I really hope TypeSafe AI works with an edge network provider to improve the co-location of models and reduce network latency. Ultimately, these models really need to run on-device. I would even be willing to pay some kind of recurring license fee to have a great closed model running on my own hardware, just so I can reduce the TTD (Time To Decision) as much as possible. Imagine running a model like this at 60 Hz, or even 120 Hz.

At that point, we’re looking at a new kind of logic gate — we can’t even imagine what that will be like.

In summary, this one really is a game changer for everyone building AI products, and, assuming cost and latency are further improved…it’ll be a game changer for everyone doing anything.

t:
Jev、やってみてます。オンボーディングのテクニカルなことを中心にまとめました～

①どうやってはじめたか：TypeSafeで申請したあとにDMを@justKDeng さんに送って、何を作りたいか、とかを伝えたらDMに返事がなかったものの、すぐ「TypeSafe AI: Your account is ready」というメールが来ていました。やや無機質なUIで、英語が分かるとスムーズです。

②定義をしっかり与える必要あり：定義をしっかり与えるほど、回答が安定します。これは何等かのシステムに組み込んで使うことを前提としたモデルという印象です。JSON Schemaをがっつり組んだAIのAPIコールやったことがある人なら扱い易いと思います。

③ Noulが肝心：TypeSafeにおける質問タイプは Choice, Score, Noulの３つがあります。Noulってなんやねん、という感じですが、これこそJevを理解する鍵です。
敢えてBooleanではないようです。ベルヌーイ（Bernoulli）分布を覚えていますか？「結果が成功/失敗の2つしかない試行（ベルヌーイ試行）の確率を表す離散型確率分布」のことです。このNoulです。NoulはTrue/Falseではなく、確率を返します。
入力はテキストだけの模様です。

まだ手探りだと思うけど、Jev(RLCDモデル)の勘所は確信度ベースであることだと思う。
まずここまでの界隈の流れを振り返ると、LLMから正しい数字を吐かせるというタスクにおいては、数字の文字トークンの羅列出力にリニアな精度を期待するのは本来頭おかしくて、logprobsのような手法にニーズがあった。でもlogprobsがreasoning model全盛でオワコンになって、jacobian-lensから同様のことをある程度高い知能品質で出すのは仮に出来ても時間かかるという状況で、詰み感があったことを頭に入れておかんといかん。そこに、トークンスロットマシーン連荘率計算じゃなくてRLVRみたいに”計算機上の自然”にある結論側から攻めつつ、RLVRのようにトークン確率に対して0/1(コードが通る/通らない)でRLシバくんじゃなくて確信度という%なパラメータに対してシバくやり方が出てきた(これが確信度=事象の自然上発生率となるよう結論側からリニアに校正するRLCD、つまりJev)っていう歴史を把握してないと良さが掴めない。
だからJevなのにtop1だけ活用するなら超高速なローカルLLMからのstructured outputですぐ真似出来そうやんは至極当然で、どっちかというと未来予測とかマスキングされた過去の推測に対してコペンハーゲン解釈みたいな理解を得たいというネタで使わないともったいない。top2以降を捨てるだけならJevいらん。ぐらいの気迫で使いこなしたいところ。

このJevまだ勉強途中なんですが、シンプルだけど画期的で、通常のLLMは確率でテキストを生成する仕組みだけど、Jevはテキストそのものではなく、確率付きのテキストの配列みたいな構造化データを並列に提示する仕組みっぽい

——
その構造化データをソフトウェアが決定論的なアプローチ(普通に条件分岐とか)で処理することで、まずLLM(Jev)の応答速度が何十倍か何百倍くらい早いので、このマリオのプレイ動画みたいなことができる

——
LLMの出力もJSONフォーマットにできるんだけどそれはテキストの生成をする上で結果を構造的に出してるだけで。Jevはそもそもの推論ステップが違う、つまり最終的に一文のテキストを生成するのではなく、その途中の各テキストの出現確率を構造化データとして出力するように学習されて推論してるからめっちゃ早いしめっちゃ安くなる

——
このマリオの操作みたいに、今の画面の状態をインプットにして、どの操作をさせるのかを確率付きの動作パターンの配列で出すんだったら、確かに従来のテキスト生成AIよりもこっちのが良いのは直感的にわかる

——
他にも問い合わせの分類や、人間のレビュー可否の判断とかの確率に基づく処理ってそこらじゅうにあってそれらは従来のテキスト生成AIじゃなくて、Jevみたいなアプローチのが良いのかもしれない

jevの本命は、モデル置換じゃない
パイプラインの切り替えだ

classify（判断） → 構造化 → 決定論コード → 判断
この工程をを生成待ちをせず、息継ぎすることなく実行できる

従来のエージェントは判断も実行も生成も、ほぼ全てをLLMにやらせていた
プロンプトとツール一覧を渡し、ゴールまでモデルに回し続ける

確かにこれでも動くが、エージェントが迷ったり、同じツールを何度も呼んだり、状態が壊れたりと課題が多くあった

特に、LLMに全部任せる設計はAIアプリだと破綻する
プログラムで制御できる場所を考慮したり、出力が遅いときの対策などをしない限り、全任せは本番で破綻する

そこで重要となる原則が『12 Factor Agents』だ

これは、本番環境向けに信頼性の高いAIアプリを作るための原則で、要点は以下だ

良いエージェントは、巨大な一筆書きのループではない。大半は普通のソフトウェアで、LLMは曖昧な判断が必要な地点にだけ入れる

「LLMは必要な地点にだけ入る」
これがどのAIアプリでも重要な設計原則だ

そして、Jevが革命的なのが、従来はLLMでやるしかなかった「判断」を任せることができる点だ
→ Jevは文章などLLMが生成するものは生成しないが、代わりに、選択肢・スコア・真偽（yes / no）・確率といった判断結果を型付きで返す

判断はJev。実行は普通のプログラム。文章や深い・複雑な推論が必要なときだけ、LLMを使う
これが今後、AIアプリでは基本的な役割分担となる

Jevは文章などLLMのような生成はしないが、代わりに、選択肢・点数・はい/いいえを型付きで返す。向いているのは「次に何をするか決める」部分だ。

だからこそ重要なのは、より賢いモデルに全部寄せることではなく、工程を分けて、役割を分ける設計をすることだ

速くCursorやClaude Codeにも組み込まれるか、モデルとして選択できるようになったらいいな〜

t:
After playing with the model for a day I have some thoughts. Completely agree with Dr Khattab here.

There is no doubt one can build great software with JEV. If your product has a control-flow decision where the candidate actions are known beforehand - JEV is great.

That said, this model/API is severely limited - no token extraction, no ranking features, no control over complex output shapes, no way to produce nested decisions. You can't extract entities from text, coz this model is NOT a free-form token producer. But the shit is so fast and cheap that one can excuse the shorcomings - provided the usecase fits and you can work around the API.

The marketing does not mention any of that. And for good reason.

I am testing it inside my recommender system for pbd - and it works! As long as you can programatically/statically construct a list of choices, you can pass a context string + these choices into JEV, and it will give you the probability to pick each choice.

I think whats happening is that people who have been around deep learning can recognize what is going on under the hood with this model, and that these ideas have existed in the past as well. For years.

Some people who got into AI through API calling and ChatGPT are seeing the magic of token-level classification for the first time. And this idea of "parallel token processing" is absurdly attractive to them.

There is also the twitter cookie monsters who have jumped on the hype train and getting their cookies while the topic is still viral. I'm seeing some of the most nonsensical demos that have no real application in the real world beyond an eye-catching demo. They all go viral because they are indeed super impressive to look at. This is part of the problem for overselling what this model can do/what it actually is.

Once you start incorporating the model into a real product, you will quickly realize what the strengths are, and what the limits are.

Spent an hour on YT livestream today with the Jev model via the typesafe API. Thanks to typesafe team for helping out with credits.

The main use-case for this LM is to predict context aware decisions when the decision space of the problem is known apriori.

The biggest downside is that you CANNOT generate new tokens - it only works as a classifier + confidence-predictor. You cannot use it even for extraction or form-filling stuff. You always have to pass in a list of candidate answers as well.

IOW, you must programmatically create a candidate list BEFORE calling the API - and the model will output the probabilities for each entry given the context. You can send few shot examples and instructions too... dspy-style... but the output schema is fixed into 3 types of things: Choice (enums), Noul (boolean+probability), and Score (ordered value)

We also went into masked LM and parallel constrained decoding. We discussed theories about how the model functions - and how it happens so quickly.

Random thought: I feel like the next version of this model is probably going to be running small autoregressive/diffusion heads over the output token embeddings. This way prefill can still remain parallel, but arbitrary token output is also possible.

Jev should probably be all over your GTM stack...

Here are 10 high-value use cases for it:

1) Inbound lead qualification

Every time a lead comes in, Jev looks at:

• Company size
• Role
• Intent
• Source
• Website activity
• CRM history

Then decides:

• Route to sales
• Drop into nurture
• Send self-serve
• Ignore

Your reps stop wasting time sorting leads.

2) Outbound account prioritization

Instead of blasting a static list, Jev continuously scores which accounts are worth touching right now based on:

• Hiring activity
• Funding
• Website changes
• Intent signals
• Past engagement
• ICP fit

Your outbound team always works the best accounts first.

3) Next-best sales action

After every call, email, or CRM update, Jev chooses what should happen next:

• Call
• Email
• Wait
• Send proof
• Bring in a founder
• Move to nurture
• Close lost

This is where sales automation gets much more interesting than "send another follow-up."

4) Discount approval

A rep asks for 20% off.

Jev checks:

• Deal size
• Margin
• Account value
• Stage
• Competitor pressure
• Company rules

Then returns:

• Approve
• Counter
• Hold
• Escalate

You can give reps far more autonomy without letting margins get destroyed.

5) Lead response timing

Not every lead should get the same sequence at the same speed.

Jev decides whether the next touch should happen in:

• 5 minutes
• 2 hours
• Tomorrow
• 3 days
• Never

Based on intent and everything that happened before it.

6) Ad budget reallocation

Every few minutes, Jev can decide where the next dollar goes.

Campaign A is converting.
Campaign B is getting expensive.
Campaign C has better downstream revenue.

Jev shifts spend based on the outcome you actually care about, not just clicks.

7) Sales call escalation

During a live sales conversation, Jev watches the state of the deal and decides when to:

• Bring in an AE
• Pull in technical help
• Offer a case study
• Surface pricing
• Book the next meeting
• Do nothing

The useful part isn’t generating another sales script.

It’s choosing the right move at the right moment.

8) Churn intervention

A customer’s usage drops.

Jev looks at:

• Account value
• Product activity
• Support history
• NPS
• Contract date
• Previous interventions

Then decides:

• Ignore
• Send education
• Trigger CSM outreach
• Offer help
• Escalate internally

Now retention teams only step in when the intervention is actually worth it.

9) CRM automation

Most CRM automation is basically:

"If X happens, do Y."

Jev lets you make it:

"If X happens, inspect everything we know and choose between Y, Z, A, or nothing."

Lead ownership, lifecycle stage, follow-ups, alerts, and handoffs can all become decisions instead of hard-coded rules.

10) Human review queues

This might be the biggest one.

Let AI handle thousands of GTM actions, then have Jev decide which ones actually need a person.

• High-value account?
• Low confidence?
• Large discount?
• Unusual behavior?
• Important customer?

Send it to a human.

Everything else keeps moving.

LLMs can write the email, analyze the call, and generate the plan.

Jev decides what the GTM system actually does next.

It is probably still an attention mechanism, because we need to semantically process variable-length inputs, and the real jev is a foundation model in the sense that its large enough to be general-purpose.

t:
TypeSafe「Jev」、面白そう👀
タスクを細かく分解して、ここを判定し判断軸を持たせるということのよう。

元OpenAIのDiogo Almeidaらが
「チャットではすでに超人がいるのに、なぜ仕事は自動化されないのか」と問い、2年かけて出した判断専用モデル。

・入力は問い合わせ文やアプリの状態。
・返すのは「どの部署か」「緊急か」「基準を満たすか」といった型付きの答えと、その確率と信頼度。

文章は書かない。
その代わり速く、安く、プログラムがそのまま読める。

チャットの進化形ではなく「コードの中で使える賢いif文」。
それが正体。

既存LLMとの差は、強さの種類にある。

「LLMは人向け」
返信の下書き、要約、対話、長い推論は強い。
だが遅くて高く、JSONが壊れたり、自信過剰になったりする。
人が読んで直す前提が残る。

「Jevは機械向け」
出力の形を先に固定し、校正された確率だけを出す。
壊れた文字列で処理が止まらない。
自信が低ければ、そこで自動実行を止められる。

知能を増やす話というより、ソフトウェアが信頼して分岐できる形にした話のようだ。

LLMとの使い分けは置き換えではない。
・決まった計算や権限はコード
・意味の判定を何度も回すならJev
・文章を生む工程だけLLM

たとえばサポートなら、
・返品期限の判定はコード
・緊急度と担当部署と返金可否はJev
・お客様への返信文はLLM

エージェントなら、
・LLMが調べて書き、
・Jevが「正しい文脈を拾ったか」「出力は基準を満たすか」を途中で検査する

大きな問いを一発で投げず、狭い質問に分解してコードで合成する。
そこが本番に載るかの分かれ目になる。

これから変わるのは、画面のチャットより裏側だ。
判断が安く何度も呼べると、生成のたびに検査し、怪しいときだけ高いモデルや人に渡せる。

自動化は「一発で賢い答えを出す」ことから、「安く検証しながら進む」ことへ寄っていく。

競争も、何でも話せるかより、コードに埋め込んで止まらず動くかへ移る。

これは「神を作り出す」という話ではなく「現場の分岐を信頼できる部品にする」というストーリー。

t:
Jev : retour d'expérience.

Allez, moi aussi je me lance. J'ai testé le modèle de TypeSafe qui ne génère pas de texte.

J'ai monté 3 outils avec : un tri de tickets de support, un taggeur d'articles de blog, un classifieur de catalogue produits.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BEhbglltMSw

our first two jev use cases:

1. when you comment on a PR from Detail, we have an LLM check for whether the comment is asking Detail to do something (e.g. "remove this test") vs not (e.g. "hey teammate does this look right?") and when we interpret a comment as an ask, we react with an 👀 to ack that we're working on it. this is now happens in 400ms instead of 1200ms thanks to jev.

2. when we find a bug, we check if it's a dupe of a bug we've already reported. this can be tricky because unrelated code change can move the "same" bug to a new location, and we don't want to report twice in that case. but two bugs can be nearly identical in structure but in different places, and we want to flag both of them, e.g. the same missing auth check in two different routes. this is now a jev check.

in both cases, backtesting showed ~99.5% agreement with models that were 30x as expensive.

q.t:
JEV 的能力边界慢慢开始暴露了

前几天，Browser Use 创始人 @gregpr07 开源的那个爆火 Demo（7 秒订机票、成本 $0.0039）刷爆全网

但后面他亲自用 JEV 跑了一轮长链路任务实测，发现正确率很低，远远落后于GPT luna：

 • Luna：17 / 20 
• Jev Agent：1 / 20 

20 道复杂的现实任务，JEV 整整挂了 19 道……

那它之前为什么能做到 7 秒订机票？它到底强在哪里？

✅这是JEV擅长的：输入需求 ──> 填表 ──> 选航班 ──> 提交成功（毫无分叉，全是直道）

💥这是JEV做不到的：
【真实复杂长任务】
输入需求 ──> 弹窗拦截？ ──> 验证码？
                ↓               ↓
            [死胡同]         [死胡同]
               │                │
     JEV：零推理不会回溯，直接原地死锁 💥
     Luna+推理模型：回退上一步（Backtrack），切换策略绕行 ✅

客观来说，JEV 确实快到不可思议，但一旦进入真实的复杂环境，逻辑就全崩了：

Browser Use 创始人说： 浏览器交互从来不是简单的元素点击，而是极其复杂的【高维状态空间搜索】

在真实网页里，一个合格的 Agent 必须具备两个核心底层行为：
停下来深思（Think hard）
走不通时原路回退（Go back / Backtrack）
而 JEV 的推理能力（Reasoning）完全为 0。

看来Jev还有很长的路要走啊~~

q.t:
Jevのキラーアプリ、「意味で探す grep」を作った。

semgrep -e "顧客が怒っている" と打つと、"angry" も「怒」も含まない行まで拾ってきます。

正規表現の代わりに、TypeSafe AI の Jev（System One モデル）に 1 行ずつ「この行は○○の意味に合うか」を yes/no 確率で答えさせる。Jevの特性を活かして30 行をまとめて 1 リクエスト、200 行のログが 1 秒弱で返ります。依存ゼロ、Node 1 ファイル。

grepに準じるオプション体系。

・-e A -e B で OR、-a で AND、-v で AND NOT
・-r で再帰、-l でファイル名だけ、-A/-B/-C で前後の行、--color
・確率の閾値は --level loose / strict で調整

ベクトル検索と何が違うかというと、否定検索もできるし、話題の近さではなく「命題が成り立つか」を見るところです。「返金してほしい」と「返金処理が完了しました」は埋め込みではほぼ同じ距離ですが、「顧客が返金を求めている」という意味で引くと 0.98 と 0.10 に分かれます。だから AND や NOT がそのままブール演算として効きます。「返金の話だが要求ではない行」なども 1 コマンドで検索できます。

問合せは「意味」でおこなうので、多言語検索が普通に可能。日本語と英語の区別もフランス語もロシア語も、その混在文書からも検索できます。仏・露・独・西・中・韓14行を4言語（日・英・仏・露）の意味クエリで検証した結果、取りこぼしも誤爆もゼロで、どの言語で意味を書いても同様に機能します。

Spent some time testing #Jev from @typesafeai  on a use case I care about: matching a resume against real job descriptions.

I built a small demo called Rolewise. @metix_ai handles job retrieval; Jev handles the fit decision.

The setup:
- Parse the resume and generate editable search filters.
- Retrieve jobs and full descriptions through the Metix AI API.
- Send each resume–JD pair to Jev, with 20 requests in flight.
- Ask for one decision: suitable or not suitable.

One run: 838 jobs evaluated in 61.3 seconds. That excludes parsing and retrieval.

I started with multiple scoring dimensions, then simplified the task to a single fit decision. For this demo, I wanted to see whether Jev could help someone narrow a list of opportunities without adding another scoring system to interpret.

The recording shows actual requests completing—no simulated progress. Retrieval and evaluation are separate steps, so you can inspect the jobs before running Jev.

This is a throughput result, not an accuracy benchmark. I haven’t established how reliably those decisions agree with a human reviewer yet. That’s the next thing I’d test, especially on borderline cases.

Sharing this as a concrete Jev example. If you’re building something similar, I’d be curious how you’re defining “fit” and checking the results.

Job data/API: https://platform.metix.ai

想知道JEV的具体应用场景？可以参考这里的思路🤔

Jev 不是更好的聊天模型。它是系统里的判断层，官方文档其实已经写了五个应用场景：

一是自动化软件：代码管流程，它只做判断，后台可以跑百万次，不用人盯

二是实时应用：一百多毫秒出结果，能塞进界面、游戏、下一步动作

三是大数据处理：便宜到可以对海量文本做搜索、分类、抽特征

四是万能校验：查 prompt、推理、工具调用、幻觉、越狱，比再调一次大模型便宜得多

五是 Agent 工程：模型路由、挑上下文、报错检测、护栏，给 harness 加一层快决策

t:
After half a day with Jev, my mental model is simple:

LLMs are great writers. Jev is great at multiple-choice questions.

LLMs generate, explain, and reason through problems. Jev takes a situation and a list of possible answers, picks one, and tells you how confident it is. Your software can act on that answer.

That makes Jev a good fit for automation built around lots of small decisions.

An agent playing a game has to keep choosing whether to jump, dodge, attack, or move forward. A web crawler does the same kind of work: follow this link, skip that page, classify this result.

I once built a crawler to collect job listings from companies' official websites. It had to decide whether each link led to a job, whether the listing had expired, and which category it belonged to.

I want to rebuild it with Jev and see how it holds up.

I've been seeing a lot of fake looking demos online of people using Jev to play video games perfectly in real time.

I'm hella suss'd by the demos so i'm trying to build one right now. So far its kind of shit tbh especially since I don't have raw game state from WOW.

I'm essentially trying to recreate the game state from pixel data of key elements of the game and have Jev just make decisions on what to do next.

The issue is even if it decides what to do next I'll need an entire bot code that handles playing the game itself.

So if you had these two elements
1. perfect game state
2. bot code that knows how to play the game already

Then Jev is the perfect decision maker to give commands to the bot.
And to be very clear I have nothing against TypeSafe, it’s a great idea. I just run a healthcare startup which means we need control over deployments, so we can’t use Jev.

If you work at an enterprise or VC-backed startup building AI workflows:
1) DM me your email to get fast tracked off the waitlist
2) We’re hosting a 20 person exec dinner on October 14th around TechCrunch Disrupt - DM me if you’re interested

这两天一直在关注 Jev，我做的导航站现在已经收录了 287 个相关项目。

如果你刚拿到 Jev API，还不知道能拿它干什么，我建议优先看下面这 20 个：

（我没有按 Star 排，主要挑了三类：能马上跑起来的、能明显看出 Jev 优势的，以及脑洞特别大的。）

1. jev-ultrafast
Browser Use 做的高速浏览器 Agent。Jev 每一步只负责判断「做什么、点哪个元素」，需要输入文字时再叫小模型。Google Flights 搜一次航班完整跑完约 7 秒。

2. fast-jev-compaction
给 Claude Code 做上下文压缩。每次工具调用都先让 Jev 判断还有没有用，没用的直接删，留下来的原文不重写。

3. json-render + Jev
Vercel Labs 拿 Jev 试验实时生成 UI。Jev 不逐 Token 写 JSON，只负责选组件、属性和布局，火车票界面从 3.21 秒压到了 0.88 秒。

4. typesafe-mcp
最适合刚拿到 API 的人。直接把 Jev 接进 Claude Code、Claude Desktop、Codex 和 Pi，让大模型随时调用它做 Choice、Score、Noul 判断。

5. jev-mcp
更像一套现成的 Agent 判断工具箱。已经封装了事实核验、内容筛查、Prompt Injection 检测、语义排序、分类和信息提取。

6. SemDecide
把 Jev 做成命令行工具。可以直接在 Shell 里做分类、打分、过滤和判断，很适合接爬虫、CI 和数据流水线。

7. Jev Codex Router
先让 Jev 判断这一轮编程任务有多难，再决定该交给哪个档位的模型。很直观地展示了 Jev 做模型路由的玩法。

8. Winnow
给 Claude Code 做「上下文垃圾回收」。Read、Bash、Grep 吐出一大堆内容时，Jev 先判断哪些真的和当前任务有关。

9. Jev Review
代码审查前先过一遍 Jev，把高风险改动挑出来，再交给更贵的大模型或者人仔细看。

10. Blink
把 Jev 当代码库导航器。每走到一层目录，就判断哪些文件和当前问题最相关，再继续往下找。

11. jev-desktop
把 Jev 用到桌面自动化。它读系统无障碍树，判断下一步该操作哪个按钮、菜单或输入框。

12. typesafe-mario
让 Jev 玩《超级马里奥》。不看截图，直接读模拟器 RAM 里的结构化状态，再决定跑、跳和躲避。

13. jev-drone
拿 Jev 控无人机。底层飞控继续负责稳定和安全，Jev 只做爬升、刹车、穿越障碍这类上层判断。

14. OneVOneJev
直接做了一个 1v1 FPS。Jev 每个决策 tick 都要判断走位、视角、瞄准、开火和跳跃，很能体现低延迟的意义。

15. jev-trader
在 Monad 测试网上做高频做市。Jev 根据价差、收益和主动成交方向，判断下一步买还是卖。

16. Prism
更偏量化策略。它不直接让 Jev 下单，而是让 Jev 判断 toxic flow、市场压力、均值回归之类的状态，再交给原来的策略处理。

17. neo4jev
把 Jev 塞进知识图谱里。每走到一个节点，就让它判断下一条最值得走的边，再一路找下去。

18. jev-curate
拿 Jev 筛训练数据。大量 JSONL、Parquet 数据先做质量、相关性和风险判断，再决定哪些值得进后面的训练流程。

19. Canny
专门防 Coding Agent「嘴硬说自己做完了」。它会看工具输出、代码 Diff 和测试结果，再判断 Agent 的完成声明到底靠不靠谱。

20. killmyidea
这个最适合随手玩。输入一个创业点子，Jev 会从多个维度打分，最后给你 KILL、FIX 或 SHIP。

---

看下来，你就明白了：Jev 最适合的不是写文章、写代码，而是反复做那些「要不要、选哪个、打几分、下一步干什么」的小判断。

真正需要生成和长链推理，再交给大模型。

我已经整理了 287 个 Jev 开源项目，每个都核过公开源码和实际接入点。想继续翻的可以直接去这里搜（还有好玩的抽卡机制）：

https://logicrw.github.io/awesome-jev-projects/?v=1

拿到 Jev API 还不知道怎么玩的，基本能在里面找到一圈思路。

GLiClass gained 100 GitHub ✨ overnight. I suspect the buzz around Jev played a big part, and it’s exciting to see more interest in models that turn natural-language instructions into structured decisions.

Back in June 2023, we wrote about our first generalist zero-shot model for classification tasks:
https://blog.knowledgator.com/the-new-milestone-in-zero-shot-capabilities-its-not-generative-ai-9b5a081fbf27
Our long-term vision has been to push these models toward a broader range of tasks, including agentic decision-making. We have also worked on RL agents for path-based reasoning over knowledge graphs.

So, how might Jev work, and how does it compare with GLiClass?

TypeSafe describes parallel structured outputs and a training method called Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). Its launch materials do not disclose the exact architecture, parameter count, or complete training recipe. What follows is my hypothesis about the design space:
https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev

There are several plausible approaches, and we have explored multiple designs for related tasks:
• Bi-encoders that align text and label embeddings;
• Cross-encoders that jointly process each text–label pair;
• GLi*-style models that jointly encode text and multiple labels;
• Diffusion-based structured prediction;
• Multi-stage encoders with dedicated structured-output heads;
• A larger encoder with a small, constrained decoder.

These choices can also be combined. The trade-offs depend on input length, the number of questions and choices, interactions between labels, and whether representations can be cached and reused.

Given latency and performance characteristics, I would guess the size of the model is a few billion parameters, but it can be easily much larger well optimzied model.

My hypothesis would be broad supervised training followed by decision-focused RL, potentially using rewards from multi-step workflows. That could reinforce choices that improve task completion, while calibration would require attention to the quality of the predicted probabilities.
For GLiClass, we have already published an RL training approach that adapts PPO to multi-label classification:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.07662

For agentic workflows, state can live in the application and be passed into each model call—as structured context, history, or a compressed summary. Persistent behavior does not require persistent memory inside the model.

I also wouldn’t make “encoder or decoder?” the central question. Bidirectional encoders are a strong fit for classification, while causal backbones can also score decisions and benefit from incremental caching. The right choice depends on the workload and training setup.

On multimodality, Jev’s published Doom demo uses structured text state rather than images. Its documented interface currently focuses on text and structured state.

We remain focused on pushing open-source models toward frontier-level capabilities across more tasks. Stay tuned.

As a weekend project I set out to determine the prime factors of happiness also known as RSA-255.

I sent 1000 agents using Astra X high on newly freed up spare GPU capacity from workloads moving from LLMs to Jev and this is what they came up with

问了问NewMax，用Jev如何做Marketing：

1. 线索与客户分层（最直接的钱）
线索评分：官网表单、聊天记录、邮件往来 → "是否有明确采购意向？""预算是否 ≥ X？""是决策人吗？"每条线索几百毫秒出分，销售按置信度排序跟进

ICP 匹配：拿公司描述、职位标题判断是否符合目标客户画像，替代人工筛 LinkedIn / 展会名单

意图信号识别：从客服对话、社区发言中判断"正在比较竞品""准备续约""有流失风险"

CRM 清洗：行业归类、公司去重（A 和 B 是同一家？）、职级标准化——过去营销运营最头疼的脏活，一次跑全量

2. 内容生产流水线的"质检员"
Jev 不写文案，但可以给 LLM 或人写的文案当闸门：

品牌合规：语气是否符合品牌调性、有没有用禁用词、有没有夸大宣传（"最好""第一"）、是否触碰广告法

平台适配：这条是否适合小红书/公众号/X 的风格；标题党程度打分

多版本预筛：LLM 生成 50 个标题，Jev 按"清晰度 / 点击欲 / 品牌一致性"打分，人只看 Top 5

法务前置：医疗、金融、教育等受监管行业，每条内容先过一遍"是否含承诺性表述"，高置信直接拦，中间转人工

这一条的价值在于把审核从瓶颈变成默认步骤——以前一天审 50 条，现在每条内容生成时自动过。

3. 用户生成内容与社媒监听

评论/提及分类：情感、是否投诉、是否询价、是否提及竞品、是否需要回复。上千条评论几秒跑完，运营只处理需要动作的

舆情预警：实时判断"这条负面是否可能扩散"（KOL 发的？带截图？情绪激烈？），达到阈值才报警

UGC 素材筛选：从海量用户晒单里判断"画面里有产品吗""可以用作宣传素材吗""涉及未成年人吗"

KOL/达人初筛：内容垂直度、受众匹配度、有没有争议性历史发言——按维度打分，替代人工翻主页

4. 投放与实验

广告素材预打分：上线前对几百个创意变体打"和落地页一致性""视觉是否清晰""是否符合平台审核"，减少被拒和无效花费

搜索词/关键词分类：SEM 里几万个搜索词判断意图（品牌词 / 竞品词 / 信息型 / 交易型），自动决定否词和出价策略

落地页-广告匹配检测：判断点击后的页面是否兑现了广告承诺（影响质量分）

A/B 实验的定性维度：量化指标之外，用 Jev 给每个变体的用户反馈打标签，快速看出"为什么 B 赢"

5. 个性化与实时触达
这是 Jev 延迟优势最能兑现的地方：
站内实时决策：用户浏览行为 + 上下文 → "现在弹优惠券吗""推哪一类内容""该不该触发客服介入"——100 ms 内能进页面渲染链路

邮件/推送的发送门控：每封自动化邮件发出前判断"这个用户当前状态还适合收这封吗"（刚投诉过的人不要发促销）

对话式营销的路由：聊天机器人中判断用户当前阶段（了解 / 比较 / 犹豫 / 准备下单），决定走哪条话术分支，LLM 只负责生成那句话

动态受众分群：不用等数据团队建模，运营用自然语言定义分群规则（"近期表现出价格敏感的高价值用户"），Jev 全量打标

6. 竞品与市场情报
竞品官网、发布会、社媒的变化监控：这条更新是否涉及定价 / 新功能 / 目标市场变化

行业新闻分类：是否与我们相关、紧急程度、该推给哪个团队

电商竞品评论挖掘：竞品用户最常抱怨什么（按预设维度打标），直接变成自己的卖点文案素材

7. 效果归因与报表的"语义层"

客服记录、退货原因、NPS 开放题——过去只能看数字，现在把开放文本编码成结构化列，直接进 BI

销售通话摘要打标：客户最在意的三个点是价格、交付还是服务

Browser Use 把 Jev 接进网页 agent，做出了一个约 7 秒查出苏黎世到伦敦航班的 demo。计时从初始页面观察完成后开始，包含后续操作和加载，任务到查出航班结果为止。

之前聊 Jev，我的疑问是 classifier 已经很成熟了，拿个 base model 做后训练，究竟差在哪里。现在实际案例多了，至少可以具体讨论它在 agent 里能接手什么工作了。

这个 demo 会先读取网页 DOM，把按钮、输入框、下拉选项整理成带编号的元素表。Jev 根据任务和页面状态，选择下一步操作以及目标元素，再由浏览器代码执行。需要填写文字时，另外调用 Mercury 生成内容。

原本开放的网页操作，被程序整理成了一组选择题。

从接口行为理解，Jev 在做的接近于 p(选项 | 状态、问题、候选项)。候选项可以跟着页面变化，这一页是选出发地，下一页可能是选航班。它需要理解这些选项的含义，不用为每个页面重新训练一个分类器。
这比固定标签分类多了一层泛化要求，但动态候选项和语义分类本身，也算不上全新的研究方向。

它在这个场景里能快起来，还因为多个问题可以一起算。

程序同时问下一步做什么、如果要点击该点哪里、如果要输入该填哪个框。结果回来后，假如选了点击，就只使用点击目标，其他分支直接丢掉。

官方把这个叫 speculative fan-out。提前计算可能用到的分支，省掉先拿到一个答案、再发下一次请求的等待。Jev 又直接返回结构化决策，不需要逐 token 写出一段动作描述。

这里并行的是同一页面状态下的问题。点击后页面发生变化，下一步还是得重新观察，不能把整条操作流程一次算完。

所以在能够可靠读取 DOM 的网页上，Jev 可以承担一部分原本交给通用 LLM 的动作选择。程序已经把可操作对象列出来了，模型选编号就行，执行前再由代码检查元素是否还有效。

但它没有解决通用 computer use 的全部问题。这个 demo 的决策过程不看截图，遇到 canvas、只有图像的界面，或者拿不到结构信息的桌面软件，还是需要视觉理解和定位。Jev 选出了合法编号，也照样可能点错按钮。

DOM 加元素编号本来就在 browser agent 里使用了。Jev 带来的变化，是把其中反复发生的选择做得更快。效果也很依赖外围工程，同样的模型，Browser Use 优化运行代码后，三组对照的中位耗时从 9.45 秒降到了 7.09 秒。

其他人的体验也能看到这种取舍。

Every 用 12 段合成文本做写作检查，Jev 每段中位耗时 0.35 秒，Fable 5.1 high 是 8.83 秒。但预设的 7 个问题，Jev 找出 6 个，Fable 全部找到，漏掉的那个 Jev 连测三次都没发现。

Pi 社区也有人尝试用它检查 agent 的工具调用。使用者的反馈是便宜、快，但问题得写得明确，还要设计问题之间的组合。模型负责判断哪些动作有风险，开发者仍然要定义检查什么、结果怎么处理。

至于 RLCD，目前公开说明主要讲它要训练出经过校准的概率。比如大量被赋予 80% 概率的事件，实际发生比例也应该接近 80%，这样程序才有依据决定自动执行还是升级处理。具体训练方法和底层架构，公开资料还不足以还原，不能直接脑补成某种分类头就算解析完了。

我觉得这些案例已经能说明实际用途。一个 agent 连续操作很多步，每一步都只是选按钮、判断是否完成、检查有没有问题，把这些调用做快，整个任务的等待就能少很多。

不过，之前关于 base model 后训练的疑问还在。现有实测主要拿它和通用生成模型比较，还缺一个认真训练过的小模型或分类器，在相同输入、相同候选项和接近成功率的条件下，对比延迟与成本。这个比较才能说明，Jev 的优势究竟有多少来自模型方法本身。

q.t:
TypeSafe 新发布的 Jev，主打不生成文字，只返回选项、概率和置信度。光看这些功能，我确实会觉得，拿个 base 模型后训练，再接个分类头，也能做啊。分类器已经是很成熟的技术了。

预训练模型接分类头，本来就可以直接输出分类概率。把答案限制在 A/B/C，也能保证它不会输出 D。所谓零幻觉如果指的是这个，和模型能不能选对是两回事。

Jev 允许开发者用自然语言定义问题和候选项，可以理解为估计 p(选项 | 输入状态、问题、候选集)。这比只认固定标签的业务分类器通用，但同样可以作为 base 模型的多任务后训练目标。难点在于换到没训练过的任务以后，判断质量还能保留多少。
它把同一份输入上的多个问题独立、并行求值，省掉了逐 token 写出完整答案的过程。直接给候选项打分，确实可能比生成一整段 JSON 快很多。但分类头本来也不需要生成文本，单凭这个对比看不出新架构的贡献。公开材料也没说明底层如何共享计算，一次 API 调用不等于只跑一次前向传播。

它的训练方法 RLCD 强调概率校准。给出 80% 概率的那组预测，长期看应该大约有 80% 正确。分类准确率高，不代表概率可信，一个正确率 90% 的模型，也可能动不动就报 99% 的把握。

这个目标有实际意义。程序需要根据概率决定自动执行还是转人工，同样选 A，51% 和 99% 应该触发不同处理。

但校准也有成熟方法。交叉熵、Brier score 可以用于训练概率预测，温度缩放可以做后处理。目前这些公开材料没有给出 RLCD 的奖励函数、训练配方和消融实验，还没法判断它相对常规训练加校准，多解决了什么问题。

Jev 的 confidence 也是从选项概率分布计算出来的统计量。分布很集中，说明模型偏向某个答案，不能单凭这一点认定它可靠。

如果它能让开发者直接用自然语言定义分类任务，省去准备数据、训练和部署的工作，同时保持低延迟、低成本，这个产品当然有意义。成熟技术做成好用的服务，本身就能解决问题。

不过，既然主张新架构和新训练方法，就应该和经过多任务后训练、带分类头和校准、支持批量推理的模型比较。在未见任务上测准确率、校准误差，以及相同错误率下能自动处理多少请求，再比较延迟和成本。这样的结果才能说明 Jev 到底做到了什么。

Jev is now open to everyone.

Here's what it actually is.

AI models read your text and write text back. Then your code has to parse that text and hope it's in the right shape.

Jev skips that. It reads plain text or JSON, but it never writes a paragraph. It answers with typed decisions your code can use directly.

Say you are building an email agent and this lands in the inbox: "Loved the demo! Can you send pricing? We want to start next week." You give it to Jev and ask:

– Which team should get this? (a choice)
– How excited is this person, 0 to 10? (a score)
– Is this a hot lead? (yes/no with a probability)

It answers all of it in one go, in about 70 to 500 milliseconds, with a confidence level on every answer. So your code can act when it's sure and send it to a human when it's not.

Think of it as an AI you call like a function, not one you chat with.

Super cheap: input costs $0.042 per million tokens. Output is free.

q.t:
Jev from @typesafeai is great, but way overhyped.  

I fine-tuned an open-weight model on my Mac that beats Jev by almost 10pp, and is 8x faster.

It took less than an hour and runs on my local CPU.  Yes, it's task-specific.  Meaning it doesn't beat Jev on every task.  But that's ok:

Jev is pretty good at zero-shot general classification, but a quick fine-tuning run allows GLiNER 2.5 (open weights, built by @fastinoAI) to beat it on a specific task as a specialized classifier.

In this experiment, I tested default GLiNER 2.5 vs Jev vs Fine-tuned GLiNER 2.5 on the Banking77 benchmark from @huggingface.  

Default GLiNER 2.5 trailed Jev by ~9pp, despite being 10x faster. 

After fine-tuning GLiNER 2.5 on ~10k training samples (this took about 51 minutes on my M4 Max), I retested.

Fine-tuned GLiNER 2.5 gained ~18pp of classifying accuracy on the task, beating Jev by ~9pp. 

I'm betting that while Jev thrives as an easy plug-and-play endpoint for non-recurring classification tasks, most teams shipping to production will just take a little bit of time of front to fine-tune open-weight classifiers for tasks.  

If you can spend an hour fine-tuning to get:
- 8-10x speed boost
- 10pt accuracy lift
- AND it can run locally on your hardware?  

That seems like a no-brainer.  

So yes, @rileybrown, it seems like you can fine-tune  your own "jev" on your data :)
