q.t:
you can make any open source model behave like jev with just a bit of inference engineering.  

it's shockingly easy. to prove it, we built a new endpoint we're calling deepseek-v4.1-flash-jev. see the demo below. here's how it's done:

sglang (an inference engine) offers a scoring endpoint in addition to the normal generation one. in scoring mode, given an input & set of possible answers, it forces the model to produce probabilities for each one. example:

> input: what is most common letter in abcccde?
> possible answers: a, b, c
> output: (c, 0.9), (b, 0.0.5), (a, 0.05)

getting the above behavior instead of streamed output is as simple as using sglang's /v1/score endpoint instead of /generate. there's just one other trick required.

for deepseek, you have to add a closing think tag before the response. this forces a direct answer instead of  a reasoning trace. if you want reasoning, you can do that too, but imo that makes things too slow to be worth it.

dsv4.1 flash is not as good as jev, but if we had enough spare compute to experiment with this same approach for a larger model then i think the decision quality would be at least as good, if not better.

also, somewhat unrelated, i think decision-making models kill all prospecting & sourcing work. i would have absolutely killed to have jev or similar when i was recruiting @mintlify. absolutely incredible.

q.t:
Top 5 Jev Alternatives:
__

I have been running a benchmark since this morning on every Jev alternative against Jev. So far, none have been it on accuracy but some have slightly less accuracy with better speed. So far, here are my rankings... And be mindful, there are 40 still in queue + I am automatically scraping for more on X which get placed in the queue by my agents. 

1. djev - Slightly lower accuracy and slightly faster speed than Jev. Worthy tradeoff. (https://djev.dev/)
2. Simplejev-qwen38-27b - Best open source model you can replace Jev with today but requires the ability to run a 27B model. You may need a DGX Spark or similar. (https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B). I have a feeling the Simplejev version of Qwen Flash Next will beat Jev on speed and accuracy. @MiaAI_lab I would love if you can Simplejev your fantastic model and beat Jev with open source! (Simplejev-qwen36-35b-a3b is basically interchangeable and you should always choose the former). (https://simple-jev.featherless.ai/)
3. Reflex-4b - This is actually one of my favorites. It is a great tradeoff between speed and accuracy. It is 2-3x faster than Jev but 5% or so less accurate. That said, I bet somebody can tune it or something. It is apache 2.0 for reference.  (https://huggingface.co/YannQi/R-4B)
4. Decider-2b - I love this one because it did the whole test in like 4 minutes or something ridiculous. It is about 10x faster than Jev and completely local. It's accuracy is a 5% less... So it is up to you if that tradeoff is worth it. Considering the size, you can slap this thing on a work computer and get stuff done quickly. Love this one. (https://huggingface.co/Mapika/decider-2b)
5. Lastly is Laya... It is the historical model that did not get enough love. It does not seem to be as good as Jev, but is is very fast on a GB10 GPU... It's accuracy is 62.5% which is not worth it to me. I would say anything less than 70% is a nogo. Definitely not worth the tradeoffs when we consider a faster and higher accuracy model like decider-2b.

Do not let people convince you that Jev is not special or is a tool we always have. It is the frontier of this paradigm... But it is losing ground quickly and I might find a better model by tomorrow. 

The benchmarks are automatically updated here. If you want my agents to test one, please send the name below and they will pick it up!

http://bench.jakecuth.com

q.t:
大开眼界，跑完交易回测算法，我见识到了 Jev 交易决策的效率和质量，况且只是简单地跑了几个算法，77 天收益率高达 +6.71%。

跑完之后剩一个问题：这一堆 JSON 怎么给人看？

我把可视化设计稿丢给蚂蚁百灵刚开源的 Ling-3.0-flash-VL，让它照着写前端，最后输出视频。

我没给它设计稿标注，也没给它组件库。它自己看图，直接构建出动态仪表盘页面：净值曲线、三个策略的持仓条、当日决策流、右上角的加速倍数。然后它用 playwright 逐帧截图，390 帧压成 13 秒，浓缩了 95 天的新闻与行情。

说到具体的方法论：我把 NewsHub 攒了三个月的投资日报，一天一份丢给 OpenRouter 上的 Jev 1.13。我给它当天的日报和当前持仓，它能迅速输出每个标的买、卖还是不动，附带三个选项的概率和置信度。后面的程序拿着这些概率去调仓、按 Binance 真实小时级别 K 线成交、算净值、对账。

77 天，3 个策略（动量、逆向、宏观），5 个标的（BTC / ETH / SPY / QQQ / XAU），1155 个决策。全程只花了 $0.09（Ling-3.0-flash-VL目前在OpenRouter免费😺），跑完 87 秒，单次调用 1.1 秒，零次失败。

当然，现在还远没到干死基金经理的程度。动量策略 +6.71%，但同期等权买入持有是 +13.2%，它没跑赢。而另外两个策略表现比较拉胯，一个 −1.0%，一个 −10.3%。

🔥 Jev 和多模态 Ling-3.0-flash-VL，一个负责判断，一个负责看懂和展示。
Ling-3.0-flash-VL 总参数 124B，但 MoE 每 token 只激活约 5.5B。

这对 Visual Agent 很重要，极为广阔的知识，以及极低的激活，能做到又快又好。

一个1500粉的号，两年没发声，9月15日一句 “After co-inventing ChatGPT” 把stealth产品、新模型类别、DCVC领投的4000万融资一次性打出去，主帖收获两千万+浏览。创始人履历确实很硬，InstructGPT核心作者，但是确实话术也做了包装，RLHF不是他一个人发明的，与此同时，ChatGPT也没有所谓的发明人。

1/ 宣发并非自然爆发，而是高投入冷启动

http://doomers.ai 接了内容策略、发布包和当天seeding。创始人号从约1500涨到9万+，官号从200到6万+。宣发预算打满后，在发布后第一小时就铺天盖地把工程师和founder们时间线填满了Jev内容。

冷启动种子是买的，但后面几千万浏览是算法主动承接。一场大约十万美元级别的发布战役，撬出平均launch二十多倍的曝光，ROI可以说非常好了。

2/ 创作者侧的模版化生产

用心留意的朋友，应该会观察到Jev相关内容反复出现同一套结构：先一句“LLM写字 / Jev做决定”，再塞工单路由、风控、agent选工具，最后一段屏幕录像。Mario、Doom、Browser Use找航班，全是同一套演示语法。

还有一句比RLCD好传播一百倍的产品句：输出token定价为零。创作者不需要理解训练方法，复述“$0.042/M输入、输出免费、70–500ms”就够了。

模版的作用是让技术观众在不同账号上反复撞见同一个可理解的差异。看起来像有机讨论，但底层是可复制、低成本的叙事零件。

3/ 第一批技术群体跟上，铺量后飞轮效应出现

英文圈先行发动，Vercel高管公开测分类任务，有人开源约束解码复刻，有人把Jev接进browser agent。三天内社区冒出LiteLLM透传、Instructor预设、Pi路由插件、jev-browser、两个MCP server，中文圈接着快速承接。

而真实用户，吐槽也不少，比如有人拿到key之后发现打游戏泛化不如Astra，强项是快和便宜，这种帖比重复200x口号更真实可信。

4/ 渠道接棒，平台开始借它给自己引流

9/16 Vercel AI Gateway上架，官方称付费团队24小时渗透约13%，历史最快，随即把Jev免到9月25日

9/18 OpenRouter上架 typesafe/jev-1.13，只走Decisions端点，chat/completions直接拒绝

这些平台在用当下最快冷启动的模型给自己的Gateway获客，飞轮效应进一步加速。

5/ 链路复盘

创始人给一句可核验的身份，适当包装
产品差异压成对比句和一个反常识定价，让创作者能直接套模版
发布当天只服务第一小时，剩下交给算法
发动顶级平台一起 co-PR，启动互利飞轮

How to use it:

- Make an API key
- Call the decisions endpoint: /api/alpha/decisions
- Set the model to ~typesafe/jev-latest
- Send it a "state" (what's going on) and "questions" (what you want decided, plus the options)

ChatGPT and Claude write you an answer word by word. 

Jev doesn't write at all. You give it the options and it sends back a probability for each one, plus how confident it is.

- "My card was charged twice" went to billing, 100%, in about a second
- We hooked it up to Tetris and it picked every move in about half a second
- A whole game cost less than half a cent

"DiffusionGemma as Jev" showcases the power of non-autoregressive architectures.

While Jev demonstrates the value of rapid decision models, running DiffusionGemma in this paradigm leverages canvas diffusion to evaluate structured choices in a single parallel pass:

⚡ ️Massive Parallelism: Denoises across an open canvas in a single step instead of sequential autoregressive token generation (~0.2s on a DGX spark).

🧠 Full Bidirectional Attention: Allows every option to attend to the full context concurrently, yielding well-calibrated decision distributions.

👁️ Multimodal Grounding: Inherits Gemma 4's spatial vision capabilities for complex visual and text decisions.

Read more about this approach here:

t:
Jev is genuinely interesting.

It compresses a workflow we’ve spent decades doing in data science, including building a clean dataset, training a classification or regression model, evaluating it, calibrating it, and deploying it, into an API call.

It could democratize a major part of applied data science, and that’s awesome.

But it is NOT a singularity, and “nobody saw this coming” is just plain silly.

The foundational ideas have existed for years. Jev appears to combine them with genuinely impressive speed, cost, and ergonomics.

But “decision models may become bigger than LLMs” is currently just an unsupported prediction.

LLMs were revolutionary because they created a general interface to both humans and technology. Text becomes code, code uses tools, and tools can operate practically anything.

Jev doesn’t have that interface. It makes predefined decisions inside systems that programmers still have to build.

ChatGPT was an insane leap for technology and humanity as a whole. Jev may become extremely valuable infrastructure, but it is not the revolution that hype influencers want you to believe it is.

For context, I have a master’s in AI from VU Amsterdam, spent a decade working in data science and machine learning, and previously worked at @turinginst.

q.t:
Mark my words: @typesafeai JEV is not only the new hottness, it's a genuine phenomenon as a whole new wave of normie programmers learn how to plug fast, cheap intelligence into their otherwise normal codebases.

Feels like Xmas 2025 all over again. I predict that all the major frontier labs will have JEV-style offerings within the next few months. I will not be surprised one bit if decision models end up being bigger than LLMs in the long run.

If you think I'm being hyperbolic, consider that hacking LLMs into production codebases has literally been my focus for over 3 years now and I wrote the definitive book on the subject: Patterns of Application Development Using AI

We are definitely in a singularity, because nobody I know saw this coming.

Turned @typesafeai’s Jev into a next-word predictor over 30k words.

It can’t generate text. For every word, it picks 1 of 254 meaning groups, then picks the word.

Sometimes it’s weirdly right:

“what day comes after monday” → tuesday
“how many legs does a spider have” → viii
“is the earth flat” → no
“i am sad” → sorry you sad understand

The fun part is where it breaks: the answer is often in there, but the sentence falls apart.

“what is the biggest animal” → is the is im is whale
“who wrote hamlet” → is was william
“tell me a joke” → sure tell joke chicken
“what is 2 plus 2” → two

Jev picks. Jev does not write.

tr: Jeth is different than ChatJPT or Claude in one big way. He can't write. It is a really good classifier. You describe your categories in plain English and it gives back responses in one or three ways. One, it can pick from the list you give it. Is this support ticket for billing or technical or sales? And it can respond back like consider technical 85% sure. Two, yes or no? They call it null, so a question like is the customer asking for refund? And Jeth's response could be 0.95, which means it's leaning heavily towards yes. Three, a score on a scale you write. Like how angry is the customer? Calm, frustrated or furious? Jeth could save 1.6 between frustrated and furious. Now because it can't write, it cannot invent answer, it cannot hallucinate. And it comes back in a fraction of a second at the fraction of the cost. So the bottom line is ChatJPT is built for your chatting or talking, whereas Jeth is built for your structured logical statements.

Jev makes a strong case for a dedicated decision layer in application design and marketing work.

a surprising amount of that work comes down to a small judgment:

→ which model should handle this request?
→ which topic or hook fits this post?
→ does this draft need human review?

here's how the pieces fit:

Jev: take the relevant context, answer bounded questions, return choices and probabilities.

code: apply rules and thresholds, enforce permissions, route the work.

LLM: write the response, draft the campaign, or handle deeper reasoning.

independent questions can run together. uncertain decisions can go to a stronger model or a person.

the part worth getting right is the handoff. a valid label can still be wrong. confidence needs checking against your own examples.

start with one low-risk decision. run it beside the current workflow. count the mistakes and review work alongside the model cost.

that's how a cheap model earns a place in the workflow.

tr: ways to think about policy engine. If you're trying to apply like RBAC or other things is effectively classification of the action. And then the life cycle that goes around that right. So that is basically can we decide what this thing is trying to do and then also enforce whatever action based on our policy that we need to take. So when I saw Jeff, the first thing that came to mind was basically a policy engine because it handles the semantic classification really, really well. And so what you're seeing on screen is basically Claude is preparing the browser use action to fill in like a particular field. And then Jeff is basically looking at the proposed code that is being executed and deciding whether or not it's going to allow or deny each one based off of the role. And so this particular scenario, we are an editor. We have the ability to both do things as well as like log in. And you'll notice that basically Jeff is effectively everything through, right? But if we go and end this and we spin up another session, we're going to switch over to our read only role and we're going to see what the difference looks like. And so in this case, what happens is that our task is the exact same. Our website is the exact same. So Claude is going to take all the same actions. It's going to fill in the username, fill in the password dynamically. Jeff is going to allow those. It's going to allow it to look around. The store. But then what's going to happen is Claude is going to try to add to the cart. And in this particular scenario, what Jeff is going to flag based off of the context of the action that's happening, the website that we're on and the tasks that the user is given, it's going to identify the fact that adding to cart is actually not allowed within that read only action. And I think this is a really kind of exciting thing to explore. Because doing like semantic policy evaluation at runtime is both something you need to be super low latency. But also be incredibly accurate. And so we can see on the right here, this was blocked because it violates kind of what this role is allowed to do, which is to kind of change state. And you'll notice that we just didn't execute that click this time.

q.t:
I used Jev to classify 1,018 AI research papers.

The result: $0.08 total cost and 256ms median end-to-end latency per paper.

The pipeline was:

1. Summarize each paper with DeepSeek V4 Flash
2. Send the title + summary + 24 possible topics to Jev
3. Use Jev to classify each paper
4. Visualize everything on http://1kpapers.com

The summaries cost $3.99 on @togethercompute. The classifications cost $0.08 on @typesafeai.

So for just over $4 of inference, I ended up with a pretty useful way to explore the top AI research papers from the past year.

I think this is where things are heading: different models for different parts of the workflow, instead of using one model for everything.

I’m running evals on the Jev classifications before replacing the current ones, but the site is already live: http://1kpapers.com

q.t:
Frankly I didn’t get this until today

Here’s the non-technical friendly way to understand Jev: 👇🏼

Problem: LLMs often feel slow for a lot of app work because developers force it to “write” an answer every time 

Like asking someone to write a full paragraph just to say yes or no. 

Then the app/ software has to read that paragraph, pick out the answer, and hope LLMs didn’t invent something weird.

Jev is a fresh new take that skips the writing. Built by the @typesafeai team. One of them Diogo who is on the video below co-created ChatGPT while at OpenAI.

You give Jev a situation, ask a clear question with clear options, and it comes back with a decision plus how confident it is.

Jev’s comparision with LLMs are wild:
• 20–200x faster
• 40–400x cheaper (and output tokens are free because they are too cheap to meter. What?!!!)

So Jev is not a better chatbot. More like a smart yes/no button decision maker your app can press a thousand times.

Hope that helps? Lmk if you got any Qs below

q.t:
this is the easiest way to understand Jev:

LLMs generate answers.

Jev makes decisions.

that sounds like a small difference, but it actually changes the entire use case.

say you give a normal LLM this:

“here’s a user, their account history, payment behavior, support chats, device data, etc.

tell me if this looks risky.”

the LLM might reason through it and return:

“yes, this looks high risk.”

maybe in JSON if you ask nicely.

with Jev, you define the possible decisions upfront:

risk:

* low
* medium
* high

manual review:

* yes
* no

and Jev returns something closer to:

risk = high (96%)
manual review = yes (91%)

that’s basically the product.

it’s not trying to be another ChatGPT.

it’s more like an AI-native if statement.

instead of:

if transaction > $10,000:
review()

you can start thinking more like:

if “does this behavior look suspicious?” > 95%:
review()

and that opens up a pretty interesting category of software.

a few assumptions I had at first that turned out to be wrong:

1. “so it’s just a classifier?”

kind of, but that undersells it.

the input can be messy real-world context, and you can ask multiple typed questions about that state at once.

fraud?
churn?
escalate?
eligible?
priority?

all from the same input.

2. “so it replaces GPT / Claude?”

not really.

I actually think the interesting architecture is:

Jev decides WHAT needs to happen

Claude / GPT reason or generate WHEN deeper intelligence is needed

normal code executes the deterministic stuff.

Jev becomes the routing layer.

3. “it can’t hallucinate?”

this one needs nuance.

if your allowed answers are:

LOW
MEDIUM
HIGH

Jev won’t suddenly invent:

“EXTREMELY HIGH 🚨”

the output structure is constrained.

but it can still be wrong.

HIGH at 92% can still be the wrong decision.

so “no hallucinations” doesn’t mean “always correct.”

4. “why not just force an LLM to return JSON?”

you can.

we already do this everywhere.

but you still deal with generation latency, schema validation, retries, weird outputs, confidence estimation and a lot of glue code.

Jev is designed around the decision itself rather than text generation.

5. “why should I care?”

because most software is ultimately a giant tree of:

if this → do that
if this → route here
if this → escalate
if this → reject
if this → ask a human

Jev is basically asking:

what if those if statements could understand messy human context?

that’s a much more interesting framing than “another AI model.”

I can see this being very useful for:

fraud / risk
support routing
moderation
PR / QA automation
lead scoring
compliance
workflow orchestration
agent routing

especially as the cheap + fast decision layer sitting in front of larger reasoning models.

early tech, obviously.

but the category itself makes a lot of sense.

Who decided to call it Jev and not Instinct

With the launch of the Matrix model back in March, I was fairly close to a Jev-like architecture. 

Here is where I was
- Frozen pretrained backbone + small trained heads. 
A Judge head, a domain-router MoE, a complexity head, etc., ~278M trainable params. That is exactly the architecture the Jev teardown points to (a pretrained decoder + a decision readout).
- Score in one forward pass, no text generation. The Matrix model did not generate, it read a score straight off a pooled representation in a single pass. That's the defining Jev principle ("don't generate a verdict, read it from the representation"), applied to reranking instead of action-choice.
- Reading decisions from internal representations, not generated tokens. Jev teardown framed the whole proposition as "retain a pretrained LLM's knowledge
but replace generated confidence claims with decision probabilities read directly from its internal representations." That's literally what Matrix's Judge head and reranker do.

Here is what Jev taught
- RLCD, Calibration as the training objective: training the probabilities to be calibrated via proper scoring rules.
- A general "typed questions over shared state" surface. Jev generalized: encode any state once, ask many typed questions sharing the KV cache. Matrix stayed domain-specific.
- Options that interact. Jev scores the whole option list at a final-position head, so adding a 5th option shifts the others. Matrix's reranker scores each query-doc pair
independently.

So I was on the right track: frozen backbone + scoring head, no generation, before Jev launched. 🤷‍♂️ What it taught is the objective (train for calibration) and the generalization (typed questions over shared state).

Jevons Paradox
Now I am taking all these learnings, for a local, on-device Jev-like model as part of the Hyperspace agentic system. It's called Paradox. Already built it's v1 to validate the possibilities: that a local, API-free, Jev-accurate decision engine runs on a laptop and decides real pages correctly in a hybrid setup; measured that
its weak spot is multi-step decision quality which will be solved by Paradox v2. 

More abundance of this type of a model, from Jev's datacenters to running it on-device, the better it will be for society. 

h/t @NielsRogge, @harshagundal, and @4rcherhume (architecture deep-dive) and @CompleteSkeptic 🫡

Seems to me that the best application for @typesafeai System One models will be: *the AI router / controller* of the system. Let me explain... 

This demo by @allietheicon of Jev's real-world capabilities is incredibly cool.

Traditionally in automation engineering there are 3 main building blocks: sensors (get info), actuators (perform actions) and controllers (decide what to do). It seems to me that a very compelling AI system design going forward will have System One-like model right at the input of the system playing a role of controller/gateway/router that then decides incredibly fast: 1) perform a deterministic action, 2) delegate to an LLM, 3) loop back or exit.

Performance characteristics match well with a general concept of a router. In a way it's reminiscent of Karpathy's "cognitive core" idea

It'll be interesting to see the architectures that will pop-up: system-one + LLMs + code-mode + realtime. https://x.com/karpathy/status/1938626382248149433

q.t:
高频使用了几天JEV，慢慢摸到了它的能力边界

几天高频实测下来，我最大的感受是：Jev 是一个极其依赖使用者的工具。它能发挥多大价值，完全取决于你给它定的约束有多严格，把复杂的开放任务交给它是行不通的

--Jev 的中文适配能力较差。官方文档明确标注 CJK（中日韩）准确率偏低。英文短文本表现相对稳定。我实测过，JEV中文的准确率简直就是在乱来......

--Jev 没有推理能力。典型的例子是 Browser Use 创始人 @gregpr07 实测的长程浏览器交互，Jev 最终测试结果为 1/20，落后于具备推理能力的 Luna（17/20）。浏览器操作涉及状态空间搜索与路径回溯，Jev 不具备多步状态推演能力

--Jev 无法应付真实复杂的非沙盒网页。X上公开展示的流畅演示，多运行在结构规范、无干扰的封闭沙盒中，包括我自己的邮件分发演示，主要用于直观展示其执行速度。面对真实网页中未清洗的 DOM、异步加载与突发弹窗，JEV缺乏应对能力

--Jev 的“零幻觉”并不代表判断正确。官方文档说明其仅保证输出符合预定义的 JSON Schema 数据类型，CEO 亦确认模型存在自信选错的情况..

--Jev 无法胜任动态参数的工具调用。在实际 Agent 工具调用通常需要动态生成参数（例如指定代码修改行号、生成代码片段或自定义检索词），此类无限维的参数空间JEV的能力无法覆盖

--Jev 高度依赖清晰的边界限制。在规则复杂的任务下，低延迟与低成本是事实，但前提是必须建立在定义明确的封闭边界上，否则输出的大多是错误决策

--Jev 无法输出推理依据。它仅返回最终的选项或数值，不包含思考过程（CoT）。在需要解释决策原因、人工复核或合规审计的场景中，无法提供追溯依据

总结来说，Jev 的适用场景非常细分，而且高度取决于开发者如何去定义它的运行环境，所以我觉得非常需要高手们开发一个Jev harness....

ar.tx:
文章を1文字も書かないAIに、判断だけを任せる。使いどころから弱点まで、コードが書けない人向けに
ChatGPTにメールを1通渡して「これ、急ぎ？」と聞く。ちゃんと答えてくれます。
でも、それが1日1000通だったらどうでしょう。1通ずつChatGPTに読ませるのは遅いし、もったいない。急ぎかどうかを決めるだけの仕事に、文章もコードも書ける頭脳を毎回呼び出しているわけです。
そこに出てきたのがJevです。Jevは文章を書きません。1文字も書きません。やるのは「選ぶ」「YESかNOか決める」「点数をつける」の3つだけです。
そのかわり、速くて安い。海外では「メール500通を数秒で仕分けて、かかったのは3.5セントだった」という開発者の報告も出ています。
先に正直に書いておきます。JevはChatGPTのように、開いたその日から仕事に使える製品とは違います。
2026年9月19日時点で順番待ち制です。チャット画面もありません。本格的に使うには、プログラムから呼び出す必要があります。しかも公式が「日本語は英語より精度が低い」と明記しています。
それでも今、知っておく価値があります。AIの使い方が「1体に全部やらせる」から「役割で分ける」へ変わり始めていて、Jevはそのための部品だからです。
この記事は、コードが書けない人に向けて書きました。System Oneのような専門用語の解説はしません。渡すのは次の4つです。
・Jevが何者かを、30秒で人に説明できる言い方
・自分の仕事のどこにJevを置けるかの見つけ方
・順番待ちの間に、今日ChatGPTやClaudeでやっておける準備（依頼文は8章に置きました）
・飛びつく前に知っておく弱点4つ
全体像 この記事の地図
全部で9章です。前半で「何者か」、中盤で「どこに使うか」、後半で「どう触るか、何が危ないか」の順に進みます。
・1章 30秒で分かるJev。ChatGPTとの違いを1枚の図で
・2章 なぜ今注目されているのか。速さと安さの数字と、その割り引き方
・3章 聞けることは3種類だけ。選ぶ、YESかNOか、点数
・4章 仕事なら何に使えるか。入口になる10個
・5章 問い合わせ1通をJevに通すとどうなるか。公式サンプルの実際の答え
・6章 「ChatGPTにやらせればよくない？」への答え
・7章 最大の武器は速さではなく「自信のなさ」
・8章 コードが書けなくても使えるのか。近づき方を簡単な順に3段
・9章 飛びつく前に知っておく弱点4つ
時間がない人は、1章、3章、9章だけ読んでください。何者で、何ができて、何が危ないかは、そこで足ります。
1章 Jevは「書くAI」ではなく「決めるAI」
30秒で説明するなら、こうです。
ChatGPTやClaudeは、考えて文章を作るAI。Jevは、情報を見て判断するAI。
図にするとこうなります。
ChatGPT・Claude
　　↓
考える
文章を書く
コードを書く
Jev
　　↓
選ぶ
判定する
点数をつける
メールで言えば、Jevはメールを書くAIではありません。メールを見て、大事な用件か、どこに回すか、どれくらい急ぐかを決めるAIです。
公式サイトのFAQに「Jevは小さいLLMなのか」という質問があります。LLMは、ChatGPTやClaudeのような、文章を作るAIの総称です。公式の答えは「小さくもなければ、LLMでもない」でした。
言葉は理解する。でも自由な文章は生成しないし、チャットボットとしては動かない。公式がそう言い切っています。
https://typesafe.ai/
ここで1つ、勘違いしやすい点があります。JevはChatGPTのライバルとして出てきたわけではない、という点です。
AIエージェントの開発基盤で知られるLangChainも、公式ブログでこう整理しています。JevはLLMの置き換えにはならない。自由な推論と文章の生成はLLMが受け持ち、途中で何度も出てくる速い判断をJevが受け持つ。補い合う関係だ、と。
https://www.langchain.com/blog/building-a-harness-with-jev
誰かに「Jevって何」と聞かれたら、「ChatGPTは書くAI、Jevは決めるAI」と答えれば足ります。
余談ですが、Jevという名前は経済学者のジェヴォンズから来ています。蒸気機関の効率が上がったら、石炭の消費は減るどころか増えた、という話で知られる人です。知能が安くなれば、使い道はむしろ増える。そういう意味を込めた名前だそうです。
2章 注目されている理由は、小さな判断がほぼタダになったから
Jevを作ったのは、サンフランシスコのTypeSafe AIという会社です。公式ブログでの発表は2026年9月15日でした。
創業者のDiogo Almeidaは、公式ブログで自分の経歴をこう書いています。OpenAIで、言語モデルが指示に従って人と会話できるようにする手法づくりに関わった。それがChatGPTの裏側の研究になった、と。
会話するAIを作る側にいた人が、今度は「会話しないAI」を出してきた。まずここが面白いところです。
公式が出している数字はこうです。
・速さ：判断型のタスクで、従来のLLMより193.6倍高速
・安さ：同じ比較で444.6倍低コスト
・料金：入力100万トークンあたり0.042ドル。出力は無料
・応答時間：70〜500ミリ秒
トークンは、AIが文章を数える単位です。ざっくり文字数のようなものだと考えてください。
https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev
ただし、この数字は割り引いて読んでください。193.6倍と444.6倍は、TypeSafeが自社で作った評価での結果です。
公式ブログ自身が「現実の改善幅としては高い側の結果だと見ている」と注記しています。評価に使った仕事の流れは自社メンバーが作ったので、偏りがありうる、とも書いています。
自分に不利な注記を自分で書く会社は、わりと信用できます。それでも自社評価は自社評価です。
なので、第三者の数字も1つ見ておきます。OpenRouterという、いろいろなAIモデルをまとめて呼び出せる中継サービスが、Jevの応答時間を測って公開しています。直近3日間の中央値はおよそ0.22秒。100回のうち99回は0.52秒以内に返っていました（2026年9月19日確認）。
https://openrouter.ai/typesafe/jev-1.13
公式の言う70〜500ミリ秒と、ほぼ一致しています。少なくとも速さは本物です。
じゃあ、速くて安いと何が起きるのか。答えは「小さな判断を、量を気にせずAIに任せられる」です。
1通のメールが急ぎかどうか。1件のレビューが悪質かどうか。こういう判断は、1回なら人間がやれば済みます。でも1日1000回になると、人間には無理で、ChatGPTには高くて遅い。その隙間に、Jevがぴったり入ります。
ちなみに公式は、Jevに昔のゲームのDoomを遊ばせるデモも出し

不要把长达几万 token 的代码历史交给路由模型去“猜”意图。

为 Pi Coding Agent 开发的 Pi Jev Router 接入了 TypeSafe Jev 进行任务边界路由，但核心策略是极度的“保守”与“克制”。

关于它如何使用 Jev 模型的 3 个事实：

• 绝对的上下文隔离：只向 Jev 发送任务原文和可选摘要（最多 6000 字节）。不发送历史正文、工具输出、系统提示词或图片内容。
• 明确的模型职责：固定调用 jev-1.13.0，Jev 仅负责判断任务档位、上下文充分度与潜在后果。最终换模决定由本地程序结合真实缓存比例与可用性做出。
• 允许模型“放弃”：如果 Jev 返回 Unknown、低置信度或判定上下文不足，系统不会强制切换，而是直接保留当前合格模型，拒绝暗中降级。

扩展默认处于 Shadow 模式且默认关闭 Jev 网络调用。适合在连续编程中对 Token 成本和上下文稳定性极度敏感的开发者。

q.t:
We just ran Jev on our WebMCP benchmark.

The result: basically broke the benchmark.

Jev + Mercury 2.5 (a fast, low-cost LLM) using WebMCP solved 100% of the tasks at roughly 112× lower model cost than GPT-6 Astra using computer use with code execution. Compared to Astra using screenshot-based computer use, the model cost was 245× lower (!). 

We also compared Jev operating the browser with and without WebMCP. 

We used Browser Use’s open-source Ultrafast, with some improvements to the harness to make it more reliable across the benchmark. 

Jev’s browser-control accuracy on its own was not amazing - adding WebMCP nearly doubled the number of solved tasks, from 25/49 to 49/49, while reducing model cost by 18% (more on why below).

The benchmark and methodology are fully open and reproducible.

Full results: https://webmcp.com/benchmark

A few words on how the Jev + WebMCP harness works and why this is exciting:

Jev receives text as input and a set of discrete options it can choose from.  With WebMCP, those options are the tools exposed by the website. At each step, Jev sees the task, the available tools and previous results, then picks what to do next.

The limitation is that Jev can’t generate arbitrary text, which you need for tool arguments. For example, it can choose the search_products tool, but it can’t generate the search query itself.

So we split the work: Jev picks the tool and Mercury 2.5 generates the arguments if needed. 

This works well because turns out most of the cognitive load in these tasks is around choosing the right action. The argument generation itself is relatively simple, so we can delegate to a small and very fast model. We used Mercury, which outputs 1,000+ tokens/sec and is very cheap.

The result is a pretty simple combination: Jev for tool selection + Mercury for arguments + WebMCP for the interface. It ends up being very reliable, very fast, and very cheap.

A few words about Ultrafast and why do we think it underperforms:

Without WebMCP, Jev chooses from the page’s controls: which button to click, which field to fill, or which option to select. 

But choosing a valid button is different from choosing the right next step. The agent still has to navigate menus, understand forms, recover from errors  and recognize when the task is actually complete.

Our hypothesis is that WebMCP makes the decision space much simpler. Instead of figuring out a sequence of clicks through a website, Jev chooses explicit actions that directly advance the task. 

@typesafeai itself documents weaker accuracy on questions requiring multiple reasoning steps. WebMCP moves much of that complexity into the website’s tools, leaving Jev with clearer decisions and fewer opportunities to go wrong (in a sense WebMCP "compresses" a sequence of clicks into one tool call).

Our modified Ultrafast setup solved 25/49 tasks - that is a result for our particular implementation and benchmark, not a universal limit on Jev or Browser Use. We are open to more harness optimization to get this result to perform better, feel free to directly contribute to the benchmark here: https://github.com/nekuda-ai/WindTunnel

Browser-use ultrafast: https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast

我实际演示了一下，用 JEV 和 DeepSeek 做同一个任务：从当天的海量实时新闻流里，为 15 个品牌快速匹配有没有适合借势的公关热点，并打上结构化意图分类标签

结果是：28 秒内，Jev 狂刷完了整整 428 条数据，并完成了全部的目标分解与分类；而同一时间跑在同样任务上的 DeepSeek V4.1-flash，才刚刚完成 6/428 条

速度被拉开了几十倍，答案甚至在你读完第一行字之前就已经返回了....

为什么会产生这么恐怖的差距？底层逻辑是：

• DeepSeek 这种通用模型本质上是在“逐字写文章”：
哪怕你只让它做个最简单的“是/否”判断，它在后台也必须一个词一个词往外推，硬走一遍漫长的生成流程，延迟按秒起步

• Jev 官方定位是“System 1（快决策）”模型，从根上就根本不会写字：
它彻底抛弃了逐字吐词，底层直接一次性并行出结果。不输出半句废话，70 到 200 毫秒内直接甩出代码需要的最终答案（对/错、打分、分类）

demo参考@elvissun Github开源：https://github.com/elvisun/newsjack

建议大家试试JEV，越用越觉得牛逼.....

Jev 这个 waitlist 还是很给力的，昨天申请，今天就能用上。

给已经拿到 API、但还不知道怎么玩的人整理了一份 Awesome Jev，目前我能确认到的 Jev 项目基本都在这里：

1. jev-ultrafast
Browser Use 做的高速浏览器 Agent。Jev 负责每一步判断「做什么、点哪个元素」，需要输入文字时才调用小模型。Google Flights 搜航班完整跑完约 7.1 秒。
https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast

2. typesafe-mcp
把 Jev 直接接进 Claude Code、Claude Desktop 和 Codex。Agent 可以随时调用 Jev 做 Choice / Score / Noul 这类结构化判断。
https://github.com/itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp

3. jev-mcp
另一个更偏实用工具的 MCP，已经封装好事实核验、Prompt Injection 检测和语义排序。
https://github.com/jkudish/jev-mcp

4. SemDecide
把 Jev 做成 Unix 命令行工具，可以直接拿来做语义判断、分类、打分、过滤和 Guard。很适合塞进脚本、CI 和数据流水线。
https://github.com/sharziki/semdecide

5. Jev Codex Router
先让 Jev 判断每一轮编程任务有多难，再自动决定交给便宜模型还是更强模型。作者用 237 个真实 turn 回放，自测成本降低约 60%。
https://github.com/0xNatoshi/jev-codex-router

6. Winnow
给 Claude Code 做「上下文垃圾回收」。Read、Bash、Grep 输出太长时，先让 Jev 判断哪些内容真的跟当前任务有关，再决定哪些需要进上下文。
https://github.com/GhalebDweikat/winnow

7. Jev Review
用 Jev 做代码审查前置筛选，先判断 correctness、security、reliability、兼容性和测试风险，再把重点问题交给更重的模型处理。
https://github.com/devagrawal09/jev-review

8. Blink
用 Jev 在代码库里做语义寻路。每到一层目录，就判断哪些文件或文件夹最可能和问题有关，再把更多 walker 分配过去。
https://github.com/ellipsis-dev/blink

9. neo4jev
把同样的思路用到知识图谱。Jev 给每条候选边打概率，再用 beam search 一步步找到最可能的路径。
https://github.com/jexp/neo4jev

10. jev-desktop
把 Jev 接到桌面自动化里。它读取 Accessibility Tree，判断该操作哪个控件、执行什么动作，再交给本地执行器。
https://github.com/lahfir/agent-desktop

11. TypeSafe AI Playground
一个专门拿 Jev 做实验的 Rust CLI，已经做了 PHI 检测、代码注释审查、实时语气分析、职业和行业分类等玩法。
https://github.com/markjaquith/typesafe-ai-playground

12. Prism
目前我看到最接近量化/交易场景的项目。它让 Jev 判断流动性池的 toxic flow、市场压力、均值回归可能性和流动性分布方式，目前默认还是 shadow/advisory，不直接驱动交易。
https://github.com/irfndi/prism-liquidity-agent

13. 1v1 Jev
直接做了一个 FPS，让 Jev 大约 9Hz 判断移动、瞄准、ADS、开枪和跳跃。属于最直观展示 Jev 低延迟决策能力的项目之一。
https://github.com/emrickgarrett/OneVOneJev

14. TypeSafe on Neon
拿 Jev 做模型 Router。请求先由 Jev 判断属于哪种任务，再转给 Grok 4.6 或 GPT-6 Astra 等模型执行。
https://github.com/andrelandgraf/typesafe-on-neon

看完这些项目，你大概也知道 Jev 可以怎么玩了，就是拿它反复做「要不要、选哪个、打几分、下一步干什么」。

真正需要生成代码、写文章和复杂推理时，再把任务交给传统大模型。

t:
Nice to see my timeline finally discovered and learned what a classifier is.

Those things exist for decades.

The only thing that makes Jev great is that its general purpose, and you don't need to train it.

ここ数日、X の AI 界隈は Jev の話でもちきりになっている。TypeSafe AI のローンチポストは3日ちょっとで3,500万回以上表示されて、日本でも 9/17 の夜あたりから勉強会や社内ブレストが同時多発している。元 OpenAI の Diogo Almeida さんが立ち上げた会社のモデルで、チャットもしないし文章も書かない、ソフトウェアの中で使う「判断」だけを返すというものなので、気になって OpenRouter から実際に叩いてみた。

・状態と、答えの型を決めた質問を投げると、yes/no・選択肢・段階のどれかで確率付きの答えが返ってくる

・1つの状態に何十問でもまとめて聞ける。実測で1回0.2〜0.3秒、費用は0.0016セントくらい

・入力は100万トークンあたり0.042ドルで、出力は無料

・OpenRouter だと chat/completions ではなく /api/alpha/decisions という専用の入口に投げる(ここでハマる人が多そう)

注意しておくと、速さや安さの倍率は TypeSafe 自身の評価で、「ハルシネーションしない」というのも答えが定義した型の外に出ないという意味なので、判断の中身が正しいことまでは保証していない。

日本語の精度が落ちるとも公式に書かれていて、試してみたら、はっきりした質問は英語と同じ答えになる一方で、判断が割れる質問では日本語のほうが確率が0.5に寄って、自信のない答えになった。

それでもおもしろいのは、LLM を置き換えるのではなく、LLM の横に置いて判断だけを任せる、という立ち位置のほう。エージェントを何体も動かしていると、届いたメッセージをいま読むべきか、どのエージェントに回すか、この結果を成功とみなしていいか、のように文章はいらなくて判断だけほしい場面がけっこう多い。

先日書いた「Monitor が30分で切れる」件も、張り直すかどうかをエージェントの判断に任せた結果だったので、ああいう判断を型の決まった yes/no として外に出せるのは、エージェント間のメッセージ基盤を作っている側としてはかなり追い風だと思っている。

実際に叩いた手順と結果は記事にまとめた。

t: Jev is a great example of -- "if you offer something compelling that's cheap and fast, people will experiment and build cool shit" @typesafeai

speed is always fun

jev proves it

i'm excited about Jev for generative interfaces because if you can remember back before transformers were invented, we did generative interfaces with decision trees & constraint solvers. it wasn't fully deterministic—i think having probability over fixed answer is GOOD—but things were more repeatable

of course, LLMs were kind of better at learning and parsing intent than anything before them, but no matter how good LLMs get at generating interfaces, they're always black boxes that are sometimes magical, sometimes abysmal, and always Incredibly Frustrating To Nudge As A Designer

I actually yearn for more control over my systemized design environments than the blackbox Slop Or Not randomness that LLMs inherently provide

anyway, i am extremely excited about the new possibilities Jev is opening up in Determinishtic Interfaces, and in intelligent software composition in general

Playing with Jev made me want a new kind of model: one whose whole job is to find what's ambiguous, ask the questions that resolve it, and name the decisions a human or agent actually needs to make.

LLMs don't reliably do this, probably because of benchmaxxing and RLHF. When they encounter something unclear, they tend to make assumptions so they can keep going, rather than stopping to ask.

Giving models tools for asking questions isn't really sufficient in my experience.

I hope something like this is in the pipeline for @typesafeai!

Typesafe 的 jev 基础知识(一)：问题的三种类型，理解了这个，你才能理解browser use 如何使用jev(最后面）

1️⃣  Noul（是非题）：true 或 false。
2️⃣ Choice（单选题）：在不同类别里选一个，比如“香蕉、苹果、梨”，或者“牛马、中层、高管”。
3️⃣ Score（打分题）：衡量同一属性的程度，像温度计上的刻度（分数）
这是最难理解的类型，例如情绪：["冷静", "沮丧", "暴怒"]。

它看起来像类型２的Choice(单选题），但在这个打分设定里，是同一个属性“情绪”，设冷静是 0 分，沮丧是 1 分，暴怒是 2 分。JEV 给出 1.3 分，就表示处于沮丧和暴怒之间，更靠近沮丧。

所以，别只看选项是不是文字，要看它表达的是类别，还是刻度。

4️⃣所以browser use是用哪种呢？

它主要用类型２,　把相关的无障碍树的节点列表让jev选（单选题），当你问它我要点击登录按钮，应该选择哪个节点，jev会从这些节点里快速选出那个

This could be a nice architecture to explore:

Use @typesafe Jev as a tool call coordinator for LLMs.

LLMs are now better at tool calling than they were, but it's still an ugly hack in the coding harnesseses. System One models could likely decide better when a LLM needs to perform a tool call to either get more info or to perform an action - like a LLM's decision side-car of sorts.

I imagine a kinda "cyber-LLM" loop that a System One model controls:

1. LLM just does token prediction (let's say 1k at a time)

2. System One model decides if the token stream would benefit from one or more tool calls (issues tool calls, injects input+output into the LLM token stream)

3. go to step 1

q.t:
Okay, everyone wants us to give the unbiased facts.

Jev compaction here has a lot of problems. The biggest problems:

- When I ran it on our public compaction eval (that you can run too), it resulted in a programmatic rule, that you dont need any Jev or other model for - it simply removed all tool calls from the chat history
- This means you could do it for free, first of all, but second of all, it means you run into a viscious cycle.
Every compaction, there are less and less tool calls to remove from the chat history, meaning it compacts less and less tokens, until there is no room for compaction, and you hit a hard stop, and can't compact anymore.
- And, if you are cycling like this, every compaction breaks your cache, so you're paying 10x the price on input tokens, and keeping more input tokens each round means a higher baseline cost after compaction as well.

Here's the full reproducible eval that you can run against Hermes Agent between the two (Hermes' vs Jev's):

https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/116246

Jev looks like a really natural fit for graph sharding in OpenServ v3.

Graph sharding already lets us intelligently break down and route execution across large agent graphs, but having a decision layer this fast and cheap could make those routing decisions dramatically more efficient — potentially allowing us to make many more intelligent decisions throughout execution without paying the latency and cost of additional LLM calls.

We’re definitely looking at integrating it.

q.t:
I got access to Jev earlier today (thank you @hackgoofer).  I have run ~5,000 requests so far, (which cost me around $2!), across classification, model routing, intent, steering, and many other things.

tl;dr, Jev enables a new intelligent decision-making primitive, separate from deterministic code and LLM calls.  This allows a class of decision-making that was neither suited to dumb, unintelligent code, nor to slow, expensive LLMs.

It is super fast and cheap, and I think I will likely end up making a few Jev calls to every LLM call I make in my product. I think probably any company using LLM requests today can probably add a Jev call pre and/or post LLM calls to quite literally make their product much better for free, and have better tool calling behavior in many cases.  

I happened to have a personal benchmark for this as I’d been working on a ton of proactivity and classification tasks.  I have been using the deepseek flash and more recently gpt 5.6 luna family of models as reasonably smart classifiers with low latency.  Think questions like:

- Did this conversation output contradict something they’ve mentioned before?
- Should we send a followup message to this user based on our rules?
- It’s been a few seconds of silence.  Should we proactively send a message?

In the past, I’ve been forced to write a bunch of what I call decision chains, mostly because an LLM classification call is very expensive in TIME (avg 4s), and less importantly can cost quite a bit if run on every message.

Imagine a normal chat app.  If you added 4s to every response to figure out if the response is good before sending it out, that ends up being pretty bad.  So instead, I usually have to write some code that is a crude heuristic that runs quickly and decides whether to run the classifier.  Obviously this sucks because you call the classifier many times that you don’t want to, which makes your p95 bad, and you also miss cases with the heuristic, and you also have to manage all of these weird chains.

With Jev, it’s cheap enough, and fast enough (p50 ~150ms, p95 ~350ms in my testing!) that you can easily run it every turn.  Heck you can reasonably run it before generation AND post generation, for any application that isn’t realtime voice, and still feel snappy.

But this is just one use case.  Think: smarter model routing, better context packing, better responses, better observability for intent/tags/safety, smarter retries and so much more.  By simply thinking about the inputs and outcomes you want to enforce, you can use Jev to supercharge most model calls and reduce bad user outcomes.  The more “quirks” a model has, the more valuable it ends up being.

It’s a bit weird and unintuitive using Jev.  Generally, you want to decrease the # of questions you ask a classifier, or it makes more mistakes.  In fact, you might want to ask your questions kind of in a compound way, because the reasoning happens in a shared scratchpad of sorts.  Adding questions muddies the scratchpad and makes it take longer.  

With Jev, you feel incentivized to go the other way, to formulate your query as a set of independent questions.  It doesn’t feel like adding more questions decreases your performance on others.

You can go a bit deeper to improve tool calls.  Many model tools are things like turning on settings, or other things.  You can easily improve models that are not very good at tool calling with Jev, by simply figuring out when to run them.  You can do a pre-LLM call to figure out when to unfurl different tool definitions, in order to make your main LLM run better, you could run a background task with Jev + another LLM to reduce tool and context burden on your main LLM, and free it to be responsive.

I’ve only scratched the surface of my testing but very excited!

q.t:
I was super intrigued when I noticed that JEV returns not just probs for candidate choices, but also a CONFIDENCE SCORE of it's prediction...

I was wondering if TypeSafe AI brought back Bayesian Networks or something to learn uncertainty.

Turns out - NO. Acc to their docs, confidence is just a derived metric from the classification scores. It carries ZERO extra information. Their demo page shows:

 confidence = (3 × largest probability − 1) / 2

Confidence is tightly coupled with the classification scores it is measuring the uncertainty for.

There is no magic here. The model can produce high probability on a wrong choice and just be confidently wrong.

I used Jev to classify 1,018 AI research papers.

The result: $0.08 total cost and 256ms median end-to-end latency per paper.

The pipeline was:

1. Summarize each paper with DeepSeek V4 Flash
2. Send the title + summary + 24 possible topics to Jev
3. Use Jev to classify each paper
4. Visualize everything on http://1kpapers.com

The summaries cost $3.99 on @togethercompute. The classifications cost $0.08 on @typesafeai.

So for just over $4 of inference, I ended up with a pretty useful way to explore the top AI research papers from the past year.

I think this is where things are heading: different models for different parts of the workflow, instead of using one model for everything.

I’m running evals on the Jev classifications before replacing the current ones, but the site is already live: http://1kpapers.com

t: Use code wherever you can, use System One when rules stop being practical, and use LLMs for what remains. https://x.com/i/article/2101427861668392960

ar.ti: Pyramid of AI Workflows
ar.tx:
With the release of Jev and System One models, people have been wondering where they fit into the agent workflows they already use.
The Bitterest Lesson pyramid by @typesafeai inspired me to make one of my own
https://x.com/devagrawal09/status/2100718323495489795
This is roughly what I think hybrid AI workflows should look like.
- Code is the most efficient and reliable way to encode a workflow. It should make up majority of the system, especially the parts where you need hard guarantees. The downside is that code is also the most verbose way to describe behavior. You have to spell out every decision.
- LLMs are useful when the task is messy, the answer is not known ahead of time, or you need the system to work through something for a while. They can do things that would be impractical to fully specify in code, but they are slower, more expensive, and less reliable.
- System One models, like Jev, sit somewhere between them. They are faster and cheaper than LLMs, while still being able to make decisions that would be annoying or impossible to write as rules. So it makes sense that they also sit in the middle by usage.
The sizes of the layers matter. Most of the work should happen in code. System One models should handle the parts that need some judgement. LLMs should be reserved for the smaller number of tasks where the other two are not enough.
This is not saying every system needs to follow the same sequence. There are many ways these pieces can work together. The pyramid is mostly about how much you should expect to depend on each one.
There is also two directions of movement in the diagram.
Context flows up
Input from the outside world should usually meet code first.
Code can fetch data, remove things that are not relevant, and put limits around what gets passed along. A System One model can look at that smaller view and make some judgements. If an LLM is needed, it gets the specific information needed for its task instead of everything the system knows.
This also means each layer does not need to understand the entire system. It only needs enough context to do its part.
Instructions flow down
Instructions move the other way.
An LLM might come up with a plan or request an action. A System One model can evaluate that request, and code can make the final decision using both the model output and its own rules.
Not every instruction has to pass through all three. Sometimes code is enough. Sometimes code needs one model decision. Sometimes you really do need a full LLM or agent.
The basic idea is simple: use code wherever you can, use System One when rules stop being practical, and use LLMs for what remains.

q.t:
Jev from @typesafeai is great, but way overhyped.  

I fine-tuned an open-weight model on my Mac that beats Jev by almost 10pp, and is 8x faster.

It took less than an hour and runs on my local CPU.  Yes, it's task-specific.  Meaning it doesn't beat Jev on every task.  But that's ok:

Jev is pretty good at zero-shot general classification, but a quick fine-tuning run allows GLiNER 2.5 (open weights, built by @fastinoAI) to beat it on a specific task as a specialized classifier.

In this experiment, I tested default GLiNER 2.5 vs Jev vs Fine-tuned GLiNER 2.5 on the Banking77 benchmark from @huggingface.  

Default GLiNER 2.5 trailed Jev by ~9pp, despite being 10x faster. 

After fine-tuning GLiNER 2.5 on ~10k training samples (this took about 51 minutes on my M4 Max), I retested.

Fine-tuned GLiNER 2.5 gained ~18pp of classifying accuracy on the task, beating Jev by ~9pp. 

I'm betting that while Jev thrives as an easy plug-and-play endpoint for non-recurring classification tasks, most teams shipping to production will just take a little bit of time of front to fine-tune open-weight classifiers for tasks.  

If you can spend an hour fine-tuning to get:
- 8-10x speed boost
- 10pt accuracy lift
- AND it can run locally on your hardware?  

That seems like a no-brainer.  

So yes, @rileybrown, it seems like you can fine-tune  your own "jev" on your data :)

【Monadエンジニアが作った「Jev自動売買デモ」まとめ】

MonadのAIエンジニア Jarrod Watts が、TypeSafeの新モデル「Jev」でトレーディングボットを公開した事例です。
文章を生成せず、買い/売りと確率だけを約100msで返すAIを、約300msのブロックに直結しています。

デモ
https://jev-trader.vercel.app/

ソース
https://github.com/jarrodwatts/jev-trader

■ 核心
普通のChatGPT型AIは「理由を長文で書く」。
Jevは「buy 80% / sell 20%」みたいな型付き判断だけ返す。
だからブロックごとに判断→注文→再判断が回る。

対象は Monad 上のオンチェーン板 Kuru の MON/USDC。
毎ブロック、板を見て方向を決め、スプレッドの内側に指値を置き、前回注文をキャンセルする。
自分から高く買って安く売るのではなく、相手がぶつかってきた時だけ約定する設計。

■ 何が新しいか
・AIが毎ブロック判断している様子を公開ダッシュボードで見られる
・推論がだいたい70〜180ms。ブロック時間に間に合う
・作者の想定では、1時間のAI利用料 約$0.20、同時間のガス 約$2〜5
・「AIの方がガスより安い」を可視化したデモ

■ 注意（ここ重要）
・今の戦略はかなり単純。作者も「ショーケース」と言っている
・公開デモはシミュレーション/代替モデルの可能性が高い
・動画時点のPnLはマイナス。勝てるBotの証明ではない

q.t:
Jev + Kimi K3 for fraud detection!

TLDR: Jev classified 100 emails in 1.42 seconds, then I routed the uncertain cases to Kimi K3. The full pipeline got 96/100 correct for only ~$0.07.

Video is not sped up, check out the live run!

Here was my process:

I gave Jev 100 emails to classify (a mix of 50 legit & 50 fraudelent emails). It classified all of them in 1.42 seconds.

An underrated feature about Jev is it will give you the confidence score for a classification, so I routed any prediction under 95% confidence to Kimi K3 to be fully sure.

31 emails fell below that threshold. After routing those to Kimi K3, the combined pipeline reached 96% accuracy.

The full run took 16 seconds & ~$0.07 in inference costs:

- $0.068 from Kimi K3 on @togethercompute
- $0.003 (1/3 of a cent) from Jev on @typesafeai.

I think this is a really interesting pattern: use a fast specialized model like Jev for the narrow task, then route the uncertain cases to a larger LLM.

I feel like this kind of approach could be a game changer for use cases like fraud or anything realtime. You can use the speed & low cost of Jev while having a larger LLM as a fallback to ensure high accuracy.

一篇新闻刚上线，一次点击都没有，你能猜到它会不会火吗？

我们花了 5 美分试了一下

微软的 MIND 新闻数据，3,448 篇文章，只给 TypeSafe Jev 看标题和摘要，不给任何点击数据，问它五个问题

三个发现

01｜问"有用吗"，反而猜反了

越被判定为实用的文章，前 100 次曝光的点击率越低，ρ 是 -0.129

问"情绪化吗"，才是五个问题里最准的，+0.210

直接问"读者会点吗"，只有 +0.154

描述文章是什么，比直接让模型预测结果更靠谱

02｜一个零样本问题，顶 500 条标注

一个文本模型要用大约 500 篇带点击数据的文章训练，才追得上 Jev 一个零样本问题

把 Jev 的五个回答当特征加进去，50 条标注的效果就超过不加 Jev 的 400 条

03｜冷启动多拿 25% 点击

放进 Thompson 采样的冷启动，同一个模型加上 Jev 的回答，比不加多拿 25% 点击，比完全没有先验多拿 73%

这是半合成实验，用的是离线日志，不是线上 A/B

这是同系列的第三篇。换到新闻领域，和我们在 Agent 技能仓库上看到的规律一致：零样本 Jev 抵得上几百条标注，有了标注以后，它最好的位置是当一个额外特征

MIND 数据集按微软研究许可不能转发，仓库里只放了文章编号、点击率和 Jev 的回答

t:
I imagine 100% of the frontier labs have an urgent "Jev" meeting today

And I imagine 100% of the good engineering teams have a "how do we use Jev" meeting today

Did I just beat TypeSafe AI's Jev on calibration with an 11-second TF-IDF baseline ?!

Here is what happened: my 151M model initially scored 26.10% on LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions (400 cases, 2,000 decisions). Uniform random chance on that split is 29.85%.

Before touching model weights, i audited the evaluation harness and caught three bugs:

Appended __insufficient_evidence__ to every schema on a benchmark with zero ground-truth abstentions.
Dropped criteria on binary Noul queries, predicting "true" 100% of the time.
Appended (Value: X) to score levels, breaking label matching.
To establish an honest reference floor, we trained character 3-6 n-gram TF-IDF + Logistic Regression on the 1,200 training cases. It ran in 11 seconds on a CPU.

Here is where the 11-second baseline beat Jev:

Calibration error across all workflows (ECE, lower is better):
Overall: 0.0207 (vs Jev 0.1440)
Security Incidents: 0.0238
Invoice Processing: 0.0290

Customer Service accuracy:
TF-IDF hit 69.00% accuracy, clearing Jev's reported 68% overall benchmark average on CPU text statistics alone.

Binary Noul judgments:
75.83% accuracy with 0.0464 ECE, proving that binary decision criteria do not need billion-parameter attention to calibrate.

Why did classical ML win on calibration?

Logistic Regression directly optimizes convex Bernoulli log-loss against empirical class frequencies. Its predicted probabilities naturally match empirical hit rates across every confidence bin without teacher-distillation distortion or post-hoc temperature hacks.
Clean wiring and empirical reference floors matter more than pretraining compute.

Full breakdown, benchmark logs, and reproducible script are live on GitHub: link in comment

q.t:
TypeSafe AI came out of stealth with Jev, and access is behind a waitlist.

I built an open source version Verdict (Open-jev) you can run right now in a browser tab: And its a real post trained model..(link in comments)

It is a post trained 151M parameters model. ModernBERT-base with a GLiClass head. Instead of token-by-token autoregressive decoding or JSON string parsing, it takes an input text and candidate options, then returns calibrated probabilities and an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome in a single forward pass.

Some of The numbers:

Calibration: 0.83% adaptive expected calibration error on 1,000 held-out cases. I trained with a multi-class Brier score term, then tried standard post-hoc temperature scaling. Temperature scaling degraded the metrics, so the model ships with temperature 1.0.

Order invariance: reversing the option list flips 3.0% of predictions across 1,000 cases. For reference, another open Jev reproduction measured a frozen Qwen3.5-4B at 27.8% flips on the same perturbation, though on their own 36-case fixture rather than mine. Full bidirectional attention evaluates the candidate list simultaneously instead of scanning left to right.

Shuffled-context control: Pairing questions with the wrong document drops accuracy from 95.0% to 22.4% and drives abstention from 21.8% to 72.7%, confirming the model actively conditions on the context.

Latency: 89ms median in-browser via WebGPU, and 35.6ms via ONNX on CPU at 5 candidates.

The negative results:

I ran 12 use cases on public data across both checkpoints and three label framings three passed the promotion gate. Passage re-ranking hit 11.9%, jailbreak screening 34.9%, and phishing detection 57.5%. 

On 337 cases from TypeSafe's public evaluation set, Jev reaches 90.8%, a 26B diffusion model reaches 88.4%, and Verdict reaches 48.1%.which is expected since its just 151M param model but working on trying it on bigger scale as well.

A 151M encoder is calibrated, order-invariant, and fast, but it lacks broad world knowledge. 

In a tiered architecture where a cheap model gates an expensive one, knowing exact failure boundaries is essential. 48 of the 50 classification errors fall below a 0.95 confidence threshold, making the gate predictable.

For the next steps i will be testing the same harness on a larger backbone a bigger model with more params to see whether order invariance holds at scale or depends strictly on bidirectional attention.

Demo and repository links are in the first in the first reply.

Will be trying this on a bigger variant soon, let me know your thoughts what i can do better

would love to know your thoughts as well @CompleteSkeptic @typesafeai

とりあえず Jev がどういう問題クラスに対して、どれくらいのインプットまで適切に回答できるかを検証。
(Size rank については2枚目)
Parity が 8bit ですら低すぎるのが気になる。

① Lookup：ビット列の、指定した位置が1か。
② Majority：ビット列の中で1が0より多いか。
③ Parity：ビット列に含まれる1の個数が奇数か。
④ Product bit：二進数で与えた2整数を掛け算し、積の指定した桁が1か。
⑤ S5 composition：5個のラベルの並べ替えを順に適用し、すべて元の位置に戻るか。
⑥ Boolean formula：真・偽をAND／ORで組み合わせた式が、最終的に真になるか。
⑦ Undirected reach：無向グラフで、始点から終点へたどり着けるか。
⑧ Directed reach：有向グラフで、始点から終点へたどり着けるか。
⑨ Circuit value：0と1をAND／OR／XORで順に計算し、途中の結果も再利用する回路で、最終出力が1か。

this is going take forever to spend with jev @typesafeai

I've been looking for a cheap Memoizer with Semantic Invalidation Conditions (MSIC) for months now

in our react-inspired harness we were initially doing classical checksum-based invalidation and then later we were doing semantic state invalidation using generative models. what we really needed was a runtime-configurable classifier for this job.

in fact, the state invalidation code was ugly and inelegant and was my central annoyance with Reactor/Press, it stood in what felt like a carve-out juxtaposition across from all the real generative calls... but it's actually super elegant if you think of this system as a generator-classifier weave

time to dig this back up now if the right primitive is here...

the idea is to use a general classifier like jev as cheap attention-over-time, classifying whether world state meets or does not meet an OpenProse contract. when it decides it's invalid, it re-kicks the fulfillment providers (née terraform), aka renderer (née React)--in our case agents--to go and modify the world to make the contract true again

q.t:
everyone is building an agent or a tool

you don't want an agent or a tool, you want a reactor

I've been working on something cool and I think you'll like it

it's simple: an agent session DAG that keeps a declared world-model up to date in an efficient (memoized) render

each render node is an agent session: you declare the desired state with OpenProse markdown files

once invoked, each agent session acts as the provider. the agent session uses the open source openai-agents-sdk, extensible however you like with any model (I use with opus, sonnet, haiku)

the facets of the world-state are memoized, so not every agent has to run on every event, saving you on inference

if that sounds a lot like React or dataflow, that's because even in our brave new world the wisdom of the agents holds fast

I've put Jev into my ranking, retrieval, and LLM-as-a-judge workflows.  Video on why it's so useful to me, and why it's better than previous options.

tr: There's a new model called Jev by TypeSafeAI that I think is actually a step forward, not an incremental improvement like most models are. It brings this general purpose intelligence that our coding agents or chat GPT gives us. And it gives it in JSON as a classifier that's extremely fast. And so we get two big benefits. And I'll explain why these matter. One is it's much faster and cheaper. And two, it gives us structured outputs that we can use in software to make decisions. And for example, a user puts in a query, and a classification step might be, should I proceed to the next step? Do I want them to continue? Or do I want to ask a clarifying question? And that's not easy to do. And so usually we use something like Gemini Flash or Luna, which is fairly slow, take several seconds to run just to do this. And whether it's a tool call or a workflow, we basically just ask it very nicely to give us JSON and give us stuff in the right shape. And that works surprisingly well. And so we can't do that everywhere, because we can't have people waiting two to three seconds every time we click a button. But with Jev, now you can because it's super fast. These things can take 10th of a second or three tenths of a second to make these small determinations and classifications for all the things with Jev, you define the decision and the possible answers for classification. And then you get back this typed judgment with all the probabilities. And then my code can use that directly. No one capability is new, we could train these small fast classifiers before. But what's new is that we don't have to train it for every task. And it works on a wide range of things. I've already put this in my workflow for things like ranking, retrieval re-ranking and LLM as a judge workflows. And it works extremely well. And it's fast enough that I can put it inside a software and see it happen live rather than adding significant latency. So this is why I'm excited about Jev. There's so many places where software needs little bits of understanding and language to figure out what we should do next. We have these if statements that are powered by this LLM intelligence. And so really we have this like entire new foundational programming construct to use in software. And I'm using it myself. I wrote details on six ways that I'm using Jev in my workflow and how I replaced Gemini Flash and other things with Jev and how that worked out both latency wise and accuracy wise on my evals.

Classified 1,018 AI research papers for 8 cents.

Ran every paper through DeepSeek for summaries then Jev for classification across 24 topics. 256ms per paper. Total cost for all 1,018 papers: $0.08.

q.t:
I used Jev to classify 1,018 AI research papers.

The result: $0.08 total cost and 256ms median end-to-end latency per paper.

The pipeline was:

1. Summarize each paper with DeepSeek V4 Flash
2. Send the title + summary + 24 possible topics to Jev
3. Use Jev to classify each paper
4. Visualize everything on http://1kpapers.com

The summaries cost $3.99 on @togethercompute. The classifications cost $0.08 on @typesafeai.

So for just over $4 of inference, I ended up with a pretty useful way to explore the top AI research papers from the past year.

I think this is where things are heading: different models for different parts of the workflow, instead of using one model for everything.

I’m running evals on the Jev classifications before replacing the current ones, but the site is already live: http://1kpapers.com

簡單來說，這跟你熟知的LLM不同，我覺得有點像「有腦子的RAG」。還需要時間思考一下使用方式，但我認為會在許多場合非常實用。

q.t:
People look at this and keep saying "you need to sell/market yourselves well" (pro tip: none of the ppl saying this, understand what this is all about)

But, that's what the laya author is actually doing right now pretty cleverly (or naively) by overstating and broadening the claims of their work, because their 2025 work wasn't "Jev/Jev-like" at all. It shared "one" ingredient with jev, RL for a non-generative prediction, but it was not the general jev-like system now being implied, and even that wasn't novel.

First, Jev isn't just "a classifier + RL". It takes arbitrary state + typed questions (yes/no, choice, score) and returns calibrated probability distributions in parallel. RLCD trains for calibrated decisions and the same model is meant to generalize across many task types.

Their sales RL agent was embeddings -> small network -> PPO -> one 0-1 sales conversion probability, trained on synthetic sales chats. RL Classification itself wasn't new as well. DQN Classifiers were done in 2020, PPO multi-label classifications were demoed in 2022, much before their work, so it was building on that work already, not a novel approach.

Looked deeply into Laya. It's interesting.

The timeline claims are fuzzy and benchmarks are mixed but the model is worth following.

Laya, as compared to Jev by the author and @benchmarkheaven:

-#4 overall w/ 70.1 vs Jev’s 75.4
-Much stronger cost score: 86 vs 52
-Weaker intelligence, calibration + speed
-34% vs 74% on hard questions

Most interesting result comes from Laya’s own 2,000-decision benchmark...

When *fine-tuned* its typed-decisions checkpoint scored 0.766 vs Jev’s published 0.727.

Laya trained on 6,000 decisions from the same 4 synthetic workflows, whereas Jev ran zero-shot. 

This is a narrow, same-distribution win, to be super clear. But ~0.36 base → 0.766 fine-tuned is a big jump. Expect us to go hard on fine-tuning open weight models.

Lots of caveats on these benchmarks and more empirical methods are definitely needed. But closed weight models can't be fine-tuned. 

Whoever can create a highly fine-tunable Jev-like model will win the market.

There is a swarm of jev made this, jev made that on the timeline, and it might look like it is just another fun tool that takes in the hype and goes away once the algorithm stops the momentum.

But the real builders and thinkers are already looking at their application pipelines and workflows and finding ways to make it cheaper and faster for the users. That is where @typesafeai shines, the boring workflows.

q.t:
There has been a lot of talk around Jev as a next gen 'model', which cannot be far from reality.

Let me try and explain with an analogy of airport:

LLM = the pilot.
It can reason about a complex situation, make a plan, communicate, adapt, write things, use tools, and solve novel problems.

Jev = the air-traffic control system around the pilot.
It constantly makes small decisions:
Which runway?
Is this request risky?
Which model should handle this?
Is confidence high enough to continue?
Does this need escalation?
Did the previous step succeed?

You wouldn't replace the pilot with air-traffic control.

And you wouldn't want the pilot personally answering 10,000 little routing questions every second either.

Very exciting that we have a new infrastructure to make LLMs more reliable and consistent.

Got access to Jev and tested it on a simple use case: does this bookmark belong in this collection, given the rules its owner wrote?

Before: An LLM model answered with a sentence I had to parse into a boolean, taking 1–3s per call.

Now (with Jev): It returns a probability:
Above 0.85: Files it automatically.
Below 0.35: Drops it.
The middle: Goes back to the user as a judgment call.

A sweep over 500 bookmarks takes 13s and costs $0.017.

q.t:
you can also use Jev to cut costs and token usage!

make your agents more efficient by compacting shell and large file output before it reaches the LLM

passing only necessary tokens to the model and carrying fewer tokens through the rest of the conversation

you can just ask a model a question that requires a given output, from a list of up to 50,000 outputs, and then naively parse the next token it generates to do the same thing...?

"200x faster" okay yeah you're generating one token  and running a deterministic system with the output, good job?

am I completely misunderstanding this thing? seems not super impresssive. 

I do like the basically parallel instead of sequential inference idea, but you can do that with LLMs to by just putting the parallel processing you need in the prompt rather than having the model think through it. 

The whole "tiny straw of autoregression" thing is completely ignoring that you can just load yourself up 100 different KV caches and inference them all at once for one token. You don't have to use LLMs like a chatbot!?! 

this is among the reasons why we need to keep completions apis, and we just need better tooling for them....

this is one of my favorite under-used ways to inference LLMs, and it's exactly how the original DATA Browse would narrow down from 1000 potential sources to the 20 pages we actual read and parsed fully to conserve tokens, but it is *not* ...like.... new?

GPT-3 did this really well. all groq models do this brilliantly. 

you can get type safety and the rest off it by just inferencing in parallel in json mode with an affordable model. one token output 200 times is in fact nearly free, but it seems like with Jev and with other models you pay out the ass for context. such is life.

tr: add a red diamond here. I'll make it bigger. Move this over here. This viral jev demo you may have seen. This is fake. This demo too. Very fake. The internet right now is slittered with tons of fake demos about jev. With every type of claim, including iBuilt Tesla full self-driving. What? Now jev by typesfai is actually very cool. But it's a decision model, not an LLM. It's fast, it's cheap, it's a new type of model which we don't see very often. But oh my god people are posting so many demos that are so fake it's killing me. Let me explain to you what jev actually does. How these demos are cheating in completely unviable ways. And show you some actually cool things you can do with jev and how they work. Here's the list of the coolest and most BS jev demos right now. Now let's go back to jack. Now jack is not a developer. When people ask how does this work, he just says i don't really know fable did it for me. And that's fine to be honest. But let's see what's actually going on here. Jev only makes decisions. It can basically tell you a probability of yes, no, or a choice from a set of options. So you can see in the UI below what's actually happening. So the trick most of these demos use is they hard code a bunch of options, and they have jev pick from the options, and they go wow look what jev did. So for instance in this case we're hard coding a bunch of components in static prob options. They're saying wow jev designed the UI. Jev did not design the UI. Jev chose card button and one of a few pre-configured text options. This is not useful. This does not give you generative UI, the ability to give you dynamic UIs on the fly. It lets you pick from a set of pre-built options. This is not like here's the future demo. It'll get better as we get better with it. This is just not what the model does. This doesn't get better unless you're going to make infinity options, which truly for this use case of design a UI generation makes no sense. But going back to our first video, how do they map this to a set of options? They kind of fake it. The set of options that are clearly here are things like add circle. Now again it's a drawing program, but you don't actually get to choose the size of the circle, the position of the circle. It just adds circle where cursor is. He moves his cursor, asks for blue square, it gives you square, that is blue. Not a precise blue, just the hard coded blue, and it places it. Diamond two. And a few other hard coded actions. Move here, undo, select. This is not a demo of the future of how to use jev for programmatic application use. This is your typical misleading AI demo where you hard coded some options, and then you ran through them and acted like this will extend to real workflows, but it truly doesn't. This will not extend to real workflows. Real workflows, you need to put things in precise places and drag them to precise sizes and choose precise colors and arrange them in precise compositions. It's not what jev does. Jev doesn't give you that control flexibility precision. Again, it's choosing from a set of finite options. Let's take full self-driving. First of all, jev cannot take in images or video input. So when you see things like jev playing doom or jev driving a car, jev is actually being passed internal game state. It can't see pixels, so you need to use a custom version of a game where it can look at internal state and choose between usually the controller options, like the fire button, move left button, move right button, etc. For driving, it just sees the state and decides turn left, turn right, etc. Maybe it's a little more advanced than that, but it's nowhere near what this guy is saying that it's full self-driving. And maybe that's a joke, and maybe jack didn't intend for this to be taken the way it did or Chris or anyone. But the reality doesn't change. People are walking away thinking jev does all kinds of things it does not. This is a cool example of something it kind of can do. It's still pretty much not realistic and probably will never actually be used realistically in this way. But yes, jev is deciding to add floor tiles and probably from a fixed set of heights. So there's height 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, blah, blah, blah. And that's pretty cool. It's assembling a simple level, but this will only work for a very simple game that probably get very monotonous because again it's choosing from a fixed set of options every time. Now let's take this demo from Zaki. This is a super cool interesting idea where you just have a jev postgres function write in natural language and query and filter all rows based on that. Using jev to classify basically likely yes likely no on every row. When I first saw this I thought this is a pretty exciting idea because it is very fast and very cheap. But realistically this is only going to work on very small data sets. It's going to be far too expensive and slow to run AI even a fast AI on every single row of a real production size database. tr: Archibald, meet Mappity. It's a map you can just talk to. A talking map? Marvelous. Does it also do my taxes? Watch, my kid is melting down and needs sugar. Immediately. Every place you see just answered with a probability. 400 judgments, about a second, a fraction of a cent. 400 opinions in one second, like my family, but useful. On the left, Needle, a tiny local model, thought sugar was a landmark. Jev gave that one percent. Overruled. They mark each other's homework, I approve. Next, cozy coffee, within five minutes' walk of the aquarium. Needle pulls out the aquarium, and the five minutes. Code does the geography, Jev decides what cozy means. One that no category can answer. Somewhere I'd feel fine walking to, alone, at 11 at night. Jev decided the street matters, so we asked Mappillary what its cameras saw. Each place is judged twice, itself and its street, and code multiplies the two. So those little specs are actual lamp posts, good heavens. Very worthy, but can it do anything frivolous? Let's play a guessing game. It's now thinking of one of these 60 places. Can I eat there? I only hear one answer. But every place answered, so the odds shift across the whole map. Does it serve alcohol? Bayes theorem, as a pub quiz. Stand back, I shall guess. I demand a recount. Open street map, Mappillary, type safe Jev, and cactus Needle. About a second per question. No chat bot anywhere. Splendid. Now ask it where one finds a decent cup of tea.

So this allow to use Jev in the tool call loop directly and mitigate the issues in the current set of changes causing issues in down stream code gen.

diogo almeida’s new model, jev, makes structured decisions inside software. typesafe claims 20–200× faster and 40–400× cheaper performance than llms on those tasks.

$0.042 per million input tokens. free outputs.

it returns choices, scores and probabilities in parallel. developers can use those signals to automate routine decisions and send uncertain cases for review.

two details matter:

• its workflow evals use other frontier models’ answers as the reference, rather than independently verified ground truth.
• “zero hallucinations” means guaranteed output structure. it can still make wrong decisions.

t:
GLM 5.3 Flash vs Hybrid (GLM 5.3 Flash + Jev) on a turn-based strategy game (Halite 2)

The hybrid approach is 13x faster, 56% of the pure GLM 5.3 Flash API cost, and gains a slight edge in performance.

In the hybrid approach:
-GLM 5.3 Flash handles strategic judgment of which planets matter, who expands, who fights, when to re-plan. 
-Jev handles the ship-by-ship execution.

GLM 5.3 Flash alone defeats Jev alone 82% of the time.

This is obviously just a single example and some of the first things I've tried to make use of Jev as an augmentation to an LLM. Could potentially make even more gains in cost, speed, and performance, but using what I've figured out here, I am compelled to try some ideas with robotics next.

q.t:
I am becoming less skeptical of Jev.

it appears to be a solid augmentation of LLMs, saving on total token/iter time. still measuring & trying to determine if a hybrid approach can stay faster + result in no loss (or improve) perf. I am not yet seeing that, but it feels likely.

tr: Here we have a demo of using the TypeSafe API to create a smart home assistant. We're able to issue commands to the smart home and using only TypeSafe to evaluate what should be done on the devices in the home. So we can do turn off all of the lights and over here in our mock smart home we can see that all the lights turned off. We can say turn on the living room lights and those turned on. We can say shut off all the music in the house and the smart speaker turned off, get the coffee boiling and the coffee maker turns on. So on the right side here we have the full trace of exactly what's happening on every call. So we just did get the coffee boiling. So let's look at how we actually made that decision. We're actually only calling the TypeSafe API one time in all of these requests but we are supplying a whole bunch of prompts in that one call to the API with everything that we need to make the evaluation for a multitude of different commands. So in this particular case we're using a choice primitive to decide what is the user's intent. So is it a smart home command? Is it an information request or is it a smart home query like asking the status of a device? In this case it's a smart home command. We determine that it is not a compound request so it does not contain multiple commands in one. We do that with a new primitive. We say what is the scope of the request in the case of the coffee maker? It was a specific device. What kind of device is being targeted? It's an appliance. Which specific device should receive the command is the kitchen coffee maker? And then finally what should happen to the appliances which is turn on? So we're turning on the kitchen coffee maker and that becomes the one action. But what's notable here is that in that same call to the type safe API we also asked other questions like what should happen to the fans? What should happen to the locks? What should happen to the speakers? But our code didn't even look at the responses to those because we already know we're targeting a specific device. It's an appliance. It's the kitchen coffee maker. So this is an example of speculative prompting. So we asked what should happen to the locks and the type safe API returned a bit of an unknown response like it's got 79% likely unlocked 21% likely lock. It makes sense that it's not certain about it because the command didn't have anything to do with locks at all. But we ask it anyway because in the case that it did have to do with locks, we're going to have that answer already available in our code without having to do another round trip. So if I say lock up the whole house in this example, what should happen to the locks becomes pertinent and the what should happen to the appliances is not pertinent. So in this case of locking up the whole house we can see it was also a smart home command. The scope was the whole house and the kind of device being targeted was a lock. This shows that by leveraging the fact that type safe returns very, very quickly and very inexpensively when you cram as many prompts as you need into a single API call, you can get the advantage of getting all of the intelligence back at once and relying on your code to branch where you want. But let's get into a couple other patterns that we show in this example. So here is turn off the kitchen lights and lock the office door. This is a compound request. In this particular case, we're doing something a little bit trickier. We got to scroll up a bit more to see here. So one of the earliest things that we evaluate is does this request contain multiple commands and it does 98% probabilities. So yes, it absolutely does. We're asking about the kitchen lights and locking the office door, which we can already see it did it correctly. This is a case where we're using the strength of type safes very, very fast primitives pairing with a traditional LLM when actual text extraction is needed when text generation is needed. So as soon as we determine that this request contains multiple commands, we decide to kick it out to an LLM to say split this into the discrete sub commands. And the LLM returned one is to turn off the kitchen lights and two is to lock the office door. And then we're running each of those against the same logic that we run all of our commands. So we can see up top at the timing here, we have the type safe API returned in 178 milliseconds, we then called Claude Haiku to just get as quick as possible to get the split into two commands. And then we did two parallel requests to type safe for each of those two split commands. And now we were able to fully evaluate the answer. And then finally, the other pattern that we have here is showing how if we ask who won the World Series in 1989, we are just looking for a general intelligence question is the kind of thing that you would want an LLM to answer. We can put type safe as the first has the responsibility to look at the response immediately very, very quickly determine where to

q.t:
Yes, classifiers existed. BERT, DeBERTa, GLiNER, fine-tuned heads. Most of them were specialized. Pick the labels, train, ship. Changing the rules at runtime meant another training run.

What we did not have was a general-purpose classifier at Terra / Sonnet 5 level intelligence.

You could fake it by asking an LLM for JSON, but that was slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated.

Jev is that missing piece. Labels defined in code, typed answer plus confidence, no extra LLM call.

Classification is not new. What is new is a general-purpose classifier this intelligent, this fast, and this cheap.
