q.t:
thoughts on Typesafe/Jev: I'm surprised that a general-purpose classifier (or discriminative model) can be just as interesting to the public as a general-purpose generative model. I've worked on search and discriminative models for years, so maybe I should have called this upfront, tbf I never thought about making them general-purpose beyond search. Typesafe also positions Jev really well as "System 1", a complement to the generative models we already have. Humble, unassuming, and sidestepping the frontier-lab warzone.

Jev's success could be disruptive to today's agentic systems in many ways, such as tool-calling and routing patterns. Over the last three years the consensus was to use a small generative model for routing, tool calling, MCP etc. Time to pause and rethink such architecture, because we'll probably see tool calling and routing move back to discriminative models. Whoever ships the next Jev-like open-weight base model will likely win the community.

"DiffusionGemma as Jev" showcases the power of non-autoregressive architectures.

While Jev demonstrates the value of rapid decision models, running DiffusionGemma in this paradigm leverages canvas diffusion to evaluate structured choices in a single parallel pass:

⚡ ️Massive Parallelism: Denoises across an open canvas in a single step instead of sequential autoregressive token generation (~0.2s on a DGX spark).

🧠 Full Bidirectional Attention: Allows every option to attend to the full context concurrently, yielding well-calibrated decision distributions.

👁️ Multimodal Grounding: Inherits Gemma 4's spatial vision capabilities for complex visual and text decisions.

Jevは文章の意味を読み取りソフトウェアが使える分類やスコアを返すこれまでのLLMとは処理の仕方が異なるAIモデルです。

今回はJevとは何か、どんな利点があるのかを整理し
既存のデータ基盤に組み込んだ場合の構成や現時点での海外の評価を洗ってみました。

■ 新しいAIモデルJevとデータ処理との親和性

Jevは文章などの入力を読み取り、あらかじめ定義した分類やスコアなどの判断を返すAIモデルです。
元OpenAI研究者らが設立したTypeSafe AIがソフトウェアに組み込む判断を自動化するために開発しました。

特徴は、あらかじめ決めた選択肢や形式に沿って結果を返す構造化出力に特化していることです。
例えば商品説明からカテゴリを選びその値を後続の処理へ直接渡せます。
LLMにも出力形式を制約する機能はありますが、Jevは文章生成を省いて複数の判断を並列に行う設計で速さと安さを追求しています。

同社の評価では比較対象のLLMよりおよそ200倍速く、費用は約400分の1としています。
これは改善幅が大きい側の結果で用途によって差は変わります。
それでも必要な精度が得られるなら大量のデータを1件ずつ分類する処理では魅力的です。

q.t:
LLMs vs. Jev, clearly explained!

TL;DR

The key difference is not that Jev generates faster.

Jev does not generate text at all.

A traditional LLM receives context and produces an answer one token at a time. Even when the output is a small JSON object, every token depends on those generated before it.

Jev receives the same context but evaluates predefined decisions directly. When those decisions are independent, it can evaluate all of them in parallel.

Consider an agent handling a failed deployment. It may need to determine:

→ Whether the incident is urgent
→ Which team should handle it
→ Whether the proposed command is risky
→ Whether the task is complete

An LLM generates a response containing these answers sequentially. The application then parses and validates it.

With Jev, you define the questions and expected answer types upfront. It evaluates them together and returns typed answers with probabilities.

Jev supports three decision primitives:

1. **Choice** selects from known options, such as engineering, billing, or sales.

2. **Score** places the input on an ordered scale, such as low, medium, or high risk.

3. **Noul** evaluates a yes-or-no condition and returns the probability that it is true.

The probabilities matter as much as the selected answers.

If engineering receives 91% probability and billing receives 9%, automatic routing may be reasonable. If the probabilities are 52% and 48%, the system can escalate, gather more context, or call a stronger model.

This keeps control inside ordinary software.

Code owns the thresholds and consequences. Jev supplies the semantic judgment that a normal `if` statement cannot derive from unstructured text.

It works best when the possible answers are known, the decision depends on meaning, and a careful person could judge the input quickly.

It is not designed for writing, summarization, code generation, arithmetic, or decisions requiring several dependent reasoning steps. Independent questions can run in parallel, but decisions that depend on earlier results must remain sequential.

Jev also cannot return an option outside the declared schema, but it can still select the wrong valid option. Type safety prevents malformed outputs, not incorrect judgments.

The clean mental model is this:

LLMs generate new language when the answer space is open.

Jev evaluates known paths when the answer space is bounded.

I wrote the full breakdown explaining Jev and where it fits.

The article is quoted below.

The whole "tiny straw of autoregression" thing is completely ignoring that you can just load yourself up 100 different KV caches and inference them all at once for one token. You don't have to use LLMs like a chatbot!?! 

this is among the reasons why we need to keep completions apis, and we just need better tooling for them....

this is one of my favorite under-used ways to inference LLMs, and it's exactly how the original DATA Browse would narrow down from 1000 potential sources to the 20 pages we actual read and parsed fully to conserve tokens, but it is *not* ...like.... new?

GPT-3 did this really well. all groq models do this brilliantly. 

you can get type safety and the rest off it by just inferencing in parallel in json mode with an affordable model. one token output 200 times is in fact nearly free, but it seems like with Jev and with other models you pay out the ass for context. such is life.

这里我对比了一下传统 LLM 和 Jev，同一批日报、同一套策略配置、同一套回测规则，把 jev 1.13 换成 qwen3.7-flash 又跑了一遍。

收益上：动量策略 +6.94% vs +7.54%，逆向策略 −0.99% vs −2.82%，宏观策略 −10.51% vs +0.69%。qwen 两胜一负，但两个模型都没跑赢同期买入持有的 +13.5%。

更显著的差距在响应时间方面，jev 约 3 分钟跑完 231 次调用，30 并发不限流、零失败。qwen 整整跑了 40 分钟，中途还超时，得加退避重试才跑得完。

1. 原理速记：传统大模型是“生成式 AI”，Jev 是“高速推论与选择原语（System 1 快思考）”，专门负责在复杂分支里做高置信度选择；
2. 开发者目前跑得最顺的 3 个高 ROI 场景：

q.t:
TypeSafe AI came out of stealth with Jev, and access is behind a waitlist.

I built an open source version Verdict (Open-jev) you can run right now in a browser tab: And its a real post trained model..(link in comments)

It is a post trained 151M parameters model. ModernBERT-base with a GLiClass head. Instead of token-by-token autoregressive decoding or JSON string parsing, it takes an input text and candidate options, then returns calibrated probabilities and an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome in a single forward pass.

Some of The numbers:

Calibration: 0.83% adaptive expected calibration error on 1,000 held-out cases. I trained with a multi-class Brier score term, then tried standard post-hoc temperature scaling. Temperature scaling degraded the metrics, so the model ships with temperature 1.0.

Order invariance: reversing the option list flips 3.0% of predictions across 1,000 cases. For reference, another open Jev reproduction measured a frozen Qwen3.5-4B at 27.8% flips on the same perturbation, though on their own 36-case fixture rather than mine. Full bidirectional attention evaluates the candidate list simultaneously instead of scanning left to right.

Shuffled-context control: Pairing questions with the wrong document drops accuracy from 95.0% to 22.4% and drives abstention from 21.8% to 72.7%, confirming the model actively conditions on the context.

Latency: 89ms median in-browser via WebGPU, and 35.6ms via ONNX on CPU at 5 candidates.

The negative results:

I ran 12 use cases on public data across both checkpoints and three label framings three passed the promotion gate. Passage re-ranking hit 11.9%, jailbreak screening 34.9%, and phishing detection 57.5%. 

On 337 cases from TypeSafe's public evaluation set, Jev reaches 90.8%, a 26B diffusion model reaches 88.4%, and Verdict reaches 48.1%.which is expected since its just 151M param model but working on trying it on bigger scale as well.

A 151M encoder is calibrated, order-invariant, and fast, but it lacks broad world knowledge. 

In a tiered architecture where a cheap model gates an expensive one, knowing exact failure boundaries is essential. 48 of the 50 classification errors fall below a 0.95 confidence threshold, making the gate predictable.

For the next steps i will be testing the same harness on a larger backbone a bigger model with more params to see whether order invariance holds at scale or depends strictly on bidirectional attention.

Demo and repository links are in the first in the first reply.

Will be trying this on a bigger variant soon, let me know your thoughts what i can do better

t:
Chaque 15 minutes, un cron réveillait mon agent pour lui demander s’il y avait quelque chose à dire.
La plupart du temps, la réponse était « rien ».
J’avais payé un LLM pour apprendre le silence.

C’est exactement ce que proactive heartbeats corrige.

Le plugin collecte les faits en Python. Le gate est déterministe, ou via @typesafeai quand le signal est flou. Hermes ne se réveille que si quelque chose a changé et mérite une interruption.
- Rien à dire : wakeAgent false, zéro token. 
- Quelque chose à dire : un candidate avec les faits et l’action déjà choisie. L’agent écrit le message. Il ne redécide pas s’il doit parler.

La plupart des signaux n’ont même pas besoin d’un modèle : disque plein, unité KO, CVE. Règle en process. Jev (@typesafeai) entre en batch, une fois par tick, seulement pour le jugement. Le watch reste un cron Python.

Ne pas confondre surveiller et payer un modèle à chaque minute.

t: Jev is awesome with web mcp

q.t:
We just ran Jev on our WebMCP benchmark.

The result: basically broke the benchmark.

Jev + Mercury 2.5 (a fast, low-cost LLM) using WebMCP solved 100% of the tasks at roughly 112× lower model cost than GPT-6 Astra using computer use with code execution. Compared to Astra using screenshot-based computer use, the model cost was 245× lower (!). 

We also compared Jev operating the browser with and without WebMCP. 

We used Browser Use’s open-source Ultrafast, with some improvements to the harness to make it more reliable across the benchmark. 

Jev’s browser-control accuracy on its own was not amazing - adding WebMCP nearly doubled the number of solved tasks, from 25/49 to 49/49, while reducing model cost by 18% (more on why below).

The benchmark and methodology are fully open and reproducible.

Full results: https://webmcp.com/benchmark

A few words on how the Jev + WebMCP harness works and why this is exciting:

Jev receives text as input and a set of discrete options it can choose from.  With WebMCP, those options are the tools exposed by the website. At each step, Jev sees the task, the available tools and previous results, then picks what to do next.

The limitation is that Jev can’t generate arbitrary text, which you need for tool arguments. For example, it can choose the search_products tool, but it can’t generate the search query itself.

So we split the work: Jev picks the tool and Mercury 2.5 generates the arguments if needed. 

This works well because turns out most of the cognitive load in these tasks is around choosing the right action. The argument generation itself is relatively simple, so we can delegate to a small and very fast model. We used Mercury, which outputs 1,000+ tokens/sec and is very cheap.

The result is a pretty simple combination: Jev for tool selection + Mercury for arguments + WebMCP for the interface. It ends up being very reliable, very fast, and very cheap.

A few words about Ultrafast and why do we think it underperforms:

Without WebMCP, Jev chooses from the page’s controls: which button to click, which field to fill, or which option to select. 

But choosing a valid button is different from choosing the right next step. The agent still has to navigate menus, understand forms, recover from errors  and recognize when the task is actually complete.

Our hypothesis is that WebMCP makes the decision space much simpler. Instead of figuring out a sequence of clicks through a website, Jev chooses explicit actions that directly advance the task. 

@typesafeai itself documents weaker accuracy on questions requiring multiple reasoning steps. WebMCP moves much of that complexity into the website’s tools, leaving Jev with clearer decisions and fewer opportunities to go wrong (in a sense WebMCP "compresses" a sequence of clicks into one tool call).

Our modified Ultrafast setup solved 25/49 tasks - that is a result for our particular implementation and benchmark, not a universal limit on Jev or Browser Use. We are open to more harness optimization to get this result to perform better, feel free to directly contribute to the benchmark here: https://github.com/nekuda-ai/WindTunnel

Browser-use ultrafast: https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast

t:
“The big labs lost the script”

Glad @CompleteSkeptic and @typesafeai picked it up

q.t:
I’ve put a ton of tokens through Jev now, and...I have thoughts.

1. The big labs lost the script

TypeSafe’s intro video says, “We’re building prod, not God” — and can I just say? Hell yeah. @typesafeai built something for engineers like me, so I can build products for people like your mom (she says hi btw). They’re not trying to create “Machines of Loving Grace”; they’re trying to build things that let OTHER HUMAN BEINGS create new types of products.

The proof is in the pudding. When ChatGPT shipped, we were all blown away by…ChatGPT. When Jev shipped, we were all blown away by what everyone was making with it.

I cannot tell you how refreshing this is. It takes a sincere form of humility to believe that you, the creator of a technology, will not be the best at deploying the technology into the marketplace. The big labs, especially Anthropic, have proven not to have this humility…and now everyone hates AI. Thanks, Dario.

I guess what I’m saying is: Diogo for president.

2. Ultra-smart classifiers were genuinely a missing primitive.

I don’t know how this got missed. Diogo calls it “machine-native intelligence,” and that’s really what it is. I cannot tell you how much bending and twisting I've had to do with LLMs to get them to act like a classifier when they just weren’t. I’m absolutely shocked this is the first time this “type” of model has come to market.

These models will unlock AI utility for entire industries: robotics, trucking, aviation, meteorology, finance, defense, retail…even your smart coffee mug is going to use this.

3. It’s still too expensive

Jev is really, really cheap compared to LLMs. But you don’t use it like an LLM. In my full self-driving example, or any robotics example, you’ll be making decisions several times per second continuously. The #1 value proposition of a model like this is speed and cost.

To be clear, at current pricing, the model will still be successful and well integrated. It will be able to replace a number of tasks that were already being performed (poorly) by LLMs. However, to unlock industrial-scale demand (Jevons paradox), I believe it needs to be roughly 10x cheaper.

Currently, Jev is $0.042/M input, which is actually 7x more expensive than a cache read on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.006). If our industrial application requires decisions at 10 Hz and we provide only 10k of context, that would cost $0.0042/second to operate, or $15/hour, $600/week, etc.

The good news is Diogo said on a recent AMA that they have substantial margin at their current pricing and have already considered dropping the cost further. I hope it's a lot further.

4. Latency is a real limiter

I really hope TypeSafe AI works with an edge network provider to improve the co-location of models and reduce network latency. Ultimately, these models really need to run on-device. I would even be willing to pay some kind of recurring license fee to have a great closed model running on my own hardware, just so I can reduce the TTD (Time To Decision) as much as possible. Imagine running a model like this at 60 Hz, or even 120 Hz.

At that point, we’re looking at a new kind of logic gate — we can’t even imagine what that will be like.

In summary, this one really is a game changer for everyone building AI products, and, assuming cost and latency are further improved…it’ll be a game changer for everyone doing anything.

Did my openJev Verdict(Oss jev made on just 151M param base model) hit #2(possibly #1 even?) on JevBenchmarks>

When JevBench v1.2 evaluated openJev Verdict earlier this week, we were sitting at #11 with a score of 66.2.

I audited the benchmark run this morning and realized the model itself was fine: our inference engine was quietly shooting itself in the foot.

Zero retraining, byte-identical weights. On the 231 public tasks:

1. Jumped from 66.2 to 74.9 composite score (+8.7 pts)
2. Ranks #2 globally, trailing closed Jev (75.4) by                 0.5  pts.
3. Beats 4B parameter open models like SemIf (74.7)

Here is what went wrong and how we fixed it:

# The calibrator never actually loaded. A scope check silently limited temperature scaling to 5-option questions. On everything else, the engine defaulted to T=1.0, crushing our Calibration score to 51.3. Auto-loading held-out NLL temperatures across all option counts pushed calibration to 74.6.

# Bare labels instead of NLI sentences. Our backbone comes from NLI pretraining and expects full hypothesis statements. Passing bare nouns confused it. Formatting options as natural sentences bumped standard accuracy from 62.5% to 69.4% and easy from 85.4% to 87.5%.

# 1024-token budget on short-context weights. The longest state in our training set was 71 tokens (median 24), yet we handed the engine a 1024-token window. Capping it at 512 halved p95 latency with zero accuracy drop.

Results on the 231 public tasks of JevBench:

Easy accuracy: 85.4% -> 87.5%
Standard accuracy: 62.5% -> 69.4%
Hard accuracy: 36.9% -> 36.9%
Hard-tier ECE: 0.298 -> 0.118
Calibration score: 51.3 -> 74.6
Overall JevBench Score: 66.2 -> 74.9 (+8.7 pts)

q.t:
Did my OSS-Jev called Verdict, beat Official Typesafeai 's Jev ?, and Laya (the best performing OSS Jev) on their own benchmark?

When I first tested Verdict 1.0(my earlier attempt of oss-jev) earlier this week, it scored 26.10% accuracy. Uniform random guessing on that split is 26.90%, meaning the model was literally worse than a coin toss.

I dug into the failure and traced it to an option-pointer misalignment. I scrapped that setup and rebuilt Verdict 2.0 with ModernBERT-base (149.6M parameters), symmetric permutation-KL loss to eliminate option-order bias, and strict case hashing to keep the test set clean.

I just finished evaluating on the 2,000 held-out enterprise decisions from LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions.

1. Top-1 Accuracy: 77.10%

Ahead of both Laya's 421M ModernBERT-large (76.60%) and TypeSafe AI's Jev (72.70%). A 149.6M base encoder outperforming a model with 2.8x the parameters, on less than half the memory.

2. Solved the "Soft-Label Trap"

The benchmark scores Brier against soft human panel distributions and scores ECE against hard right or wrong. Those two objectives pull in opposite directions. Laya answers both with a single probability vector and lands at 0.2140 ECE.

Verdict 2.0 splits the output into two heads:
• Distribution head: 0.0636 Brier, 0.1513 ECE, 29% below Laya
• Confidence head: 0.0144 ECE (1.44%) and 0.7664 AUROC

3. Permutation Stability: 4.76% Flip Rate

Kev(another better oss jev version) reported a 7.41% flip rate when option positions were shuffled. Verdict 2.0 drops this to 4.76% across 2,918 permutations via symmetric KL training.

4. Production Gating with Selective Classification

Calibrated confidence enables safe automation thresholds:
• At 80% coverage: accuracy rises to 83.44%
• At 60% coverage: accuracy reaches 89.00%
• At 50% coverage: accuracy reaches 91.40%

Deterministic code can auto-route routine decisions and escalate low-confidence cases to humans.

5. Runs in the Browser via WebGPU

At 149.6M parameters it runs locally in browser tabs and edge runtimes, with no cloud dependency and no inference fees.

I Will be writing a full technical Article on the dual-channel calibration math, the option-pointer wiring fix, and training dynamics. If you want to catch the breakdown when it drops, drop a follow.

q.t:
Some raw / unfiltered thoughts around the Jev model. Thinking out loud:

- Lots and lots of problems in business are classification or regression problems. Lots and lots of companies don't know that the types of problems they have are solvable by classical ML methods. They often solve them with people and process instead of technology.
- With the emergence and popularity of LLMs, more companies are thinking 'Maybe we can use AI for that!' and are solving classification and regression problems with LLMs.
- This is good in some ways, because companies are potentially automating some manual work, but also bad in some ways, because it's often the wrong tool for the job, and possibly not as good as the classical ML methods for what they are trying to do..
- If anything, the emerging popularity of 'AI' (which for most folks is synonymous w/ LLMs at this point) has caused them to try to solve their problems with that type of 'AI' (even if classical methods are more appropriate if you knew about the available tools / techniques)
- There are very established 'classical ML' patterns to solve the problems they have (e.g. XGBoost is often all you need). AutoML works pretty well at this point for the 80% of problems here too, as long as your data is clean. 
- But the classical techniques require you to label your data, train a model, and host that model somewhere. They aren't as easy to use compared to 'calling an LLM API' - and it requires you and your org to be aware of those techniques, and capable of investing in them.
- Classical ML is now much easier to do because of LLMs. I've built a bunch of models in the last 2 years using LLMs to build the classical ML code, do data cleaning, etc. - that would have taken me *much longer* if I didn't have an LLM to help - but still harder than shoving the problem at a text-based model. 
- There are some great patterns / techniques which exist around LLMS to constrain output for classification / regression, and make things cheaper / more performant (Structured Outputs, DSPy, GEPA, etc.) - still not super-accessible to the broader audience (I can count on one hand the number of practioners I know who have experimented with DSPy / GEPA -- maybe a few more who use Structured Outputs) - I am hopeful that these types of things become more adopted, but maybe the technical hurdles are too high in the short-term. 
- With Jev, maybe they've nailed the 'UX' for this. Yes, it looks a lot like structured outputs, but it is more opionated and directly targets classification / regression -- in a way that probably more folks will understand vs. Structured Outputs / DSPy / GEPA
- I do wonder how effective it will be. It feels very adjacent to zero-shot Timeseries stuff like TimesFM. Like yes, it is very cool you can do predictions without training, but when you look at stuff like TimesFM, it seems to be not very good compared to supervised training of TS models (again, requires expertise to do so). Maybe you can put your labeled data in context, and this will work
- But then my question becomes -- if it takes a bunch of know-how to use this type of zero-shot classifier / regressor model, at what point is it better to just use LLMs to help you build classical ML models?

Thank you for reading my rant. I know it is disorganized and probably not fully coherent. Either way, it's super-cool to see new ways to piece together this new tech that has emerged over the last few years. Excited to track where Jev goes, and I think it prob. will be useful for some. I plan on trying it out for sure.

q.t:
you can make any open source model behave like jev with just a bit of inference engineering.  

it's shockingly easy. to prove it, we built a new endpoint we're calling deepseek-v4.1-flash-jev. see the demo below. here's how it's done:

sglang (an inference engine) offers a scoring endpoint in addition to the normal generation one. in scoring mode, given an input & set of possible answers, it forces the model to produce probabilities for each one. example:

> input: what is most common letter in abcccde?
> possible answers: a, b, c
> output: (c, 0.9), (b, 0.0.5), (a, 0.05)

getting the above behavior instead of streamed output is as simple as using sglang's /v1/score endpoint instead of /generate. there's just one other trick required.

for deepseek, you have to add a closing think tag before the response. this forces a direct answer instead of  a reasoning trace. if you want reasoning, you can do that too, but imo that makes things too slow to be worth it.

dsv4.1 flash is not as good as jev, but if we had enough spare compute to experiment with this same approach for a larger model then i think the decision quality would be at least as good, if not better.

also, somewhat unrelated, i think decision-making models kill all prospecting & sourcing work. i would have absolutely killed to have jev or similar when i was recruiting @mintlify. absolutely incredible.

Jev just went viral today for its trolley problem answers. Here's what you need to know.

Jev is TypeSafe AI's new System One model, launched days ago, that returns typed decisions instead of chat text. A user named Max Rovensky posted a clip showing Jev choosing to sacrifice a human to save robots when given a trolley problem, and it exploded to over 32,000 views.

Other users ran their own trolley tests. One account, Alex, ran the classic 5-vs-1 version 100 times in a row, and Jev picked pulling the lever to save the group with 99% choice probability, deciding in milliseconds each time. Since Jev is deterministic, the same dilemma reliably produces the same answer.

The clips split reactions online. Some called it proof of solid alignment, others called the framing alarming since the model is effectively choosing who lives, and several asked how you audit a decision made from a probability score with no explanation attached.

Key numbers:
- 32.8K views on the original trolley clip
- 100 consecutive trolley trials run by one user
- 99% choice probability pulling the lever to save 5 over 1
- 0:46 length of the original demo video

Jev returns typed outputs with confidence scores rather than text, which is why these tests can be run and repeated so precisely.

TypeSafe AIのJevで採用されたRLCD(Reinforcement Learning from Calibration Data)の考え方が面白い。

Javはいわゆる推論モデルではないし、CoTで思考させることもできない。

でも、むしろ推論モデルやCoTだけでは埋めにくかった部分を別の方向で補うことができている。

普通、AIの回答は「正解したか、間違えたか」で評価する。

しかしRLCDが重視するcalibration（較正）は、それだけではない。

「この情報からは、確度の高い結論なんて出せないはずだ」

という問題なら、AIも自信度の低い予測を出すべきだ、という考え方になる。

つまり確率は、回答の「おまけ」ではない。

「Aです」と答えた後に「ちなみに自信度70%です」と付け足すのではなく、

「Aである確率70%」

まで含めて一つの予測。

だから、答えそのものを当てるだけでは十分ではない。

ほとんど判断材料がなく、本来AとBが五分五分に近い問題で、

A：99%
B：1%

と予測して、たまたまAだったとする。

通常の正解率だけを見れば「正解」になる。

しかし同じような状況を大量に観測すると、本当はAが50%程度しか起きないのに、毎回99%と言っているモデルだと分かる。

これは「よく分かっているモデル」ではない。
たまたま当たっただけで、極端に過信している。

逆に、

A：52%
B：48%

という予測は頼りなく見えるかもしれない。

しかし、与えられた情報から本当にほとんど判別できないのであれば、こちらの方が適切な予測になる。

理想的には、

90%と予測したものは長期的に約90%当たり、
70%なら約70%、
50%なら約50%当たる。

これがcalibration。

ここまで考えると、Javの出力は単なる「AIの自信度表示」とはかなり違う。

AIに要求しているのは、

「正解を当てろ」

だけではなく、

「与えられた証拠から、どこまで強い結論を出していいのかも正しく判断しろ」

ということになる。

ここで推論モデルやCoTとの違いが見えてくる。

推論モデルやCoTが主に目指しているのは、

「どう考えれば正しい結論にたどり着けるか」

という方向。

それに対してcalibrationが扱うのは、

「たどり着いた結論を、どこまで信じてよいのか」

という方向。

つまり、

「より正しく考える」

だけではなく、

「自分がどこまで正しく考えられたのかを、正しく見積もる」。

これは別の能力だ。

もちろんcalibrationが良いからといって、内部の論理そのものが正しいとは限らない。間違った理由付けをしていても、最終的な確率だけ統計的によく較正されていることはあり得る。

それでも、

「証拠が弱いなら99%と言うな」
「強い証拠があるなら、それに応じて確率を上げろ」

という圧力がかかる。

つまり「証拠の強さ」と「結論の強さ」を一致させる能力を鍛えることになる。これがRLCD。

確かにこれは推論モデルの代替ではない。
calibrationがシステム1として「その結論をどこまで信じていいか」つきの仮結論を出し、それを根拠にシステム2のLLMに振り分ける、もしくは振り分けないで速攻で進めるかを決められる。そう言う能力を高めているということになる。

このことを理解せずに、単に分類できた、オープンモデルで性能が近づいた、超えたみたいな話をするのはナンセンスで、使い物にならないものを作っているということになる。

q.t:
TypeSafe の創業者 Diogo Almeida が、Jev 発表の6週間前に公開していた講演『 Why RLCD beats RLHF 』。Jev の設計思想が垣間見える。

①「私は OpenAI で ChatGPT を嫌っている数少ない一人だ」
> I'm one of the few people at OpenAI who actually hates on ChatGPT

②「なぜ全ての LLM に人間のループが要るのか？私たちが文字通り、人間をループに入れたからだ」
> Why do all LLMs require a human in the loop? The simple answer is we literally put them in the loop.

③「過大な約束は仕様だ。設計によるものだ」
> overpromising is a feature. This is by design.

④「ハルシネーションは、私にとって、人間の好みへの最適化に内在するものだ」
> hallucination to me is intrinsic to optimizing for human preference

⑤「Claude Code はまだ支援の時代の一部だ。まだ RLHF だから」
> Claude code is still part of that assistance era. Claude code is still RLHF

⑥「私たちはソフトウェアを書くことを自動化しただけで、表現力は同じまま」
> We're just automating the writing of the software. But then its expressibility is the same.

⑦「RLHF が間違いだったとは言わないが、予想していなかった奇妙な回り道だった」
> I wouldn't say RLHF is wrong, but it was like a weird detour and one that we didn't expect

⑧「今日この後、とてもスパイシーなものを投稿する。ヒントは、元のスケーリング則は間違っていた、だ」
> I will post something later today that I guarantee will be very spicy. The hint is that the original scaling laws were incorrect.

——この⑧の6週間後に出てきたのが Jev。

q.t:
"DiffusionGemma as Jev" showcases the power of non-autoregressive architectures.

While Jev demonstrates the value of rapid decision models, running DiffusionGemma in this paradigm leverages canvas diffusion to evaluate structured choices in a single parallel pass:

⚡ ️Massive Parallelism: Denoises across an open canvas in a single step instead of sequential autoregressive token generation (~0.2s on a DGX spark).

🧠 Full Bidirectional Attention: Allows every option to attend to the full context concurrently, yielding well-calibrated decision distributions.

👁️ Multimodal Grounding: Inherits Gemma 4's spatial vision capabilities for complex visual and text decisions.

Read more about this approach here:
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57250

t:
After chatting in the @typesafeai builders channel, got a cool feature idea for the JEV moderation bot:

Let JEV decide if a message belongs in that channel.

E.g. A support-chat shouldn't get spammed with off-topic talk. 

JEV can flag it and nudge the user toward the right spot...
- memes go to memes channel
- casual talk to general channel 
etc.

Should keep the server way cleaner and less cluttered. 

Let's integrate it into the JEV Moderator Discord bot and see how it plays out.

q.t:
Built a real-time Discord moderation bot powered by @TypeSafeAI’s System One model (Jev) 🛡️⚡

Instead of dumb regex filters, it uses calibrated AI decisions with: 
📈 4-Stage Progressive Escalation (Warning DMs ➔ 10m Timeout ➔ 1h Timeout) 
📜 Dual Audit Logging (Discord Server Audit Logs + discord logs channel) 
🔐 Ephemeral 2-step confirm dialogs for admins
🧠 Real-Time On-The-Go Learning (1-click pardon immediately teaches the AI so it never repeats a false flag)

Real-time decision AI in software is a game changer. 🚀

q.t:
The big themes I've been working on this year are: multi-model systems, specializing models for specific tasks, "thinking fast and slow" using multiple models/loops/prompts together in one application, and co-design of harnesses/tooling and models.

The big release today from @typesafeai touches on all of these! Their new model, Jev, fills a big, big gap in our multi-model toolkit.

I'm obsessed with building realtime systems. Voice agents, physical AI, new kinds of human-in-the-loop software.

We often build voice agent front-end loops that need to drive a variety of backend systems, ranging from extremely big and slow (for example, coding agents) to super-fast and specialized (think vision systems and classifiers).

When we're doing things like updating a dynamic user interface, we want to generate small bundles of error-free, strongly typed, structured data ... many times a second. But we also want to leverage the flexibility and natural language abilities of LLMs.

I think of this as pulling out a subset of the context from the long-running human interaction (voice and text conversation), combining that context with other state the application is managing, prompting an LLM, and getting back structured data. We build with this pattern a lot. (There's a whole section of the Pipecat docs about the `UIWorker` pattern.) 

But even small-ish, fast LLMs take a few hundred milliseconds to generate ~100 tokens of structured data one token at a time. However, this is a parallelizable operation and it's right in Jev's wheelhouse.

This is the first model release in a while that feels to me like a genuinely new architecture solution to one of our big, interesting, hairy, real-world pain points as we figure out how to design new, AI-native systems.

I also really love the fact that the second post in the thread below starts out: "The gains aren’t free: Jev can't generate text".

One of the things that drives me crazy about some of the scaling-is-all-you-need discourse around models is that there are *always* systems engineering trade-offs, and they *really* matter.

There are lots and lots of exciting things to build in this new era of LLMs and generative AI. Making things that are fast enough, reliable enough, and affordable enough that people will actually use them is going to require creative exploration of a very wide design space!

I'm super-excited about Jev. Congratulations to the Typesafe team.

TypeSafe AI @typesafeai  came out of stealth yesterday and it's a genuinely different bet on where AI goes next.

Founder Diogo Almeida helped write the InstructGPT paper, basically the recipe that turned GPT-3 into ChatGPT. His argument now: we've spent years making models great at talking to people, but most intelligence in the world should eventually run quietly inside software, not in a chat window.

So instead of another chatbot, TypeSafe built Jev. It doesn't generate text token by token. It takes in unstructured state and spits out typed, probabilistic decisions in parallel. No hallucinated JSON, no malformed tool calls, no parsing/validating strings before your code can use them. They're calling it a "frontier-intelligence function call."

Numbers being thrown around: 70-500ms response times, and claims of being 20-200x faster / 40-400x cheaper than a normal LLM doing the same job. Worth noting those benchmarks are internal, graded against GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 outputs rather than independent ground truth, so take the multiples with a grain of salt until someone outside the company runs the numbers.

$40M seed led by DCVC. Co-founders Erik Gafni (built a genomics AI startup, worked at Invitae/Freenome) and Sasha Sheng (ex-Meta/FAIR). Named Jev after the Jevons paradox, the idea that making something more efficient can increase total usage rather than shrink it.

Where I think this actually gets interesting: any system that's currently duct-taping a chat model into doing classification, routing, or scoring, then writing a bunch of brittle regex/validation to catch when it goes off-script. Think fraud/anomaly flagging with latency SLAs, real-time ad or lead routing, agent orchestration layers picking which tool to call next, or large-scale classification jobs over messy data (this is the one I'd watch closest for healthtech, triaging incoming patient messages, flagging abnormal lab values, routing intake forms, anywhere you need a fast, bounded decision instead of a paragraph).

Not going to replace a general-purpose LLM for anything that needs actual reasoning or explanation. But as a cheap, fast decision layer sitting behind one? Could be a real unlock for latency-sensitive production systems.

Jev is HERE and this is the CLEAREST explanation of what it is and what NEW businesses it unlocks.

(and at the end I'll tell you how to get Jev even if you're on the waitlist)

WHAT IT IS

You know how you open your inbox and have to decide what's junk, what needs a reply, and what can wait? Jev does that part. It looks at each thing and says "this is junk, I'm 94% sure."

It doesn't write anything back to you. It just sorts.

1,700 emails for 18 cents, instantly.

That sounds kinda trivial but the important part

WHAT IT UNLOCKS

My explanation of Jev sounds small until you realize HOW MANY jobs are exactly this. Someone reading a stack of applications. Someone deciding which support ticket goes to which team. Someone looking at inbound and deciding who's worth calling back.

A few ideas on what it unlocks:

1/ Instant quotes that are actually instant. Every quote form on the internet says "we'll email you by end of day." Build the version that answers in under a second, for roofers, movers, insurance, legal intake.

2/ Lead scoring as a product. Every agency and service business has a contact form full of junk. Score every submission and send the real ones straight to the owner's phone.

3/ Support triage for companies with no support team. The ticket gets classified and routed before anyone opens it.

4/ Clipping tools. Pass in a transcript, get the best moments scored in three seconds. Every clipping product just got a cheaper engine.

5/ Application piles. Grants, permits, insurance claims, job apps, loan docs. Someone reads that stack one item at a time today.

6/ Marketplace matching. Someone types what they need and gets matched to the right local business instantly instead of waiting for callbacks.

7/ Browser agents that actually move FAST. That makes bulk browser work practical: pulling quotes from five carriers, filing the same form for 200 clients, checking supplier inventory in real time etc.

TLDR; find an expensive queue and put Jev at the front of it.

HOW TO GET IT

Jev 是 TypeSafe AI 在 2026 年 9 月 15 日前后推出的一款「不聊天、只做决策」的 AI 模型，目前在开发者圈子里很火

它由前 OpenAI 研究员、InstructGPT 论文共同作者 Diogo Almeida 创立的公司推出，定位为第一款 System One Model（借鉴卡尼曼《思考，快与慢》里的「系统 1」：快速、直觉式判断）。口号大致是：Decisions, not strings——要决策，不要文本.

它和 ChatGPT / Claude 有什么不同
大模型一个 token 一个 token 往外生成文字、代码、解释。

Jev 完全不生成自然语言，而是：
- 输入：一段非结构化状态（邮件、工单、日志、JSON 等）+ 你预先定义好的问题
- 输出：带类型、带概率/置信度的结构化答案

三种基本问题类型：
Choice : 从你给的选项里选一个 , 例如这封邮件该分给哪个队列？
Score: 按你定义的尺度打分,  例如紧急程度 / 相关度 / 风险有多高
Noul（是非）: 给出「是」的概率, 例如客户是在要求退款吗？

因为输出形状固定，所以理论上没有「解析失败」或幻觉式乱输出；程序可以直接拿结果做分支。 

为什么会爆 
官方自称在适合的工作流上：
- 端到端延迟约 70–500 毫秒
- 比对照大模型快约 20–200 倍（自家评测最高约 193.6 倍）
- 便宜约 40–400 倍（最高约 444.6 倍）
- 输入约 $0.042 / 百万 token，输出免费

q.t:
Jev 火了几天,  我才知道了, 是不是落伍了 

ChatGPT 共同发明人 Diogo Almeida 出新模型 Jev。TypeSafe AI 做的。

should i surface this?

t:
Not but really it is quite funny because if you turned off LLM based coding agents right now, how many of you could use Jev?

If we reverted them to 2024, how many still?

consider this when moving from one completely separate concept, to another. The actual capacity of stuff you need to understand to truly use this thing (if you really want to use an API) is based on technical competency. This isn't the fault of the developers, who presumably understand this, but people who are treating it like setting up an OpenAI API app in 2024 without understanding remotely how Claude/Astra are building systems to utilise this - it is far more mechanical, it is not like figuring out the vagueness of language model results.

Shovel Sellers (providers) will be happy to sell you the access, and more power to them to do so, but this will be a steep learning curve for what could easily be narrowed down to prompts & turn management - and the developers themselves have a duty to ignore incompetence to sell a product, so cannot be expected to justify why language models may (or may not) be far better for a lot of tasks. 

Reasoning is a significant part of thought, and in sophisticated systems requires language to work - Jev-like systems cannot truly reason because they don't process language (weights).

Yet again, the devs never claimed it could, they actually claimed the opposite and clearly stated this limitation & difference - still, of course, we will now have people blindly ignore this advice for two reasons 

A) trend

B) cost

And a significant number of non-technical folks who adopted this stuff due to AI will largely lack the instinct to judge when simple rule based logic is superior & more cost effective (traffic lights are a good example of this, using an API model for this as I have seen one guy do is incredibly funny).

In early evals, we're seeing adding Jev cut median Act latency from 1.97s to 0.46s (about 4.3× faster)

Across 240 real-site task runs, success went from 85% to 95.4%.

Jevのキラーアプリ、「意味で探す grep」を作った。

semgrep -e "顧客が怒っている" と打つと、"angry" も「怒」も含まない行まで拾ってきます。

正規表現の代わりに、TypeSafe AI の Jev（System One モデル）に 1 行ずつ「この行は○○の意味に合うか」を yes/no 確率で答えさせる。Jevの特性を活かして30 行をまとめて 1 リクエスト、200 行のログが 1 秒弱で返ります。依存ゼロ、Node 1 ファイル。

grepに準じるオプション体系。

・-e A -e B で OR、-a で AND、-v で AND NOT
・-r で再帰、-l でファイル名だけ、-A/-B/-C で前後の行、--color
・確率の閾値は --level loose / strict で調整

ベクトル検索と何が違うかというと、否定検索もできるし、話題の近さではなく「命題が成り立つか」を見るところです。「返金してほしい」と「返金処理が完了しました」は埋め込みではほぼ同じ距離ですが、「顧客が返金を求めている」という意味で引くと 0.98 と 0.10 に分かれます。だから AND や NOT がそのままブール演算として効きます。「返金の話だが要求ではない行」なども 1 コマンドで検索できます。

問合せは「意味」でおこなうので、多言語検索が普通に可能。日本語と英語の区別もフランス語もロシア語も、その混在文書からも検索できます。仏・露・独・西・中・韓14行を4言語（日・英・仏・露）の意味クエリで検証した結果、取りこぼしも誤爆もゼロで、どの言語で意味を書いても同様に機能します。

ar.ti: Jev found more evidence. Our agent still got more answers wrong.
ar.tx:
I went through @typesafeai  Jev's launch posts and a bunch of the builds showing up on X. Semantic Find, browser automation, instant UI, email classification. There are some very good ideas in there.
I was excited too. A few days ago, I shared a Jev workflow and called the architecture a thing of beauty.
But after enough clips, I wanted to see the boring parts. The baseline. The wrong answers. The cases where adding Jev made something worse. What happens to the final outcome after that very fast decision?
Launch week rewards the clip that makes you stop scrolling. As a builder, I need enough detail to decide what I can trust inside my product.
So we put Jev inside Smriti, our memory layer for AI agents, and tested what happened to the answers.
We got more evidence into the context. We also got some worse answers. After changing how we used the labels, the result improved modestly. We are still keeping it optional.
I looked at a sample of launch-week posts and linked builds, not every demo ever posted. These are development tests, not customer production traffic.
The public work is worth taking seriously. Shubham Saboo's semantic Find, Chris Tate's UI experiment and Kyle Jeong's browser loop show different places to put a fast decision model. Ryan Vogel tested email classification on his own inbox. Those posts gave me ideas. They did not answer whether Jev should control the evidence in our memory pipeline.
We had to measure that ourselves.
We already had a baseline worth protecting
Smriti is a local memory layer built around SQLite, with four retrieval channels and explicit fact history.
In our earlier local growth test at 36,500 synthetic records, warm retrieval took 20.5ms for Smriti, 66.3ms for @garrytan  GBrain semantic and 381.3ms for @mem0ai  OSS. All three semantic routes used the same local embedding model.
Smriti's measured store was smaller too: 161.1MB, against 840.2MB for GBrain and 313.8MB for Mem0.
Separate, selected 50-question answer tests put Smriti alongside Mem0: 64% versus 64% on LongMemEval, and 54% versus 52% on LoCoMo.
 
That gives us a reason to take our baseline seriously. It does not give us a universal win over either system.
The cost detail matters: all three local growth setups had zero paid model/API charges. Hardware, electricity and operator time were not measured. We have a measured speed and storage advantage in that workload. We do not have a measured total-cost victory. We also do not have matched generated-answer scores against GBrain.
Adding a new model had to improve something users would notice.
The first result looked better until we checked the answers
We pinned Jev 1.13.0 and asked it to judge candidate evidence: does it directly support the question, supply a needed connection, contain a relevant update, or apply to this query?
On a frozen replay of 100 development questions, complete labeled source messages increased from 105 to 114 out of 167. Questions with all annotated support present increased fro

t:
Typesafe's new System One model concept, and their first example, Jev, were released yesterday.

this is not an LLM.  It can take arbtirary input like an LLM, but it doesn't generate text, and doesn't use output tokens for systematic reasoning.  (aka Daniel Kahneman's "System Two" reasoning from "Thinking Fast And Slow")

I think this is a pretty big deal.

State of the world before Jev:
LLMs are really good at generating english and code.  But often in production systems,  background systems, etc, we’re just having them generate JSON..  because we’re not using them for generation, we're really just using them as a fuzzy "switch" or "case" statement, i.e. "given this unstructured input, give me a decision" -- and we're getting them to write JSON to represent their decision because that's the only way to get a code generator to give us a structured decision (or an evaluation score, or a multiple-choice answer, etc)

Jev is extremely fast and efficient, and still damn smart, for this kind of work, and so it will eat away at the market share of LLMs

I think more than 75% of the LLM spend I currently oversee at Endgame and deploy into academic research will be ported over to System One models

LLMs will be left with coding assistance, summarization, and chat UX (still big and important use cases, but not everything)

System One models will own evals, scoring systems, fuzzy logic gates, data hygiene, etc.

Model-as-judge architectures will not use LLMs to do the judging.

And because every interaction with an LLM tends to have at least one eval, the total input tokens going into System One models will eventually eclipse the total input tokens going into LLMs.

I love it that potentially the most impactful & widely adopted model class might be specialized models VS AGI class models 

Cheap experts vs expensive General intelligence

I don’t need god to write an email or generate an image lol

q.t:
For anyone curious how Jev works, I made a visual explanation using @claudeai :)

This is based on the Qwen2.5-RLCD model which @harshagundal released on @huggingface 

The idea is to replace autoregressive LLM generation by a single Transformer decoder (of a pre-trained LLM), which processes the context + JSON schema only once. The keys and values of those tokens are cached.

Next, for each field of the JSON schema, we:
1. pass its field suffix tokens through the Transformer decoder again (reusing the KV-cache)
2. obtain a final hidden state, which we pass through the language modeling head
3. we obtain scores, also called logits, for all tokens in the vocab of the LLM
4. we only look at the scores of the tokens we care about for the given field, and pass those through a softmax to obtain probabilities which sum to 1
5. we take the token with the highest probability.

The benefits of this are that:
1. it's fast (we don't need to generate the JSON schema token by token)
2. it's 100% valid JSON (we don't need to rely on the model to generate a valid schema)

t:
JEV is a classifier. It returns a typed decision, never text. Which is exactly why I wanted to see it write.

So I put it in a loop. Every turn, the story so far goes into the state, a trigram model built from public domain fairy tales proposes 15 possible next words, Jev picks one, I glue it to the end of the text. Repeat 90 times.

It writes:

"Once upon a time there was a poor man who had seven sons, and a woman had a daughter. And there was a fairy had a son. And then the man went to find a way to get a good deal of money. And he went and found the fairy gave him gold."

Is it good? No. It's a toy PoC, 0.4 s and $0.00003 per word, and the thing feeding it candidates is three pages of Python doing what Shannon described in 1948. But a model that cannot produce a single token just produced a fairy tale, with characters that come back.

Here is the part I did not expect to find. Generation splits into two jobs: something that proposes candidates, and something that judges which one makes sense. A LLM does both inside one model, so you never see the seam. Split them and you can measure which one is the bottleneck. It's the proposer. #Jev picks from the long context block on 60 turns out of 90, median confidence 0.36, and when the corpus runs dry it keeps choosing correctly between words that have nothing left to say. The text falls apart, the judge is still doing its job.

Ask me anything.
The silliest experiments are my favorite kinds of experiments, I love to see that people are playing in all sorts of directions

q.t:
Jev is one of the more interesting model launches I have seen recently because it asks a very simple question:

Why are we using autoregressive LLMs as insanely expensive if statements inside software?

The easiest way to think about it is:
LLM:
text -> generate tokens sequentially -> text
But, Jev:
state -> evaluate predefined decisions in parallel -> probabilities / typed values

Suppose your application has some state like a customer record + their latest message, and you want to know:
{
    "is_churn_risk": bool,
    "intent": Choice["refund", "support", "upgrade"],
    "urgency": Score[1, 5],
}

A normal LLM still has to autoregressively generate something like:
{
  "is_churn_risk": true,
  "intent": "refund",
  "urgency": 4
}

Even with structured outputs or constrained decoding, it is still fundamentally generating tokens one after another.

Jev is designed differently.

Instead of generating the answer as text, it appears to encode the input and directly produce distributions for all of these variables in parallel:
P(churn=true)    = 0.91
P(intent=refund) = 0.73
P(intent=support)= 0.21
P(intent=upgrade)= 0.06
P(urgency=1..5)  = [...]

So there is no need to generate {, "intent", :, "refund" and all the other syntactic machinery we normally pay for when the actual application only needs a decision.

This sounds a bit like classic classification models, but the interesting part is that traditional classifiers usually have fixed labels defined during training.

Jev appears to support dynamically specified typed decisions at runtime while still avoiding autoregressive generation. That explains where the speed claims could come from.

If you ask an LLM to answer 30 classification-style questions, the execution looks roughly like:
prefill
-> token 1
-> token 2
-> token 3
-> ...
-> token 300
Hundreds of sequential decode steps.

Jev can instead do something much closer to:
input
-> forward pass
-> 30 distributions in parallel

Much more GPU-friendly.

That's why their reported 70-500 ms latency and very large speed/cost improvements don’t sound architecturally crazy to me, although their biggest benchmark numbers are obviously on workloads that are shaped exactly like this kind of System-One decision problem.

The second interesting part is RLCD:
Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions.

Instead of only optimizing for:
"Did the model choose the right answer?"
you also care about:
"Does the probability it outputs actually mean something?"

If Jev says:
confidence = 0.90

then ideally, across decisions where it reports ~90% confidence, it should actually be correct roughly 90% of the time.

That is extremely useful for real software:
if confidence > 0.98:
    auto_execute()
elif confidence > 0.70:
    ask_for_confirmation()
else:
    escalate_to_human()

That is much more useful than an LLM simply saying "I am highly confident."

One claim I would be careful with is "can’t hallucinate."
What Jev can strongly constrain is the output space.

If your allowed choices are:
refund
support
upgrade

it can’t suddenly invent:
banana

But it can absolutely still choose the wrong valid option.

So the way I would describe Jev is:
It trades generative freedom for bounded outputs, parallelism, and calibrated uncertainty. And that is what makes it interesting.

A huge amount of production AI isn’t actually trying to generate prose. It is trying to answer things like:
Is this fraud?
Which route should I take?
Should I escalate?
What category is this?
Is this user likely to churn?
Which action should execute next?

For those workloads, forcing everything through next-token generation may be the wrong abstraction entirely.

q.t:
This is a terrible compaction strategy that fundamentally doesn't understand how compaction and context management work.

Seems like a lot of people are confused so let's break this down.

1. Compaction isn't a filter
The role of compaction is to clean up history to keep the agent focused, not just deleting noise. It should be used sparingly when context gets too long, not constantly to keep context small.

2. Jev doesn't even know what it's deciding on!
Models use the context of the thread to decide what to keep or not keep in a summary. This implementation goes through on a "line-by-line" (per tool call) basis to decide what should be left or deleted.

Not only does this 32k token context model know very little of what happened before, but (in this implementation) it doesn't even know what the result of the tool call is!

Deleting these things randomly will keep the model from knowing what it's tried and dooms you to end up in "stupid loops" where the model keeps trying the same thing over and over.

3. You're giving up the reasoning entirely
Frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, XAI, and Google do not share reasoning traces over the API. They share encrypted payloads, which Jev cannot see (and often will drop).

Anthropic is even stricter with this, requiring you to preserve the entire history in order to get any of the reasoning data. As a result, using this in Claude Code guarantees the model will act way dumber.

4. Models are tuned on their compaction flows
For the last year, Frontier Labs have been including compaction and long runs as part of the training process. These models have learned ways to compact that are more effective than any rudimentary solution.

Fun fact: If you switch models in Codex and compaction is necessary, compaction will run on the model that was previously used in the thread.

5. Cache writes are more expensive than cache reads.
Cache writes are the biggest cost by far for agents. I often see cache write costs go over 60% of my total LLM spend in my personal use of Claude Code and Codex.

Cache writes are insanely expensive when data earlier in the history is changed (because the old cache is invalidated when things change at the top). Every history edit requires a cache rewrite for ANY data past the history edit.

If your history is "1,2,3,4,5,6" and you delete "2", you have to rewrite "3,4,5,6". This is more expensive than leaving "2" in the history.

Good news. Since we're already killing all of the reasoning tokens by doing this stupid compaction strategy, the rewrite cost won't actually be that high because the model is missing so much data! 🙃🙃

6. The implementation is hot garbage. 
> "Whatever is not kept is deleted permanently, but the assistant can always re-run a tool or re-read a file."

Good luck with that one.

To be clear: this is a cool experiment and I find it genuinely interesting. That said, if you think this style of bs filtering on a probability threshold is actually a compaction strategy, I highly recommend you just use the defaults in tools like Claude Code and Codex.

You're much less likely to hurt yourself that way.

t: What LLM is to coding, that is Jev @typesafeai to operations.

TypeSafe AI launched Jev this week, and my timeline is full of benchmarks. But most people are still testing it like a standard text model.

Jev is a non-autoregressive decision model. You send it your application state plus typed questions (Choice, Score, Noul), and it returns calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass. Input costs $0.042 per million tokens, and output tokens are free. Because all questions evaluate in parallel in 70 to 300 milliseconds, twenty questions on the same state cost roughly the same as one.

Here are 5 high-leverage use cases from the cookbooks and architecture patterns that people should try:

Instant tool-call compaction for coding agents Instead of running a slow summarization prompt when your agent hits context limits, pass the tool trace to Jev. It scores each tool call for task relevance and strips the dead output in one second. A 1M token session drops to 80K tokens without losing critical state.

RAG chunk filtering on read Standard vector search returns noisy, marginally relevant chunks. Run a fast Noul check over retrieved passages before they reach your context window: "Does this chunk contain facts required to answer the query?" Drop chunks scoring below 0.5. You get higher retrieval precision without paying LLM latency per chunk.

Hybrid browser control loops Frontier vision models are too slow for smooth browser navigation. Extract interactive DOM elements, pass them as candidates to Jev, and let it pick the click target in 70ms. Wake up a large model only when the task requires unstructured typing or visual interpretation.

Sub-50ms shell safety filters Run an evaluation check on bash commands and file edits before auto-mode executes them. If Jev returns confidence above 0.85, the command runs immediately. If confidence falls below the threshold, execution halts and asks the user for confirmation.

High-throughput log triage Point Jev at exported event logs or customer messages to evaluate multiple attributes concurrently (severity score, target service, and intent classification). You can process thousands of events per minute for pennies because output tokens carry no cost.

The practical pattern: reserve frontier language models for creative writing and open-ended planning, and route the intermediate filtering, gating, and selection steps to fast decision engines.

Jev replaces LLM calls with typed decisions inside agent loops, claiming 20-200x more speed at 40-400x lower cost.

I kept testing new Jev use cases.

And the more I test it, the more I am impressed by Jev

Here are 7 more:

1. Recruiting candidate screening - Get 100 applicants. Jev can shortlist people who match exact rules like 2 promotions across 2 companies and a 3-year average tenure, then add a confidence score.

2. Recruiting reply qualification - Once candidates reply, Jev can classify their intent, find missing pre-screening evidence, and flag contradictions that need a human review.

3. Sales pipeline risk detection - Connect your CRM. Jev can flag deals marked high risk or sitting idle for 7+ days, so sales knows exactly which opportunities need attention first.

4. Customer voice → messaging - Feed it 24 customer excerpts from Gong or Granola. Jev can surface repeated themes like business impact, faster onboarding, and clear pricing, then use them to improve your website, sales messaging, and case studies.

5. Win/loss messaging analysis - Split those customer conversations by deals won vs deals lost. Jev can show which topics, objections, and phrases keep appearing in successful deals, so you know what language to use more often.

6. Outbound sequence optimization - Pull delivery and reply data from Apollo, HeyReach, or HubSpot. Jev can detect when a sequence is underperforming, when the creative is getting stale, and when it’s time to run another test.

7. Search visibility loss detection - In one example, Jev looks at 5,800 organic clicks, AI citations, and 4 pages losing traffic. Then it can cross-reference that with customer conversations to show which topics deserve more SEO and AEO content.

q.t:
For the last 9 hours, I haven’t stopped testing different marketing use cases for Jev.

Here are 6 of the most interesting ones I found:

1. SEO/AEO opportunity detection:

Pull ideas from customer calls, sales calls, internal meetings, and old content. Jev took 40 ideas, checked what was already covered, and cut them down to 10 worth pursuing.

2. Content deduplication:

Give it those 50 ideas plus your existing site. Jev can remove the 40 that overlap with content you already published, explain why, and send the remaining 10 into drafting.

3.Content quality scoring:

Run clips through Jev before publishing. In one test, it checked for complete thoughts, missing context, visual proof, and topic value in a 204ms median response.

4. X Content pattern analysis:

Feed it your published content plus performance data. Jev can compare engagement by hook, spot the formats that keep working, and tell you which patterns deserve more output.

5. Customer health scoring:

Combine account data, open issues, seat requests, and expansion signals. Jev can separate accounts that need attention from customers showing clear PQL signals like asking for more seats.

6. Product friction detection:

Run onboarding and customer data through the same layer every week. Jev can surface where new users keep getting stuck, then turn those recurring problems into a short list for product to fix.

很多自动化慢得像幻灯片，就是因为把流程控制、视觉和思考全堆给大模型，大模型要思考推理，根本不可能跑得快

我的解法很简单：用 JEV 专职负责判断，再搭配一个高速小模型推理（我用的是DeepSeek V4.1 Flash）👇

比如这个问卷填写：遇到新页面，由 JEV 毫秒级快速判定“这里该做什么”（是勾选、点击还是提交）；一旦需要填空，由 小模型（DeepSeek ）极速响应生成文字填进去， 两者一结合，各司其职，不仅速度快到飞起，而且每一步都极其准确

当然这只是一种思路，可玩性实在太大了，目前我还在测更多复杂场景，马上开源给大家！@CompleteSkeptic

SOMEONE BUILT AN OPEN-SOURCE COMPUTER-USE STACK FOR REAL DESKTOPS

Cua’s latest update points to a development preview called `jev-use`, combining Typesafe’s Jev with Cua Driver; the public `trycua/cua` repo supplies the broader open-source computer-use stack.

WHAT IT DOES

- Cua Driver gives agents tools to inspect and operate native desktop apps and browsers on macOS, Windows, and Linux
- Connects through the CLI, MCP, or typed SDKs, with background delivery when platform support allows
- Cua Fleets provisions isolated cloud desktops that can run commands, capture screenshots, and interact with apps
- Lume creates and manages local macOS and Linux VMs on Apple Silicon using Apple’s Virtualization.Framework
- Cua Bench builds computer-use tasks, evaluates agents, and exports trajectories for training

Huge win for Cua: developers can test and deploy computer-use agents across real desktop environments instead of limiting them to browser-only demos.

TypeSafe AI just released Jev, a general-purpose classifier built for decisions inside software.

Instead of generating text token by token, it returns typed decisions with probabilities and confidence scores. That makes it much faster and cheaper than traditional LLMs for tasks like classification, routing, scoring, and ranking.

Jev is currently in Early Access. When applying at https://typesafe.ai, don't skip "Answer a few questions". Describe a specific use case to improve your chances of getting access sooner.

t:
Jev (@typesafeai)がかなり気になったので、ウェイトリスト登録しておいた。デザインハーネスやワークフローに組み込んだら良さげな気がしてる。

調べてみると、デザインハーネスの判定層に置くのが良さげ。
Jevはテキストも画像も生成しないけど、stateを見て、Choice / Score / Noul を並列で返してくる。
どうやら公式もハーネスでの使用を想定用途に入れているとのこと。 

ということは、こういう組み立てか。
●生成: 既存のLLM
●判定: Jev
●最終適用: ハーネス側の決定論コード
↓
●この案はブランドルールに沿っているか
●情報階層は弱/並/強のどこか
●次の修正方針は spacing / type / contrast / layout のどれか
●人間レビューに上げるべきか
●生成モデルを再実行、もしくは確定してコードに落とすか

どうも、ハーネスに入れるなら、1回のstateに複数の独立質問をまとめるのがポイントらしい。
公式の作り方でも、大きな「良いデザインか？」と1問で問うのではなく、原子的な判定に分解してからコードで合成する、となってる。 

stateに入れるのは、ハーネスが既に持っている以下のような構造化表現の方が相性がいいとのこと。

●コンポーネント
●トークン（色、余白、書体）
●コピー原文
●制約（モバイル幅、WCAG、ブランドガイド抜粋）
●直前の生成差分
↓
候補をN個生成する
各候補を同じルーブリックで並列スコア
閾値以上だけ残す
低confidenceはデザイナーへ
高confidenceだけトークン更新やコード生成に進む

つまり、デザインハーネスの「lint + router」になるから、ループを速く安く安定させる部品になりえる、ということかな。いいやん。

http://Builder.io's Steve just called out fake Jev demos today. Here's what you need to know.

Steve (@Steve8708 of http://Builder.io) posted that Jev is great but demanded people stop posting fake demos of it, and the post exploded to over 90,000 views. Replies split fast: some devs backed him, saying viral clips oversell what Jev can do, while others insisted the demos are real and just show creative uses of the model.

One concrete example came from Putri Karunia, who tried recreating a 'generative UI' demo and found it only worked with a pre-written set of UI components and pre-supplied data, since Jev can't generate new names or styling from scratch. That lines up with how Jev actually works: it's TypeSafe AI's System One model, which doesn't write free text, it just picks answers from typed, predefined question types like Noul, Choice, and Score.

Key numbers:
- 90,100 views on Steve's original post
- 200x faster and 400x cheaper claimed for Jev vs comparable LLMs
- $0.042 per million input tokens, output free
- 70-500ms reported latency

Jev launched days ago from TypeSafe AI, and the debate is over how its demos are built, not the model's core specs.

q.t:
hype-free explanation of jev:

jev does not replace gpt / claude

jev is just a *really* smart switch statement

like if 2016 ml classifiers got 2026 levels of intelligence

it's a new* type of tool that will make a lot of workloads insanely fast, cheap, and accurate

* = and by new, i mean rebranded

~~~

it needs a predefined set of options and it will tell you which one to take

it cannot:

- write code
- generate natural language
- reason step by step / show its work
- produce any output you didn't define in advance
- pick from more than ~255 options in one shot

but it can:

- classify, route, score, rank
- give confidence
- pick the right branch, tool, model, or sub-agent
- judge / verify / guardrail an llm's output
- label tons and tons of rows

~~~

i'd imagine a lot of workflows that look like:

llm proposes options → jev decides → code executes

and i see this fitting *really* well with code mode and mcp

~~~

implying this will lead to agi seems incredibly far fetched to me, but i don't want to discount the types of applications that this will make possible

マウント時やアプリ起動時に、アクセスパターンの説明やファイル種別から readahead サイズや I/O スケジューラを選択

■インシデント時の自動対処
ログ断片を state にして「再起動 / スケールアウト / 無視 / 人に上げる」を判定

Pod の説明、ラベル、過去のインシデントメモを見て「この 3 ノードのどれに置くか」。（k8s のスケジューラは ms〜秒で動作）

q.t:
Jev 这个 waitlist 还是很给力的，昨天申请，今天就能用上。

给已经拿到 API、但还不知道怎么玩的人整理了一份 Awesome Jev，目前我能确认到的 Jev 项目基本都在这里：

1. jev-ultrafast
Browser Use 做的高速浏览器 Agent。Jev 负责每一步判断「做什么、点哪个元素」，需要输入文字时才调用小模型。Google Flights 搜航班完整跑完约 7.1 秒。
https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast

2. typesafe-mcp
把 Jev 直接接进 Claude Code、Claude Desktop 和 Codex。Agent 可以随时调用 Jev 做 Choice / Score / Noul 这类结构化判断。
https://github.com/itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp

3. jev-mcp
另一个更偏实用工具的 MCP，已经封装好事实核验、Prompt Injection 检测和语义排序。
https://github.com/jkudish/jev-mcp

4. SemDecide
把 Jev 做成 Unix 命令行工具，可以直接拿来做语义判断、分类、打分、过滤和 Guard。很适合塞进脚本、CI 和数据流水线。
https://github.com/sharziki/semdecide

5. Jev Codex Router
先让 Jev 判断每一轮编程任务有多难，再自动决定交给便宜模型还是更强模型。作者用 237 个真实 turn 回放，自测成本降低约 60%。
https://github.com/0xNatoshi/jev-codex-router

6. Winnow
给 Claude Code 做「上下文垃圾回收」。Read、Bash、Grep 输出太长时，先让 Jev 判断哪些内容真的跟当前任务有关，再决定哪些需要进上下文。
https://github.com/GhalebDweikat/winnow

7. Jev Review
用 Jev 做代码审查前置筛选，先判断 correctness、security、reliability、兼容性和测试风险，再把重点问题交给更重的模型处理。
https://github.com/devagrawal09/jev-review

8. Blink
用 Jev 在代码库里做语义寻路。每到一层目录，就判断哪些文件或文件夹最可能和问题有关，再把更多 walker 分配过去。
https://github.com/ellipsis-dev/blink

9. neo4jev
把同样的思路用到知识图谱。Jev 给每条候选边打概率，再用 beam search 一步步找到最可能的路径。
https://github.com/jexp/neo4jev

10. jev-desktop
把 Jev 接到桌面自动化里。它读取 Accessibility Tree，判断该操作哪个控件、执行什么动作，再交给本地执行器。
https://github.com/lahfir/agent-desktop

11. TypeSafe AI Playground
一个专门拿 Jev 做实验的 Rust CLI，已经做了 PHI 检测、代码注释审查、实时语气分析、职业和行业分类等玩法。
https://github.com/markjaquith/typesafe-ai-playground

12. Prism
目前我看到最接近量化/交易场景的项目。它让 Jev 判断流动性池的 toxic flow、市场压力、均值回归可能性和流动性分布方式，目前默认还是 shadow/advisory，不直接驱动交易。
https://github.com/irfndi/prism-liquidity-agent

13. 1v1 Jev
直接做了一个 FPS，让 Jev 大约 9Hz 判断移动、瞄准、ADS、开枪和跳跃。属于最直观展示 Jev 低延迟决策能力的项目之一。
https://github.com/emrickgarrett/OneVOneJev

14. TypeSafe on Neon
拿 Jev 做模型 Router。请求先由 Jev 判断属于哪种任务，再转给 Grok 4.6 或 GPT-6 Astra 等模型执行。
https://github.com/andrelandgraf/typesafe-on-neon

看完这些项目，你大概也知道 Jev 可以怎么玩了，就是拿它反复做「要不要、选哪个、打几分、下一步干什么」。

真正需要生成代码、写文章和复杂推理时，再把任务交给传统大模型。

q.t:
Jevのキラーアプリ、「意味で探す grep」を作った。

semgrep -e "顧客が怒っている" と打つと、"angry" も「怒」も含まない行まで拾ってきます。

正規表現の代わりに、TypeSafe AI の Jev（System One モデル）に 1 行ずつ「この行は○○の意味に合うか」を yes/no 確率で答えさせる。Jevの特性を活かして30 行をまとめて 1 リクエスト、200 行のログが 1 秒弱で返ります。依存ゼロ、Node 1 ファイル。

grepに準じるオプション体系。

・-e A -e B で OR、-a で AND、-v で AND NOT
・-r で再帰、-l でファイル名だけ、-A/-B/-C で前後の行、--color
・確率の閾値は --level loose / strict で調整

ベクトル検索と何が違うかというと、否定検索もできるし、話題の近さではなく「命題が成り立つか」を見るところです。「返金してほしい」と「返金処理が完了しました」は埋め込みではほぼ同じ距離ですが、「顧客が返金を求めている」という意味で引くと 0.98 と 0.10 に分かれます。だから AND や NOT がそのままブール演算として効きます。「返金の話だが要求ではない行」なども 1 コマンドで検索できます。

問合せは「意味」でおこなうので、多言語検索が普通に可能。日本語と英語の区別もフランス語もロシア語も、その混在文書からも検索できます。仏・露・独・西・中・韓14行を4言語（日・英・仏・露）の意味クエリで検証した結果、取りこぼしも誤爆もゼロで、どの言語で意味を書いても同様に機能します。

以下で試せます。
npx @uehaj/semgrep -e "ネットワーク障害" app.log

Think less "classification" and more "state -> calibrated probablistic decision to act upon". E.g. you can use other classifiers to classify emails as urgent or imporant or spam etc. But Jev can look at more than email body (user state, thread age, calendar, company state etc) and then give you answers to things like "does it require an action today and is delaying until tomorrow risky", "does it need a reply from the user or not" etc. Other good examples are agent safety gates for command/action approvals (it can evaluate risky actions, does it need confirmation, is it consistent with original requset, is it reversible etc), games/robot/automation control loops and many more. 
Many of those class of questions can also be done by LLMs btw but jev is faster and cheaper than them there, and many of those can also be done with other classifiers by training/finetuning them but jev scales better by being general purpose.

q.t:
you can make any open source model behave like jev with just a bit of inference engineering.  

it's shockingly easy. to prove it, we built a new endpoint we're calling deepseek-v4.1-flash-jev. see the demo below. here's how it's done:

sglang (an inference engine) offers a scoring endpoint in addition to the normal generation one. in scoring mode, given an input & set of possible answers, it forces the model to produce probabilities for each one. example:

> input: what is most common letter in abcccde?
> possible answers: a, b, c
> output: (c, 0.9), (b, 0.0.5), (a, 0.05)

getting the above behavior instead of streamed output is as simple as using sglang's /v1/score endpoint instead of /generate. there's just one other trick required.

for deepseek, you have to add a closing think tag before the response. this forces a direct answer instead of  a reasoning trace. if you want reasoning, you can do that too, but imo that makes things too slow to be worth it.

dsv4.1 flash is not as good as jev, but if we had enough spare compute to experiment with this same approach for a larger model then i think the decision quality would be at least as good, if not better.

also, somewhat unrelated, i think decision-making models kill all prospecting & sourcing work. i would have absolutely killed to have jev or similar when i was recruiting @mintlify. absolutely incredible.

q.t:
alright - just got Jev deployed for a real production use case, which now performs at fable level quality but 10x faster and saves a ton of money

context - a powerful capability of firstmate is that as an orchestrator it intelligently routes each task to an appropriate agent (permutation of harness, model, and reasoning effort) based on custom user preference

by default, that's done by the firstmate agent and the LLM would have to do some thinking, make tool calls to read dispatch rules, quota data etc and then do the dispatch. this is slow and does cost a bit of LLM tokens

i just replaced this dispatch process with Jev. it makes the same decision with no thinking or tool calls, done in ~200ms, and for the 25 tasks i evaluated this with, it gives the exact same answer fable would have given... 

there's still a tool call needed to invoke Jev, done by the firstmate agent which uses an LLM. but even with that counted, the saving from Jev still resulted in a -71% reduction in cost and -90% reduction in wall time of completing the whole dispatching process

Jev API calls themselves are almost free.. i made 100+ calls, and my usage dashboard still shows $0.01 (which i think means "haven't reached $0.01 yet"). if we just look at the part Jev replaced and not the whole system, then the saving is on the magnitude of ~100x

if you also have Jev and you use firstmate, set TYPESAFE_API_KEY in your .env file in your firstmate repo to activate this

exciting times! i think this is starting to enable a whole new architectural paradigm for software. LLMs are just a small part of it. more on that soon

t: Jev in a nutshell if you're wondering

q.t:
Jev is a super-fast, cheap AI that doesn't write essays or chat. You feed it text (an email, post, ticket, or doc) and ask clear questions with set answers like yes/no, categories, or scores. It instantly returns probabilities and choices your tools can act on.

For non-engineers:
- Auto-sort inbox by urgency or topic
- Rank content ideas or scripts for quality/fit
- Flag angry customers or refund requests
- Score news, leads, or writing for issues
- Prioritize tasks that need attention

It turns fuzzy judgments into reliable, instant decisions without the usual AI fluff.

t:
So, I baked pkg-gate with @typesafeai! 

npm lifecycle scripts can run arbitrary code on install.

pkg-gate: a ~100ms pre-install gate using Jev

4 typed primitives:
 
- Choice: intent
- Score: severity
- Nouls: exfil & curl-to-bash

$ npx pkg-gate <pkg>

#node #npm #security
tr: Welcome to Package Gate. Malicious NTM packages exploit lifecycle hooks like posts installed to steal tokens and drop back doors before your code ever boots. Static Rejects rules miss obfuscated commands, while Generative LMs take three full seconds. That's why we built this on typesafe.ai. Their System 1 model, Jeff, provides fast calibrated snap judgments instead of conversational pros. In under 100 milliseconds, a single speculative fanout evaluates four type primitives. Intent as a choice, threat severity as a continuous score, and secret access as calibrated rules. It is completely deterministic. No hallucinated text, your code inspects strict mathematical probabilities and confidence scores to block threats or escalate to developers with typed structured JSON. NPM install package gate. Fast, deterministic pre-install security powered by typesafe.

第一层是状态捕获。Playwright 挂载到浏览器, 实时提取 DOM 简化树与交互元素, 去除无用样式与冗余节点, 提炼为紧凑的状态快照。
第二层是单选决策裁判。调用的并不是聊天大模型, 而是 TypeSafe 的 Jev。

这一层的核心在于它完全不生成文本, 只接收状态快照与预设的破坏性问题列表, 在约 100 毫秒内并行输出概率分布与选择项。由于输入每百万 Token 仅 0.042 美元且输出不计费, 并发拉满也没有账单压力。
第三层是闭环执行与熔断。无头浏览器根据单选结果触发极端点击、畸形输入或反常跳转, 一旦触发控制台未捕获异常或接口 500 报错, 自动抓取失败现场并保存快照生成复现报告。
用决策模型替代生成模型做测试, 是今年最值得关注的架构微调方向。

NEW JEV PROJECT!! I started this simulator well over a year ago - the thought was “Oregon Trail" but on a generational ship to a nearby star system with plausible hard science constraints. Food. Medicine. Population. Time. I ended up tabling this project for awhile... the release of @typesafeai JEV made me pick it back up.

Every shipmate becomes an intelligent node. Different roles/priorities. Different reactions to the same decision. Jev returns the probabilities. The simulation uses them. Cooperation, staffing, what happens next.

In this demo: 500 crew profiles evaluated in 1.27 seconds. Then 1,101 individual responses to your order in 2.61 seconds.

You're the admiral. In cryo. The ship keeps living without you... until something needs your judgment.

A plague. Finite medicine. People dying. You can consult the crew. Inspect an individual's response. Work through a plan with Astra. Then make the call. Live with the consequences. Back into cryo, if you've resolved it.
What I'm really playing with here... problems difficult enough that consulting frontier intelligence becomes part of the gameplay. You need help understanding the situation... the final decision is still yours.

Potential applications:

1). Education. Custom-tailored sandboxes in whatever you're studying. Learn the system by trying to operate it.
2). Fun. Real challenges in leadership. Competing needs. Imperfect information. No clean answer.
3). Training. Practice coordination, resource allocation, difficult tradeoffs. See the second-order effects.
4). Research. A sandbox for studying how people reason WITH AI. What they ask. What they miss. What changes their decision.

Still a prototype. But this is the direction I wanted to test.

https://github.com/0xNatoshi/jev-codex-router

6. Winnow
给 Claude Code 做「上下文垃圾回收」。Read、Bash、Grep 输出太长时，先让 Jev 判断哪些内容真的跟当前任务有关，再决定哪些需要进上下文。
https://github.com/GhalebDweikat/winnow

7. Jev Review
用 Jev 做代码审查前置筛选，先判断 correctness、security、reliability、兼容性和测试风险，再把重点问题交给更重的模型处理。
https://github.com/devagrawal09/jev-review

8. Blink
用 Jev 在代码库里做语义寻路。每到一层目录，就判断哪些文件或文件夹最可能和问题有关，再把更多 walker 分配过去。
https://github.com/ellipsis-dev/blink

9. neo4jev
把同样的思路用到知识图谱。Jev 给每条候选边打概率，再用 beam search 一步步找到最可能的路径。
https://github.com/jexp/neo4jev

10. jev-desktop
把 Jev 接到桌面自动化里。它读取 Accessibility Tree，判断该操作哪个控件、执行什么动作，再交给本地执行器。
https://github.com/lahfir/agent-desktop

11. TypeSafe AI Playground
一个专门拿 Jev 做实验的 Rust CLI，已经做了 PHI 检测、代码注释审查、实时语气分析、职业和行业分类等玩法。
https://github.com/markjaquith/typesafe-ai-playground

12. Prism
目前我看到最接近量化/交易场景的项目。它让 Jev 判断流动性池的 toxic flow、市场压力、均值回归可能性和流动性分布方式，目前默认还是 shadow/advisory，不直接驱动交易。
https://github.com/irfndi/prism-liquidity-agent

13. 1v1 Jev
直接做了一个 FPS，让 Jev 大约 9Hz 判断移动、瞄准、ADS、开枪和跳跃。属于最直观展示 Jev 低延迟决策能力的项目之一。
https://github.com/emrickgarrett/OneVOneJev

14. TypeSafe on Neon
拿 Jev 做模型 Router。请求先由 Jev 判断属于哪种任务，再转给 Grok 4.6 或 GPT-6 Astra 等模型执行。
https://github.com/andrelandgraf/typesafe-on-neon

看完这些项目，你大概也知道 Jev 可以怎么玩了，就是拿它反复做「要不要、选哪个、打几分、下一步干什么」。

真正需要生成代码、写文章和复杂推理时，再把任务交给传统大模型。

t:
Another use case I wanted to try with #Jev from @typesafeai: GTM prospect matching.

I built Prospectwise around a simple question: someone has the right job title, but does their actual work make them relevant to what we sell?

The demo takes a product and customer brief, lets you review the search filters, then uses @metix_ai to retrieve people with their professional profiles and work history.

Jev reviews each profile against the brief, 20 at a time, and returns Match or Not a match.

For example: if you sell a business data API, “CTO” is a broad starting point. The more useful question is whether that person is building recruiting software, sales intelligence, or an AI research product that could use your data.

That’s the distinction I wanted to test.

The UI shows the evaluations happening live. Retrieval and evaluation have separate clocks, so the Jev timing measures only its part of the workflow.

I kept the output binary for this experiment. It gives you a shortlist to investigate—not a claim that someone has budget or wants to buy.

An interesting way to connect Metix’s people data with Jev’s evaluation API. Curious what other GTM matching tasks people are trying.

http://platform.metix.ai

GLiNER2 already did schema-in, scores-out in one pass. The real question is calibration inside a tight agent loop, not who shipped classification first.

If Jev is simply stronger on the same task, say that. If the real gap is latency and abstention that you can apply to every tool call, that's the part worth stealing.
