Jevのキラーアプリ、「意味で探す grep」を作った。

semgrep -e "顧客が怒っている" と打つと、"angry" も「怒」も含まない行まで拾ってきます。

正規表現の代わりに、TypeSafe AI の Jev（System One モデル）に 1 行ずつ「この行は○○の意味に合うか」を yes/no 確率で答えさせる。Jevの特性を活かして30 行をまとめて 1 リクエスト、200 行のログが 1 秒弱で返ります。依存ゼロ、Node 1 ファイル。

grepに準じるオプション体系。

・-e A -e B で OR、-a で AND、-v で AND NOT
・-r で再帰、-l でファイル名だけ、-A/-B/-C で前後の行、--color
・確率の閾値は --level loose / strict で調整

ベクトル検索と何が違うかというと、否定検索もできるし、話題の近さではなく「命題が成り立つか」を見るところです。「返金してほしい」と「返金処理が完了しました」は埋め込みではほぼ同じ距離ですが、「顧客が返金を求めている」という意味で引くと 0.98 と 0.10 に分かれます。だから AND や NOT がそのままブール演算として効きます。「返金の話だが要求ではない行」なども 1 コマンドで検索できます。

問合せは「意味」でおこなうので、多言語検索が普通に可能。日本語と英語の区別もフランス語もロシア語も、その混在文書からも検索できます。仏・露・独・西・中・韓14行を4言語（日・英・仏・露）の意味クエリで検証した結果、取りこぼしも誤爆もゼロで、どの言語で意味を書いても同様に機能します。

Small, fast, confidence-weighted, lives inside a bigger machine.

lmk if i got it wrong.

Tried @typesafeai's   semantic-find cookbook on supplier replies for Factory Twelve, an apparel sourcing platform. Interesting first results with jev-1.13.0.

I composed three questions over the same state in one System One request:

- Choice — `where`: select the most relevant clause ID.
- Noul — `exists`: probability that the reply supplies at least one requested detail.
- Choice — `coverage`: classify the answer as `complete`, `partial`, or `absent`.

Keeping existence separate matters because the clause Choice always produces a winner. Keeping coverage separate matters because a Noul near 0.5 represents uncertainty, not a partially complete answer.

Code splits the source into clauses, preserves source IDs, versions, hashes and character offsets, then copies the selected text verbatim. No generated quotations.

First run: 12 synthetic development cases

- Existence: 12/12 correct at a 0.5 threshold.
- Clause selection: 8/8 correct on answer-bearing cases.
- No highlights shown for all 4 absent-answer cases.
- Coverage: 9/12 correct.
- Mean request latency: 455 ms.
- Total usage: 9,742 input / 1,548 output tokens.

The three coverage errors all had correct clause selection:

- `$8.50 per piece`: `complete`, despite an unspecified named currency.
- `USD 8.50`: `complete`, despite an unspecified price basis.
- `30% deposit, 70% before shipment`: `partial`, where our rubric accepts the schedule as complete.

It correctly treated “third-party testing costs extra” as a complete answer to whether testing is included. Answer completeness and requirement compliance are different judgments.

For display, code requires non-absent coverage plus Noul ≥0.7 to highlight evidence; absent coverage plus Noul ≤0.3 shows no answer; disagreement goes to review. Those thresholds are provisional and uncalibrated but based on other experiments.

Clause selection looks promising as a small, composable primitive which is super exciting. 

Unsurprisingly, completeness needs a tighter contract, potentially decomposed into individual requested details and combined with deterministic checks.

This is based off a small synthetic set, no tuning after this run, and no holdout evaluation yet. 

How others are decomposing coverage: one Choice over the whole query, or independent Nouls for each required detail?

t:
In my work as a developer, I've always stuck to one rule when building products and SaaS: AI executes, code decides. To me it's the only sane approach if you don't want the AI running your processes its own way.
That's why I find Jev, from TypeSafe AI, so interesting. The company was founded by Diogo Almeida, who worked on the RLHF methods behind ChatGPT at OpenAI. Jev is the first of a new category they call System One Models, now in early access, built for one specific job: making structured decisions at a speed and cost no traditional LLM can match.
Training doesn't go through RLHF or RLVR, the methods used to tune conversational models. TypeSafe developed its own technique, RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions), which optimizes for calibration rather than human preference: how closely the probability Jev reports matches the actual accuracy of its answer.
And that's where it lines up with my rule: the model returns a value with a probability, and the code decides what to do with it.

Top 5 Jev Alternatives:
__

I have been running a benchmark since this morning on every Jev alternative against Jev. So far, none have been it on accuracy but some have slightly less accuracy with better speed. So far, here are my rankings... And be mindful, there are 40 still in queue + I am automatically scraping for more on X which get placed in the queue by my agents. 

1. djev - Slightly lower accuracy and slightly faster speed than Jev. Worthy tradeoff. (https://djev.dev/)
2. Simplejev-qwen38-27b - Best open source model you can replace Jev with today but requires the ability to run a 27B model. You may need a DGX Spark or similar. (https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B). I have a feeling the Simplejev version of Qwen Flash Next will beat Jev on speed and accuracy. @MiaAI_lab I would love if you can Simplejev your fantastic model and beat Jev with open source! (Simplejev-qwen36-35b-a3b is basically interchangeable and you should always choose the former). (https://simple-jev.featherless.ai/)
3. Reflex-4b - This is actually one of my favorites. It is a great tradeoff between speed and accuracy. It is 2-3x faster than Jev but 5% or so less accurate. That said, I bet somebody can tune it or something. It is apache 2.0 for reference.  (https://huggingface.co/YannQi/R-4B)
4. Decider-2b - I love this one because it did the whole test in like 4 minutes or something ridiculous. It is about 10x faster than Jev and completely local. It's accuracy is a 5% less... So it is up to you if that tradeoff is worth it. Considering the size, you can slap this thing on a work computer and get stuff done quickly. Love this one. (https://huggingface.co/Mapika/decider-2b)
5. Lastly is Laya... It is the historical model that did not get enough love. It does not seem to be as good as Jev, but is is very fast on a GB10 GPU... It's accuracy is 62.5% which is not worth it to me. I would say anything less than 70% is a nogo. Definitely not worth the tradeoffs when we consider a faster and higher accuracy model like decider-2b.

Do not let people convince you that Jev is not special or is a tool we always have. It is the frontier of this paradigm... But it is losing ground quickly and I might find a better model by tomorrow.

TypeSafe AI's Jev model is under fresh scrutiny after a researcher's tests raised questions about its "no hallucination" claims. Jev is built as a systems model that returns type decisions instead of generated text, and the company says it runs 40 to 200 times faster and 40 to 400 times cheaper than frontier LLMs on classification tasks, since it only picks from valid typed options rather than generating free text.

A researcher posting as NURL_AVB found that identical prompts don't produce deterministic output, and that simply re ordering the answer choices shifted the resulting probabilities. Other users ran their own tests with mixed results. One account, rate on, said repeated identical calls can shift probability scores by several hundred points, though the final type decision usually holds unless the case is borderline. Another user, Odin, found the topic stayed consistent across runs while confidence scores drifted. A third user, now_PTR, ran small benchmarks and found that choice order barely mattered on average, contradicting the original claim.

Some defenders pushed back on the framing entirely, arguing the "no hallucination" claim only ever meant Jev can't return malformed or invalid output, not that its answers are always correct.

I used Jev to classify 1,018 AI research papers.

The result: $0.08 total cost and 256ms median end-to-end latency per paper.

The pipeline was:

1. Summarize each paper with DeepSeek V4 Flash
2. Send the title + summary + 24 possible topics to Jev
3. Use Jev to classify each paper
4. Visualize everything on http://1kpapers.com

The summaries cost $3.99 on @togethercompute. The classifications cost $0.08 on @typesafeai.

So for just over $4 of inference, I ended up with a pretty useful way to explore the top AI research papers from the past year.

I think this is where things are heading: different models for different parts of the workflow, instead of using one model for everything.

I’m running evals on the Jev classifications before replacing the current ones, but the site is already live: http://1kpapers.com

Jev by @typesafeai was ~7× faster in this controlled side-by-side test (1× speed)

Same loop on both lanes: pick a query → fork of Omnisearch mcp → official source → read → judge the evidence

End-to-end, Jev vs Lina’s model:
•  TypeSafe docs: 1.47s vs 8.96s
•  Python docs: 1.28s vs 9.22s
•  SQLite docs: 1.23s vs 6.86s
Both 3/3

Median total: 1.28s vs 8.96s

Median decision: 213ms vs 2,436ms

Boundary: Jev vs gpt-6-astra, fresh context, low reasoning 

Prepared query choices; neither generated searches freely

Jev shipped three days ago and nobody had benchmarked it. So I did.

60 real-shaped customer messages. Same questions, same conditions, zero retries.
Jev vs GPT-4o-mini vs Claude Sonnet 4.5.

Jev was right 157 times in a row. The system still failed.

Speed first, the least interesting part.

3.2x faster, 3.8x cheaper than GPT-4o-mini.
5.0x faster, 106x cheaper than Sonnet 4.5.

Published claim: 193.6x and 444.6x. Reproduced neither.

3.8x and 106x are the same model. A multiplier isn't a claim until you name the baseline.

The probabilities are the real product.

When Jev put >0.95 on a category, it was correct. 157 of 157 calls.
That's 87% of traffic you can auto-route and never look at.

Through structured output the LLMs return no probabilities. You can't build that tier with them.

Then I looked inside the 157.

49 needed a human. For 18, Jev had also said no human needed. Category right, confidence high, nobody in the loop.

One of them:
"Flight grounded by the typhoon, move tomorrow's shoot to Saturday."
reschedule 1.00. needs_human 0.42.

To catch all 18 you have to gate on the needs_human probability too. Tight enough, and automation falls from 87% to 19%.

Same model, same call. One set of probabilities was clean enough to automate on. The other wasn't.

Confidence is a property of the question, not of the model.

Caveats: 60 synthetic cases, labelled by one person, one machine, one connection. At n=60 one case moves accuracy 1.7 points, so I wouldn't call the model gaps meaningful.

1 of 380 Jev calls hung and timed out at 300s. Set your own timeout.

It basically is a smart gateway. If your code involves making certain decisions( yes/no , choose from a set of predetermined options), then TypeSafe can help evaluate that, provided you give it the relevant context. It’s extremely fast, and extremely cheap (1 output token)

Why is this better when I can ask ChatGPT/Claude to do the same thing?

Well because those models are - 

1. Expensive - you might have to figure out which model to choose for routing,  a cheaper model might hallucinate and choose an output that’s not there, an expensive model is well- expensive

2. Speed - As @CompleteSkeptic pointed in the video, LLMs are optimized for giving strings and so they’re pretty slow for cases where you only need fixed outputs.

This does seem to be one of those things that seems a little obvious in hindsight - like it’s obvious this should exist.

q.t:
I think I’ve found a pretty interesting use case for Jev (@typesafeai).

An always-on AI that knows when you’re talking to it and when you’re speaking to someone else

A thing that frustrates me about Siri/Alexa and even ChatGPT live is that there are moments that make experience feel unnatural.

With Siri/Alexa you keep saying a wake word to get their attention and then talk

With ChatGPT voice- it’s a 1:1 conversation. If someone sitting next to you says something and you reply to them, ChatGPT doesn’t understand you were talking to them.

But what if your agent could figure that out?

So here's a small demo called Toothless - where Jev figures out in real time whether something you’re saying is directed at the AI or someone else.

It does this by considering multiple aspects simultaneously - like whether this is a continuation of a topic that was discussed before, whether it’s something that uses the internet or something can be helped by AI agent and a couple of other things.

I think with a low cost classifier we are much closer to being able to have an always on ambient AI, which can jump and help us naturally, without requiring us to press buttons or keep calling out a command.

Exciting times ahead!

tr: I'm Diego Almeida, founder of Typesafe AI, and at OpenAI, I co-created ChatGBT and RLHF, the post-training algorithm behind most frontier AI. Our team trained the first models to be superhuman at instruction following, what we now call Chat. And we asked ourselves, are models that are superhuman at Chat AGI? The answer was obviously not, but the trillion dollar question is why not? RLHF has led to LMs that are optimizing for human preferences and include issues such as mode dropping, overconfidence, and an overall lack of reliability. These flaws mean that LMs require humans in the loop, and almost no true automation can be done. At Typesafe, we've spent two years building in stealth, and we're finally ready to share our new type of foundation model that's optimized for automation. System 1 models. With a new architecture, new sampler, and new training algorithm, reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions. Movements are clear if you see them side by side. Ask a System 1 model a ton of structured questions, just like you would an LM. Get the answers back near instantly. Meanwhile, LMs take hundreds of times longer to finish responding. Look at how the LM generates sequentially, which is great for a natural conversation, but totally useless for computers. LMs extract intelligence from the tiny straw of auto regression, and similar to the jump that transformers made over RNMs, We are replacing sequential computation with parallel, because that is obviously the future. Our System 1 models output decisions with probabilities and confidence instead of words, and they can't hallucinate. They're a lot more like code, reliable, fast, self-consistent, and Typesafe. This opens up a whole new world of possibilities and applications. Today, we're releasing JIV, the first public System 1 model. It's 100 times faster, so real-time AI is finally possible. This is cheaper with input tokens priced at $42 per billion tokens, and output tokens are free because they're finally too f***ing cheap to meter. JIV is super smart, and its intelligence per dollar is literally off the charts. This is just the beginning. We're excited to see what you build with JIV. As we say at Typesafe, we're building prod, not God. We're waiting seconds for responses or paying for words you never asked for. Side effects may include fewer retries, fewer parsers, fewer broken schemas, and intelligence running inside every software loop. Your software may begin moderating every message, routing every ticket, reviewing every document, and making millions of background decisions that were previously too slow or expensive to automate. Entire software categories may be rewritten in the process. As costs fall, usage may increase dramatically. Ask your developer if your industry is ready.

This project cost $23 to build on Jev.

The same token volume on Sonnet 5 or Terra would be about $1,100. On Sol, about $2,258.

There’s always a hidden tax on new ideas, which is the cost of finding out whether they’re even feasible.

At $1,000, the first prototype often never happens. You talk yourself out of it. At $23, you just build it, watch it fail, change the loop, and run it again.

This sim exists because the idea tax was low. One successful 15-drone run made 201 decisions for about $0.24. 

That’s a tenth of a cent per decision.

Jev probably doesn’t win by making ChatGPT obsolete or matching frontier-model intelligence. 

It wins by making a different class of decisions cheap enough that new use cases become possible. The ones that need millions of small decisions you would never have paid frontier prices for.

Jev + Kimi K3 for fraud detection!

TLDR: Jev classified 100 emails in 1.42 seconds, then I routed the uncertain cases to Kimi K3. The full pipeline got 96/100 correct for only ~$0.07.

Video is not sped up, check out the live run!

Here was my process:

I gave Jev 100 emails to classify (a mix of 50 legit & 50 fraudelent emails). It classified all of them in 1.42 seconds.

An underrated feature about Jev is it will give you the confidence score for a classification, so I routed any prediction under 95% confidence to Kimi K3 to be fully sure.

31 emails fell below that threshold. After routing those to Kimi K3, the combined pipeline reached 96% accuracy.

The full run took 16 seconds & ~$0.07 in inference costs:

- $0.068 from Kimi K3 on @togethercompute
- $0.003 (1/3 of a cent) from Jev on @typesafeai.

I think this is a really interesting pattern: use a fast specialized model like Jev for the narrow task, then route the uncertain cases to a larger LLM.

I feel like this kind of approach could be a game changer for use cases like fraud or anything realtime. You can use the speed & low cost of Jev while having a larger LLM as a fallback to ensure high accuracy.

t:
Just discovered Jev, and this is a really interesting shift in how we think about AI.

Jev is the first “System One Model” from TypeSafe AI, founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida.

Unlike GPT or Claude, Jev isn’t designed to generate text. You give it the current state of your application and typed questions, and it returns structured decisions — choices, scores, or boolean probabilities — with confidence estimates.

For example, an AI agent could use Jev to decide:

which tool or subagent to call next
whether to continue, retry, ask the user, or stop
how urgent or risky an action is
whether an output should be accepted or sent for human review

Instead of using a large LLM to generate and parse text for every small decision, Jev can act as a fast decision layer inside the software.

TypeSafe reports up to 193.6× faster and 444.6× cheaper execution than LLMs on its System One workflow evaluations.

It’s already available through the API and Vercel AI Gateway.

This feels less like “another chatbot model” and more like a different primitive for building AI-native software.

Every software engineer and data scientist worth their salt has a jev use-case on the tip of their tongue.

Feel like I am a second away from having a eureka moment and crashing my car all day. 

There are so many problem that can be solved by jev…

Pergunta
   ↓
  JEV  ← decide o que precisa acontecer
   ↓
Retrieval (RAG) ← recupera conhecimento
   ↓
  JEV  ← avalia/classifica evidências
   ↓
 LLM   ← raciocina e gera

t:
This is an interesting new primitive for agent systems.

Jev isn’t trying to be another model that does everything. It’s designed to make fast, structured decisions inside software.

We’ve been exploring where this fits in Apex, and the implications are bigger than just cheaper inference.

A long-running autonomous software system makes an enormous number of small decisions: classify this failure, score this context, rank these candidates, decide what’s relevant, triage this evidence.

Why spend frontier-model inference on all of them?

The architecture we’re increasingly interested in is heterogeneous:

Cheap, specialised intelligence for high-volume bounded decisions.

Frontier models for the difficult generative work.

Deterministic systems and independent verification decide what is actually allowed to survive.

If autonomous software is going to operate continuously, the economics of intelligence become part of the architecture.

Jev is a very interesting step in that direction.

t:
Jev didn't make my agents smarter.

It made the boring decisions cheap enough to run at every step.

That's the unlock. Not AGI. Not "replacing Claude." A typed yes/no decision you can afford to ask 200 times in one session.

I spent the week running it in a real loop, not a demo.

The old stack:

user goal → big model thinks → picks a tool → checks if it's done → writes the next message

It works until the bill shows up, the cache dies, or the agent quietly leaves the task.

The new stack is simpler:

1. Code owns the paths.
2. Jev judges messy text.
3. The big model plans and writes.

Three questions:

• Is the goal done?
• Which tool comes next?
• Does a human need to see this?

If the answer space is known, I don't generate. I pick.

If B depends on A, I don't batch them. I only run independent questions in parallel.

If Jev says "no" to "is this done," I don't let it keep calling tools. Freeze. Restate the goal in one line. Then continue.

Cheap verification without a brake just makes drift faster.

The practical lesson was harder:

Typed and wrong still ships.

A schema doesn't make the decision correct. A 52/48 split isn't a decision. It's a handoff.

I stopped trusting the label and started trusting the cut.

High-confidence no → stop.
High-confidence yes → go.
Gray band → bigger model or me.

Also, lock the main model at session start. Let Jev raise effort or pick a specialist mid-thread. Rerouting the main model every turn kills the cache and makes you pay twice.

What I don't use Jev for:

Code.
Thread summaries.
Inventing options.

Generate the candidate list in code. DOM, retriever, tool trace. Then let Jev pick.

That's the difference between a decision model and a chatbot in a trench coat.

For people shipping MVPs, this is the part I'd test.

A lot of agent cost isn't intelligence. It's asking a frontier model to act like a switch statement.

Routing.
Done or not.
Safe or not.
Keep or drop this tool call.

Those aren't writing jobs. We just didn't have a primitive that was fast, cheap, and could return uncertainty with a number.

Jev is that primitive.

Nimble and the rest can copy the recipe. The brand won't matter in three months. The layer will.

Weekend test:

Pick one agent you already run.

Find every call that only picks something. Replace it with a typed question. Threshold on confidence, not just the answer. Put a brake on "no."

Then look at the bill and the drift.

If neither moves, you used it like a smaller chatbot.

If both move, you put the system back in your hands.

t:
Introducing Dynamic Context Engine powered by @typesafeai Jev. 

Do your agents go off the rails when context compacts? 

Rather than compacting when context gets big, dynamically generate context from a growing infinite database using parallel Jev to build context live so you never lose anything.

1) Never lose context to compaction again = agents stop going off the rails as often and can recover from lost context. 

2) Net save money on requests by reducing unused context up to 99% without losing the important details with extremely cheap jev calls. In benchmarks we reduced 96% context and maintained 100% accuracy. Results vary on use-case. 

3) Grow infinite context that uses Jev in parallel to filter so you don’t slow down and save money. 5x faster parallel context retrieval than just a database or another context system. 

This seems like a no-brainer and everyone should be using this.

Yes, classifiers existed. BERT, DeBERTa, GLiNER, fine-tuned heads. Most of them were specialized. Pick the labels, train, ship. Changing the rules at runtime meant another training run.

What we did not have was a general-purpose classifier at Terra / Sonnet 5 level intelligence.

You could fake it by asking an LLM for JSON, but that was slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated.

Jev is that missing piece. Labels defined in code, typed answer plus confidence, no extra LLM call.

Classification is not new. What is new is a general-purpose classifier this intelligent, this fast, and this cheap.

q.t:
alright - just got Jev deployed for a real production use case, which now performs at fable level quality but 10x faster and saves a ton of money

context - a powerful capability of firstmate is that as an orchestrator it intelligently routes each task to an appropriate agent (permutation of harness, model, and reasoning effort) based on custom user preference

by default, that's done by the firstmate agent and the LLM would have to do some thinking, make tool calls to read dispatch rules, quota data etc and then do the dispatch. this is slow and does cost a bit of LLM tokens

i just replaced this dispatch process with Jev. it makes the same decision with no thinking or tool calls, done in ~200ms, and for the 25 tasks i evaluated this with, it gives the exact same answer fable would have given... 

there's still a tool call needed to invoke Jev, done by the firstmate agent which uses an LLM. but even with that counted, the saving from Jev still resulted in a -71% reduction in cost and -90% reduction in wall time of completing the whole dispatching process

Jev API calls themselves are almost free.. i made 100+ calls, and my usage dashboard still shows $0.01 (which i think means "haven't reached $0.01 yet"). if we just look at the part Jev replaced and not the whole system, then the saving is on the magnitude of ~100x

if you also have Jev and you use firstmate, set TYPESAFE_API_KEY in your .env file in your firstmate repo to activate this

exciting times! i think this is starting to enable a whole new architectural paradigm for software. LLMs are just a small part of it. more on that soon

#Jev from @typesafeai looks very promising for Observability Decision Model use cases.
 
At @edge_delta , we use frontier models for operational priority scoring, routing events, identifying recurring issues, and similar decisions. Latency adds up.
 
I tested Jev on our OperationPriorityScorer: reading an investigation thread and scoring its priority based on severity, business impact, urgency, and dependency context.
 
We selected 96 real threads, and compared Jev against GPT-5.4.

The outcome:
  • 131 ms median latency vs 4.62 seconds — about 35x faster
  • 72.9% agreement on operational priority bands
  • 19 of 24 high/critical threads stayed high/critical

GPT-5.4 also generated explanations, so the output workloads were different.

Jev tended to assign lower priority, especially for medium-priority threads. 

Still, very promising for an initial test on real observability data.

🚪 "Jeven Doors" is live

A deduction game: the AI has a secret in mind, and you guess it with up to seven yes/no questions.

The AI is Jev by TypeSafe — a model that generates no text at all. It only returns probabilities for typed questions about a state you hand it. The game leans into exactly that:
• "Is it a bird?" → "Yes 98%" — every answer comes with its confidence
• Unanswerable or double questions are detected and cost no door
• When you name the wrong thing, an off-target meter tells you how close you were (a five-level Score)
• One question = one request to Jev (~0.3 s, ~2,000 tokens, about $0.0005 per game)

13 genres — animals, dishes, countries, cities, jobs, sports, famous people, anime titles and more — with three difficulty levels. Seven doors, and one extension of seven more if you run out. UI in Japanese, English, Simplified/Traditional Chinese and Korean.

You need your own TypeSafe (or Vercel AI Gateway) API key to play — bring your own key; it stays in your browser and is never stored on the server.

Jev is seriously impressive. SERV makes it better.

We put Jev through the same benchmark we use to evaluate leading AI models, testing it both standalone and armed with SERV Reasoning.

Paired with SERV, Jev moves into the top tier of our benchmark, beating Claude Fable 5 at 30x lower cost, with cost similar advantages over GPT-5.5 (~15–20x), Gemini 3.5 Flash (~15x), and Grok 4.3 (~6–7x).

The result is clear: Jev + SERV materially outperformed Jev on its own.

Jev is extremely fast, well designed, and great at decision-making. Instead of relying on open-ended responses, it produces structured decisions with probability scores attached. SERV pushes that performance further, adding a stronger reasoning layer to improve the quality of those decisions for high volume agentic work.

The SERV Reasoning API is live, so any developer can test and deploy SERV Reasoning today in just a couple minutes. Get access at: http://openserv.ai  

The agentic economy won’t scale on better models alone. It needs better reasoning infrastructure that are finetuned to the reliability, auditability, and affordability requirements of enterprise agents. SERV is building that layer.

q.t:
This is a terrible compaction strategy that fundamentally doesn't understand how compaction and context management work.

Seems like a lot of people are confused so let's break this down.

1. Compaction isn't a filter
The role of compaction is to clean up history to keep the agent focused, not just deleting noise. It should be used sparingly when context gets too long, not constantly to keep context small.

2. Jev doesn't even know what it's deciding on!
Models use the context of the thread to decide what to keep or not keep in a summary. This implementation goes through on a "line-by-line" (per tool call) basis to decide what should be left or deleted.

Not only does this 32k token context model know very little of what happened before, but (in this implementation) it doesn't even know what the result of the tool call is!

Deleting these things randomly will keep the model from knowing what it's tried and dooms you to end up in "stupid loops" where the model keeps trying the same thing over and over.

3. You're giving up the reasoning entirely
Frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, XAI, and Google do not share reasoning traces over the API. They share encrypted payloads, which Jev cannot see (and often will drop).

Anthropic is even stricter with this, requiring you to preserve the entire history in order to get any of the reasoning data. As a result, using this in Claude Code guarantees the model will act way dumber.

4. Models are tuned on their compaction flows
For the last year, Frontier Labs have been including compaction and long runs as part of the training process. These models have learned ways to compact that are more effective than any rudimentary solution.

Fun fact: If you switch models in Codex and compaction is necessary, compaction will run on the model that was previously used in the thread.

5. Cache writes are more expensive than cache reads.
Cache writes are the biggest cost by far for agents. I often see cache write costs go over 60% of my total LLM spend in my personal use of Claude Code and Codex.

Cache writes are insanely expensive when data earlier in the history is changed (because the old cache is invalidated when things change at the top). Every history edit requires a cache rewrite for ANY data past the history edit.

If your history is "1,2,3,4,5,6" and you delete "2", you have to rewrite "3,4,5,6". This is more expensive than leaving "2" in the history.

Good news. Since we're already killing all of the reasoning tokens by doing this stupid compaction strategy, the rewrite cost won't actually be that high because the model is missing so much data! 🙃🙃

6. The implementation is hot garbage. 
> "Whatever is not kept is deleted permanently, but the assistant can always re-run a tool or re-read a file."

Good luck with that one.

To be clear: this is a cool experiment and I find it genuinely interesting. That said, if you think this style of bs filtering on a probability threshold is actually a compaction strategy, I highly recommend you just use the defaults in tools like Claude Code and Codex.

You're much less likely to hurt yourself that way.

Which Jev alternative is best?
__

Right now, I'm comparing 30 Jev alternatives to the real deal... So far, none have come close when it comes to speed, accuracy and size.

We care about speed, accuracy and size because people may say 'Laya has existed for a year'... But if it is not faster or more accurate, then it defeats the purpose. As of now, Jev seems to be genuinely better than all alternatives on my S1Bench.

There has been a lot of talk around Jev as a next gen 'model', which cannot be far from reality.

Let me try and explain with an analogy of airport:

LLM = the pilot.
It can reason about a complex situation, make a plan, communicate, adapt, write things, use tools, and solve novel problems.

Jev = the air-traffic control system around the pilot.
It constantly makes small decisions:
Which runway?
Is this request risky?
Which model should handle this?
Is confidence high enough to continue?
Does this need escalation?
Did the previous step succeed?

You wouldn't replace the pilot with air-traffic control.

And you wouldn't want the pilot personally answering 10,000 little routing questions every second either.

Very exciting that we have a new infrastructure to make LLMs more reliable and consistent.

Classification is not new. What is new is a general-purpose classifier this intelligent, this fast, and this cheap.

q.t:
TypeSafe AI came out of stealth with Jev, and access is behind a waitlist.

I built an open source version Verdict (Open-jev) you can run right now in a browser tab: And its a real post trained model..(link in comments)

It is a post trained 151M parameters model. ModernBERT-base with a GLiClass head. Instead of token-by-token autoregressive decoding or JSON string parsing, it takes an input text and candidate options, then returns calibrated probabilities and an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome in a single forward pass.

Some of The numbers:

Calibration: 0.83% adaptive expected calibration error on 1,000 held-out cases. I trained with a multi-class Brier score term, then tried standard post-hoc temperature scaling. Temperature scaling degraded the metrics, so the model ships with temperature 1.0.

Order invariance: reversing the option list flips 3.0% of predictions across 1,000 cases. For reference, another open Jev reproduction measured a frozen Qwen3.5-4B at 27.8% flips on the same perturbation, though on their own 36-case fixture rather than mine. Full bidirectional attention evaluates the candidate list simultaneously instead of scanning left to right.

Shuffled-context control: Pairing questions with the wrong document drops accuracy from 95.0% to 22.4% and drives abstention from 21.8% to 72.7%, confirming the model actively conditions on the context.

Latency: 89ms median in-browser via WebGPU, and 35.6ms via ONNX on CPU at 5 candidates.

The negative results:

I ran 12 use cases on public data across both checkpoints and three label framings three passed the promotion gate. Passage re-ranking hit 11.9%, jailbreak screening 34.9%, and phishing detection 57.5%. 

On 337 cases from TypeSafe's public evaluation set, Jev reaches 90.8%, a 26B diffusion model reaches 88.4%, and Verdict reaches 48.1%.which is expected since its just 151M param model but working on trying it on bigger scale as well.

A 151M encoder is calibrated, order-invariant, and fast, but it lacks broad world knowledge. 

In a tiered architecture where a cheap model gates an expensive one, knowing exact failure boundaries is essential. 48 of the 50 classification errors fall below a 0.95 confidence threshold, making the gate predictable.

Which Jev alternative is best?

Right now, I'm comparing 30 Jev alternatives to the real deal... So far, none have come close when it comes to speed, accuracy and size.

The problem with this model is the size. I have a DGX spark but most do not. Merging with Bonsai version of Qwen 27B may be the best way to get size, speed and accuracy that is close to Jev.

这几天看了很多 Jev 项目，我最后自己做了一个 ask-jev，专门给 Claude Code、Codex、Antigravity 这类 Coding Agent 做快速的小判断。

它目前主要做三件事：choose 从几个明确选项里快速选一个，check 对一个明确结论做二次复核，purify 从大量原文里挑出真正需要看的部分。前两个拿不准就返回 unknown，不硬给答案。

purify 和常见的生成式压缩不太一样。它不重新写摘要，只从原文里选内容，而且会强制保留代码块、Git Diff、Traceback、退出码和关键报错，避免把 Agent 后面还要用的执行证据一起删掉。

另外整次 Jev 调用被限制在 280ms 内，不做重试。超时、断网或者 API 出问题就直接回退，不让一个辅助判断把主 Agent 卡住。运行时只有 Python 标准库，也没有后台服务和本地端口。

很多 Jev 项目是在给 Agent 增加新的判断能力，ask-jev 也一样，只是它更强调边界。能快速判断的就交给 Jev，拿不准、超时或出错时，就直接交还给原来的 Agent。

https://github.com/logicrw/ask-jev

q.t:
这两天一直在关注 Jev，我做的导航站现在已经收录了 287 个相关项目。

如果你刚拿到 Jev API，还不知道能拿它干什么，我建议优先看下面这 20 个：

（我没有按 Star 排，主要挑了三类：能马上跑起来的、能明显看出 Jev 优势的，以及脑洞特别大的。）

1. jev-ultrafast
Browser Use 做的高速浏览器 Agent。Jev 每一步只负责判断「做什么、点哪个元素」，需要输入文字时再叫小模型。Google Flights 搜一次航班完整跑完约 7 秒。

2. fast-jev-compaction
给 Claude Code 做上下文压缩。每次工具调用都先让 Jev 判断还有没有用，没用的直接删，留下来的原文不重写。

3. json-render + Jev
Vercel Labs 拿 Jev 试验实时生成 UI。Jev 不逐 Token 写 JSON，只负责选组件、属性和布局，火车票界面从 3.21 秒压到了 0.88 秒。

4. typesafe-mcp
最适合刚拿到 API 的人。直接把 Jev 接进 Claude Code、Claude Desktop、Codex 和 Pi，让大模型随时调用它做 Choice、Score、Noul 判断。

5. jev-mcp
更像一套现成的 Agent 判断工具箱。已经封装了事实核验、内容筛查、Prompt Injection 检测、语义排序、分类和信息提取。

6. SemDecide
把 Jev 做成命令行工具。可以直接在 Shell 里做分类、打分、过滤和判断，很适合接爬虫、CI 和数据流水线。

7. Jev Codex Router
先让 Jev 判断这一轮编程任务有多难，再决定该交给哪个档位的模型。很直观地展示了 Jev 做模型路由的玩法。

8. Winnow
给 Claude Code 做「上下文垃圾回收」。Read、Bash、Grep 吐出一大堆内容时，Jev 先判断哪些真的和当前任务有关。

9. Jev Review
代码审查前先过一遍 Jev，把高风险改动挑出来，再交给更贵的大模型或者人仔细看。

10. Blink
把 Jev 当代码库导航器。每走到一层目录，就判断哪些文件和当前问题最相关，再继续往下找。

11. jev-desktop
把 Jev 用到桌面自动化。它读系统无障碍树，判断下一步该操作哪个按钮、菜单或输入框。

12. typesafe-mario
让 Jev 玩《超级马里奥》。不看截图，直接读模拟器 RAM 里的结构化状态，再决定跑、跳和躲避。

13. jev-drone
拿 Jev 控无人机。底层飞控继续负责稳定和安全，Jev 只做爬升、刹车、穿越障碍这类上层判断。

14. OneVOneJev
直接做了一个 1v1 FPS。Jev 每个决策 tick 都要判断走位、视角、瞄准、开火和跳跃，很能体现低延迟的意义。

15. jev-trader
在 Monad 测试网上做高频做市。Jev 根据价差、收益和主动成交方向，判断下一步买还是卖。

16. Prism
更偏量化策略。它不直接让 Jev 下单，而是让 Jev 判断 toxic flow、市场压力、均值回归之类的状态，再交给原来的策略处理。

17. neo4jev
把 Jev 塞进知识图谱里。每走到一个节点，就让它判断下一条最值得走的边，再一路找下去。

18. jev-curate
拿 Jev 筛训练数据。大量 JSONL、Parquet 数据先做质量、相关性和风险判断，再决定哪些值得进后面的训练流程。

19. Canny
专门防 Coding Agent「嘴硬说自己做完了」。它会看工具输出、代码 Diff 和测试结果，再判断 Agent 的完成声明到底靠不靠谱。

20. killmyidea
这个最适合随手玩。输入一个创业点子，Jev 会从多个维度打分，最后给你 KILL、FIX 或 SHIP。

---

看下来，你就明白了：Jev 最适合的不是写文章、写代码，而是反复做那些「要不要、选哪个、打几分、下一步干什么」的小判断。

真正需要生成和长链推理，再交给大模型。

我已经整理了 287 个 Jev 开源项目，每个都核过公开源码和实际接入点。想继续翻的可以直接去这里搜（还有好玩的抽卡机制）：

https://logicrw.github.io/awesome-jev-projects/?v=1

埋め込みは意味を理解しないけど、大量の候補から関連しそうな候補をインデックス化しておくことで絞り込める。その結果をLLMで再探索したら時間もコストもかかる。

q.t:
Jevのキラーアプリ、「意味で探す grep」を作った。

semgrep -e "顧客が怒っている" と打つと、"angry" も「怒」も含まない行まで拾ってきます。

正規表現の代わりに、TypeSafe AI の Jev（System One モデル）に 1 行ずつ「この行は○○の意味に合うか」を yes/no 確率で答えさせる。Jevの特性を活かして30 行をまとめて 1 リクエスト、200 行のログが 1 秒弱で返ります。依存ゼロ、Node 1 ファイル。

grepに準じるオプション体系。

・-e A -e B で OR、-a で AND、-v で AND NOT
・-r で再帰、-l でファイル名だけ、-A/-B/-C で前後の行、--color
・確率の閾値は --level loose / strict で調整

ベクトル検索と何が違うかというと、否定検索もできるし、話題の近さではなく「命題が成り立つか」を見るところです。「返金してほしい」と「返金処理が完了しました」は埋め込みではほぼ同じ距離ですが、「顧客が返金を求めている」という意味で引くと 0.98 と 0.10 に分かれます。だから AND や NOT がそのままブール演算として効きます。「返金の話だが要求ではない行」なども 1 コマンドで検索できます。

問合せは「意味」でおこなうので、多言語検索が普通に可能。日本語と英語の区別もフランス語もロシア語も、その混在文書からも検索できます。仏・露・独・西・中・韓14行を4言語（日・英・仏・露）の意味クエリで検証した結果、取りこぼしも誤爆もゼロで、どの言語で意味を書いても同様に機能します。

q.t:
LLMs vs. Jev, clearly explained!

TL;DR

The key difference is not that Jev generates faster.

Jev does not generate text at all.

A traditional LLM receives context and produces an answer one token at a time. Even when the output is a small JSON object, every token depends on those generated before it.

Jev receives the same context but evaluates predefined decisions directly. When those decisions are independent, it can evaluate all of them in parallel.

Consider an agent handling a failed deployment. It may need to determine:

→ Whether the incident is urgent
→ Which team should handle it
→ Whether the proposed command is risky
→ Whether the task is complete

An LLM generates a response containing these answers sequentially. The application then parses and validates it.

With Jev, you define the questions and expected answer types upfront. It evaluates them together and returns typed answers with probabilities.

Jev supports three decision primitives:

1. **Choice** selects from known options, such as engineering, billing, or sales.

2. **Score** places the input on an ordered scale, such as low, medium, or high risk.

3. **Noul** evaluates a yes-or-no condition and returns the probability that it is true.

The probabilities matter as much as the selected answers.

If engineering receives 91% probability and billing receives 9%, automatic routing may be reasonable. If the probabilities are 52% and 48%, the system can escalate, gather more context, or call a stronger model.

This keeps control inside ordinary software.

Code owns the thresholds and consequences. Jev supplies the semantic judgment that a normal `if` statement cannot derive from unstructured text.

It works best when the possible answers are known, the decision depends on meaning, and a careful person could judge the input quickly.

It is not designed for writing, summarization, code generation, arithmetic, or decisions requiring several dependent reasoning steps. Independent questions can run in parallel, but decisions that depend on earlier results must remain sequential.

Jev also cannot return an option outside the declared schema, but it can still select the wrong valid option. Type safety prevents malformed outputs, not incorrect judgments.

The clean mental model is this:

LLMs generate new language when the answer space is open.

Jev evaluates known paths when the answer space is bounded.

TypeSafe AIのJevで採用されたRLCD(Reinforcement Learning from Calibration Data)の考え方が面白い。

Javはいわゆる推論モデルではないし、CoTで思考させることもきない。

でも、むしろ推論モデルやCoTだけでは埋めにくかった部分を別の方向で補うことができている。

普通、AIの回答は「正解したか、間違えたか」で評価する。

しかしRLCDが重視するcalibration（較正）は、それだけではない。

「この情報からは、確度の高い結論なんて出せないはずだ」

という問題なら、AIも自信度の低い予測を出すべきだ、という考え方になる。

つまり確率は、回答の「おまけ」ではない。

「Aです」と答えた後に「ちなみに自信度70%です」と付け足すのではなく、

「Aである確率70%」

まで含めて一つの予測。

だから、答えそのものを当てるだけでは十分ではない。

ほとんど判断材料がなく、本来AとBが五分五分に近い問題で、

A：99%
B：1%

と予測して、たまたまAだったとする。

通常の正解率だけを見れば「正解」になる。

しかし同じような状況を大量に観測すると、本当はAが50%程度しか起きないのに、毎回99%と言っているモデルだと分かる。

これは「よく分かっているモデル」ではない。
たまたま当たっただけで、極端に過信している。

逆に、

A：52%
B：48%

という予測は頼りなく見えるかもしれない。

しかし、与えられた情報から本当にほとんど判別できないのであれば、こちらの方が適切な予測になる。

理想的には、

90%と予測したものは長期的に約90%当たり、
70%なら約70%、
50%なら約50%当たる。

これがcalibration。

ここまで考えると、Javの出力は単なる「AIの自信度表示」とはかなり違う。

AIに要求しているのは、

「正解を当てろ」

だけではなく、

「与えられた証拠から、どこまで強い結論を出していいのかも正しく判断しろ」

ということになる。

ここで推論モデルやCoTとの違いが見えてくる。

推論モデルやCoTが主に目指しているのは、

「どう考えれば正しい結論にたどり着けるか」

という方向。

それに対してcalibrationが扱うのは、

「たどり着いた結論を、どこまで信じてよいのか」

という方向。

つまり、

「より正しく考える」

だけではなく、

「自分がどこまで正しく考えられたのかを、正しく見積もる」。

これは別の能力だ。

もちろんcalibrationが良いからといって、内部の論理そのものが正しいとは限らない。間違った理由付けをしていても、最終的な確率だけ統計的によく較正されていることはあり得る。

それでも、

「証拠が弱いなら99%と言うな」
「強い証拠があるなら、それに応じて確率を上げろ」

という圧力がかかる。

つまり「証拠の強さ」と「結論の強さ」を一致させる能力を鍛えることになる。これがRLCD。

確かにこれは推論モデルの代替ではない。
calibrationがシステム1として「その結論をどこまで信じていいか」つきの仮結論を出し、それを根拠にシステム2のLLMに振り分ける、もしくは振り分けないで速攻で進めるかを決められる。そう言う能力を高めているということになる。

このことを理解せずに、単に分類できた、オープンモデルで性能が近づいた、超えたみたいな話をするのはナンセンスで、使い物にならないものを作っているということになる。
